case_title: Almeida v. Ceylon Fisheries Corporation and Others (1998)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the refusal of the Ceylon Fisheries Corporation to grant the petitioner a one-year extension of service after he reached the optional retirement age of 55 amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory treatment in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Marketing Manager of the Ceylon Fisheries Corporation, claimed that he had a long and unblemished service record and a legitimate expectation of receiving an extension of service for one year beyond the optional retirement age of 55. He argued that the Board’s refusal was discriminatory and capricious because he had previously been exonerated in a disciplinary inquiry and had even been promoted to a special grade executive post in 1996 despite the pending magistrate’s court case. He contended that several other employees had been given extensions, and therefore the refusal to extend his service violated Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
respondent_argument: The respondents submitted that the Board of Directors possessed full discretion to grant or refuse extensions of service after an employee reached the optional retirement age. At its 725th meeting on 2 September 1996, the Board had formally decided that extensions would only be granted to employees with a satisfactory record and whose services were indispensable. The petitioner was denied an extension because there was a pending criminal prosecution against him relating to forgery, and because his services were not considered indispensable. The respondents also clarified that some employees cited by the petitioner had received extensions before the policy change, while the rest received extensions only because they met the indispensability requirement.
interpretation_summary: The Court examined the petitioner’s letter of appointment and subsequent promotions, noting that none of the documents guaranteed employment beyond the age of 55. The governing administrative circulars and Board decisions clearly established that extension beyond the optional retirement age was not a right but a matter entirely within the discretion of the appointing authority. The Board had adopted a formal policy (4R1) requiring that extensions be granted only to employees who had a good past record and whose services were indispensable. The Court held that discretionary powers may be exercised so long as they are based on relevant considerations and are not arbitrary or irrational. The Board had considered the petitioner’s application and relied on two legitimate factors: (1) a pending criminal prosecution against him, and (2) the determination that his services were not indispensable. These were valid administrative considerations. The Court further noted that the petitioner failed to prove unequal treatment, as the examples he cited were either employees who obtained extensions before the new policy or employees who met the indispensability requirement. Thus, the refusal to extend the petitioner’s service was neither arbitrary nor discriminatory.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application. It held that the refusal to grant the petitioner an extension of service was based on valid considerations and did not amount to arbitrary or capricious administrative action under Article 12(1). The petitioner was not entitled to relief, and the application was dismissed without costs.
principles_established: Extension of service beyond the optional retirement age is not a right; it is a matter of discretion.
Administrative discretion must be exercised based on relevant considerations but is not unconstitutional merely because it disadvantages a particular applicant.
Refusal to grant discretionary benefits such as service extensions does not violate Article 12(1) unless the decision is arbitrary, irrational, capricious, or discriminatory.
A pending criminal prosecution is a valid consideration when deciding whether to extend an employee’s service.
Comparative claims of discrimination must show that other employees who were similarly situated received favourable treatment; mere difference in outcome is insufficient.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 310/97 (FR), decided on 8 June 1998

case_title: Amerasinghe v. Board of Directors, Co-operative Wholesale Establishment (1998)
judges: G. P. S. De Silva C.J.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether refusing the petitioner’s second extension of service based on adverse committee reports—without giving him any opportunity to respond—was arbitrary, unfair, and violative of Article 12(1).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, who had served the CWE for 26 years and was its General Manager since 1983, applied for a second extension of service after age 55. He said he had an outstanding record and had been invited by the Chairman himself to apply for the extension due to his ‘excellent service.’ His application was rejected on the basis of adverse comments made in two committee reports, even though he had never been informed of any allegations, never summoned, and never given a hearing. He claimed the refusal was arbitrary, unfair, and a violation of his rights under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that extension of service beyond age 55 is not a right but a matter entirely within the discretion of the Board and the Minister. They claimed the Board was entitled to rely on the adverse observations in the Parliamentary Committee Report and the A. L. M. Fernando Committee Report and therefore acted properly in refusing the extension.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that although extension beyond 55 is discretionary, once an employee applies, the authority must consider the application fairly, properly, and on a rational basis. The Board rejected the petitioner’s extension solely due to adverse findings in two committee reports. Yet the petitioner had never been summoned by those committees, never told of any allegations, and never given an opportunity to explain or defend himself. This violated the fundamental rule of natural justice—the audi alteram partem rule (the right to be heard). The Court emphasized that discretion cannot be exercised arbitrarily. The denial of a hearing rendered the decision unfair, irrational, and without a proper foundation. The Court distinguished earlier cases (Somipala and Perera) because those cases had not raised the issue of total denial of a hearing.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the refusal of the extension was unfair, arbitrary, lacked a rational basis, and violated Article 12(1). The Court granted relief and ordered the CWE to pay the petitioner Rs. 80,000 as compensation and Rs. 20,000 as costs.
principles_established: Even when a benefit is discretionary, the applicant is entitled to a fair and proper consideration.
Natural justice (audi alteram partem) applies even when the decision is not disciplinary—it applies whenever adverse findings are used to the detriment of a person.
Discretion must be exercised reasonably, fairly, and based on legitimate grounds.
A decision based on adverse material without giving the affected person a hearing is arbitrary and violates Article 12(1).
Fairness is a core component of equality under Article 12.

case_title: Athukorala v. Jayaratne and Others (1996)

clauses.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s sudden transfer from the Hanwella Divisional Secretariat to Homagama, allegedly due to her political opinion and activities as an elected member of the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha, violated the protection against discrimination under Article 12(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that she was transferred out of her station because she was an elected UNP member of the Seethawaka Pradeshiya Sabha, and that the 1st and 2nd respondents acted on political motives. She argued that the transfer violated section 3.7 of Chapter XXXII of the Establishments Code, which entitled her to work close to the Local Authority she represented. She alleged the transfer was discriminatory and intended to restrict her political participation.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioner’s transfer was required to ensure neutral and impartial administration at the Hanwella Secretariat. They claimed there were complaints alleging she favoured her political supporters and discriminated against others in her official duties. The 2nd respondent maintained that the transfer was necessary to prevent partisan influence and was carried out within delegated transfer powers.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that no credible evidence of misconduct had been produced, and the alleged complaints were vague, undisclosed, and untested. Section 3.7 of the Establishments Code was intended to protect elected officers by allowing them to work near their Local Authority, not to justify transfers away from it. The Court found that the transfer was motivated by the respondents’ views about the petitioner’s political opinion and activities. Acting on undisclosed allegations without inquiry was arbitrary and violated Article 12(2).
outcome: The Court declared that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(2) had been infringed. It cancelled the transfer, ordered her reinstatement to the Hanwella Divisional Secretariat, and directed the 1st and 2nd respondents personally to pay Rs. 25,000 each as compensation and costs.
principles_established: A public officer who is an elected member of a Local Authority is entitled to serve near that Local Authority under section 3.7 of the Establishments Code.
Transfers motivated by political opinion constitute discrimination under Article 12(2).
Vague, undisclosed complaints cannot justify adverse administrative action.
Even non-disciplinary decisions must follow fairness and cannot be based on arbitrary or politically motivated reasoning.
Authorities cannot indirectly penalise an officer for exercising lawful political rights.
precedents_cited: Madurapperuma v. Attorney-General, SC 90/79, S.C. Minutes 05.02.1980
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 645/95, decided on 20 September 1996

case_title: Bandara and Another v. Premachandra, Secretary, Ministry of Lands, Irrigation and Mahaweli Development and Others (1993)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the termination of the petitioners’ probationary appointments and training, based on their participation in trade union action and treated as vacation of post, was arbitrary, discriminatory, contrary to the Establishments Code, and in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, despite the ‘pleasure’ clause in Article 55(1).
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, selected as Class III Grade III Surveyors and placed on probation while following a four-year degree course at the Institute of Surveying and Mapping, claimed that their services and training were unlawfully terminated after they, following their union’s decision, submitted sick notes and joined a work-to-rule campaign. They argued that they were in fact treated as having vacated post without being informed of that basis, and were thereby denied their right under Chapter V, section 7:4 of the Establishments Code to submit explanations. They further claimed that they were singled out and punished more harshly than other surveyors and trainees who engaged in similar trade union action, and that the real reason for the action was their participation in lawful trade union activities, violating Article 12(1) and their freedoms of association and expression.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that, as probationers holding office at pleasure within Article 55(1), the petitioners’ appointments could be terminated ‘without assigning any reason’ under Chapter II, section 11:4 and Chapter V, section 6:2 of the Establishments Code. They argued that the petitioners’ conduct in absenting themselves after tendering sick notes, as part of the union campaign, amounted to serious indiscipline and misconduct justifying immediate termination, and that the safeguards in section 11:2:1 (guidance, warnings, opportunities to improve) did not apply in the face of such grave behaviour. They also sought to distinguish the petitioners from other officers and earlier batches, relying on the petitioners’ status as newly recruited salary-drawing students on a residential course and the practical difficulties and public inconvenience that would arise if similar sanctions were imposed on large numbers of serving officers.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the petitioners’ letters of appointment expressly incorporated the Establishments Code, which gives probationers not only obligations but also procedural protections, including guidance, warnings, and fair evaluation before termination. The misconduct in submitting false sick notes could warrant disciplinary action, but it was of a type that should have been dealt with under the Code, not by an abrupt termination that bypassed its procedures. Examining the internal minutes and correspondence, the Court found that the Secretary’s decision was actually to treat the petitioners as having vacated post, not to dismiss them outright, and that by misinforming them that their services had been terminated, the Surveyor General improperly deprived them of their right under section 7:4 to submit explanations which might have led to reinstatement. On Article 55(1), the Court held that the ‘pleasure principle’ is expressly made subject to the Constitution, including Article 12, and cannot authorise arbitrary or discriminatory dismissal; rules made under Article 55(4) must also conform to the Constitution and the rule of law. The phrase ‘without assigning any reason’ in the Establishments Code was interpreted to mean that no reason need be communicated to the officer, but a valid reason justifying dismissal in terms of the Code must exist and can be examined when fundamental rights are invoked. The Court further held that the real motive for the action was the petitioners’ participation in trade union activity, as revealed by the subsequent insistence on an undertaking to abstain from union activity and public statements that they had been ‘dragged into’ the campaign. Comparing the treatment of the petitioners with earlier trainee batches and with other surveyors and officers who engaged in the same union action but faced no disciplinary sanctions, the Court found no rational basis for the harsher punishment imposed on the petitioners. This differential treatment was unreasonable, arbitrary, and discriminatory, and thus violated Article 12(1).
outcome: The Court held that the petitioners had not been lawfully dismissed by the proper authority, that they were wrongly denied their right to explain a deemed vacation of post, and that they were unlawfully prevented from resuming their studies and work for participating in trade union action. It declared that their fundamental rights under Article 12(1) had been infringed, ordered their reinstatement with effect from 7 December 1992, directed payment of arrears of salary from 21 December 1992, and allowed them to resume their degree course forthwith with seniority preserved over later entrants. The State was ordered to pay each petitioner Rs. 2,000 as compensation; no personal costs order was made against the 2nd respondent because of the petitioners’ own misconduct.
principles_established: Probationary public officers are subject to, and protected by, the Establishments Code; probation cannot be used to bypass procedural safeguards such as guidance, warnings, and the right to explain alleged vacation of post.
The ‘pleasure’ clause in Article 55(1) is subject to the Constitution, including Article 12, so dismissal at pleasure cannot be arbitrary, discriminatory, or inconsistent with equal protection.

Rules made under Article 55(4) and phrases like ‘without assigning any reason’ must be interpreted consistently with the rule of law; a lawful, Code-based reason must exist even if it is not communicated, and may be scrutinised in fundamental rights proceedings.

Where other officers and trainees who participated in similar industrial action are treated more leniently, imposing the severe sanction of dismissal on one group without a rational basis amounts to unreasonable and discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1).
Administrative labelling of a situation (e.g. ‘termination’ instead of ‘vacation of post’) cannot be used to deprive officers of procedural rights expressly provided by the Establishments Code.

Adverse action taken primarily because of participation in trade union activity, rather than because of proven misconduct assessed under proper procedures, is impermissible and attracts constitutional scrutiny.

case_title: Dayarathna and Others v. Minister of Health and Indigenous Medicine and Others (1999)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the State’s change of policy which stopped the advertised Assistant Medical Practitioner (AMP) training programme, and diverted successful candidates to inferior para-medical/PHI courses, unlawfully frustrated their legitimate expectations and amounted to arbitrary and unequal treatment contrary to Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, all of whom possessed the required higher educational qualifications, applied in response to Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 to follow the course of training for the examination leading to the certificate of competency as Assistant Medical Practitioners. They sat the competitive examination on 27.12.1996 and were placed so as to qualify for training, subject only to a routine interview to verify documents (birth certificate, citizenship, educational certificates). No interview was held and no AMP training was commenced. Instead, after the GMOA wrote on 18.12.1997 opposing the restarting of the AMP training and refusing to participate in it, the Minister sought Cabinet approval to fill AMP vacancies with medical graduates and, by circular F1 dated 20.08.1998, invited the petitioners to apply for training as Pharmacists, MLTs or PHIs. The petitioners claimed (1) this substituted offer was clearly inferior in status, training and future prospects (no eligibility to register to practise medicine and surgery under the Medical Ordinance), (2) they had a legitimate expectation, based on the Gazette scheme and past practice, that they would receive AMP training if they met the published criteria, and (3) denying them that training, while earlier similarly placed applicants had received it, was unreasonable, discriminatory and violated Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents, through the Secretary to the Ministry, argued that the original need for AMPs arose when there were insufficient medical graduates to serve in hospitals, but that now around 800 medical officers passed out annually and existing vacancies could only absorb them for about two more years. They said the Government had a responsibility to provide jobs to graduates trained at public expense, and that AMP posts had historically been trained and supervised almost entirely by graduate medical officers and consultants. The GMOA had formally stated that its members would not participate in future AMP training, making it impossible, in the respondents’ view, to conduct a suitable AMP programme. On this basis the Minister submitted a Cabinet Memorandum on 11.03.1998 proposing to fill existing and future AMP vacancies with graduate medical officers, and to give high-scoring AMP candidates the opportunity, if they wished, to follow para-medical or PHI training instead. They maintained that the change of policy, driven by manpower needs, graduate employment and lack of trainers, justified discontinuing the AMP course and that no violation of equality had occurred.
interpretation_summary: The Court first compared the AMP path with that of pharmacists, MLTs and PHIs. Under the Medical Ordinance, AMPs, after prescribed periods of efficient service and further hospital experience, are eligible to seek registration to practise medicine and surgery, whereas pharmacists, MLTs and PHIs can never obtain such registration. The educational entry standards and the content, duration and intensity of AMP training (basic medical sciences, clinical subjects, extensive clinicals and clerkships) were significantly higher than those for the para-medical and PHI courses. On this basis, the Court held that inviting candidates who had already successfully competed for AMP training to instead apply for these other courses amounted to treating unequals as equals and was manifestly unreasonable and unfair. The Court also noted that earlier applicants in the same position (under previous intakes) had been given AMP training according to the same type of advertised scheme, so the departure in the petitioners’ case created discrimination between persons similarly situated without justification. Turning to legitimate expectation, the Court held that the Gazette notice, the structured scheme of competitive exam plus interview, and the consistent past practice created more than a mere hope: the petitioners had a legitimate expectation that, upon satisfying the stated conditions, they would be provided with the AMP training scheme advertised. The executive is free to change policy, but that freedom is not absolute. A change of policy that frustrates such an expectation must be (a) procedurally fair, giving affected persons an opportunity to be heard, and (b) substantively justified by overriding public interest, with means proportionate to the aim. Here, the only real driver of the policy shift was the GMOA’s refusal to cooperate and its demand that AMP training not restart, coupled with a preference to use the vacancies for medical graduates. The views of AMPs or of the petitioners were never sought; there was no structured weighing of their interests against a clearly articulated public interest. No Gazette or circular formally announced a change of policy; instead, the process simply stalled and was then redirected through F1. The Court rejected the idea that such union pressure and administrative convenience amounted to overriding public interest. It held that both the failure to give the petitioners a say and the decision to sacrifice their legitimate expectations solely to accommodate one professional group’s preferences were inconsistent with the equality guarantee and the rule-of-law values underlying Article 12.
outcome: The Court declared that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Article 12(1) had been violated by the second respondent and held that the petitioners’ legitimate expectations regarding the AMP training scheme survived the purported policy change. Document F1 of 20.08.1998 was declared to be of no force or effect in law as against the petitioners. The Court ordered the first, second and third respondents to (a) hold the interview contemplated in Gazette No. 923 of 10.05.1996 within eight weeks of the judgment, and (b) provide the advertised AMP training scheme commencing within a reasonable time not exceeding six months from the date of the order. The State was directed to pay each petitioner Rs. 5,000 as costs.
principles_established: Legitimate expectation: Where the State, by Gazette, established procedures and benefits and has consistently acted in accordance with them, applicants who meet the criteria can acquire a legitimate expectation of the promised training or benefit, not merely a hope.

Policy change and fairness: While Government may change policy, it must consider and, where appropriate, protect legitimate expectations. When a change of policy will adversely affect specific individuals, they must be given an opportunity to be heard on why the new policy should not operate unfairly against them.

Article 12 and procedural fairness: Procedural rights (like the right to be heard before a detrimental policy change is applied) are closely tied to Article 12’s guarantee of equality, helping ensure objectivity, impartiality and similar treatment of like cases.

Overriding public interest requirement: A change of policy that frustrates legitimate expectations may only be justified where an overriding public interest is demonstrated, and even then the means chosen must be proportionate. Mere pressure from a professional group or administrative convenience is insufficient.

Substantive equality: Article 12 requires substantive as well as formal equality. Treating individuals who have qualified for a higher professional track as if they were candidates for lower-tier para-medical courses amounts to treating unequals as equals and can be unconstitutional.

Consistent treatment of similarly situated persons: When earlier candidates with similar qualifications were given AMP training under a comparable scheme, later candidates cannot be arbitrarily denied the same path without an objectively reasonable and proportionate justification.

case_title: Dharmaratne and Another v. Sri Lanka Export Development Board and Others (1995)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the promotion of certain Assistant Directors to the post of Deputy Director Grade 2 by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, based on an interview and internally-set criteria, was arbitrary and irrational so as to amount to unequal treatment and a violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, both Assistant Directors of the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, applied for promotion to Deputy Director Grade 2 after vacancies were advertised in March 1993. An interview board (2nd–6th respondents) interviewed internal and external candidates. The 7th–12th respondents (internal) and 13th respondent (external) were appointed; the petitioners were not. The petitioners did not contest the external appointment (13th respondent), but alleged that the promotions of the 7th–12th respondents were arbitrary and discriminatory. They argued that (1) there was no proper scheme of recruitment or promotion in force, and the older scheme (P1) with performance evaluation was ignored; (2) the criteria used by the interview board were ad hoc, vague and subjective; (3) insufficient weight was given to seniority, as only one mark per year in Grade 3 was awarded, instead of seniority getting about one-third of the total marks; (4) there was no proper mechanism or appraisal system in place to assess experience, performance and managerial ability; and (5) too much weight was given to interview performance and communication skills, which they said were inherently subjective. They also alleged political pressure and claimed they had been treated unequally compared to the selected officers.
respondent_argument: The 7th–12th respondents (promoted internal candidates) and the 2nd respondent (Chairman of the Board, and head of the interview panel) contended that the earlier 1985 promotion scheme and the 1984 evaluation process relied on by the petitioners had been abandoned as unsatisfactory, and that the applicable framework was based on Public Administration Circular No. 15/90 and the Board’s later documents (2R2–2R3). The posts of Deputy Director were senior managerial positions requiring strong management, coordination and staff-supervision abilities, not merely seniority. The interview board therefore adopted a set of criteria: (1) seniority (one mark per year in Grade 3), (2) additional job-oriented qualifications (diplomas, MSc/MBA, PhD), (3) experience in relevant areas (export development, marketing, project appraisal, planning etc.), (4) performance (ability to identify, analyse and solve problems with practical solutions), (5) communication skills (clarity, correct language, coherent presentation) and (6) managerial ability (assessed partly by consulting the directors/head of each candidate’s division). They produced a mark sheet (2R5) showing each candidate’s scores under these heads, according to which the 7th–12th respondents scored higher overall than the petitioners (who scored 34 and 33). They argued that the process was structured, multi-factorial, reasonably objective in most criteria, and that there was no political interference. They claimed the difference in outcome was due to relative merit and suitability, not discrimination.
interpretation_summary: The Court first examined the structure and composition of the interview board and the nature of the criteria used. The board included the Chairman and senior directors of the EDB who were familiar with the organisation and the Assistant Directors from whom the internal candidates came. The board had in advance detailed schedules of each candidate’s data and each member made notes on these during the interviews. Looking criterion by criterion (as per the mark sheet 2R5), the Court held that seniority and additional qualifications were fully objective, being derived directly from service records and certificates. Experience, assessed by looking at actual work done in export development, marketing, project appraisal, entrepreneur development, planning and trade information, was also capable of objective assessment. Performance was evaluated on concrete aspects: problem identification, understanding of subject matter, analysis, use of current data and statistics, and ability to propose practical solutions. Communication skills were judged by clarity of speech, correct language use, and the coherent presentation of ideas. The Court found these criteria to be clear, relevant and not capricious. The only area with greater subjectivity was managerial ability, but for this the board had filled the gap created by the abandonment of the earlier evaluation scheme by consulting the directors of the divisions where candidates worked. The Court accepted this evidence and viewed it as a responsible way to assess day-to-day managerial capability. On this basis, the Court concluded that while the system was not perfect, the overall process was responsible and not arbitrary. On the complaint about lack of a formal promotion scheme and prior disclosure of criteria, the Court (per Fernando J.) observed that, although it is desirable that criteria and weightage be laid down and disclosed beforehand, failure to do so is not automatically fatal, and in the absence of an established scheme the interview board could legitimately formulate relevant criteria and weightage. The chosen criteria—seniority, additional relevant qualifications, experience, performance, communication skills and managerial ability—were all relevant and comprehensive; no crucial factor had been excluded. The contention that too little weight was given to seniority and too much to interview performance was rejected: weightage is a matter for the interview board’s discretion, especially for senior posts where merit, ability and performance rightly carry heavier emphasis. Further, the Court pointed out that seniority was indirectly reflected again through the experience criterion. On the argument that, without an annual performance appraisal system, performance and managerial ability could not be properly assessed, the Court held that while such a system is highly desirable and may in future become effectively mandatory in practice, it is not presently a legal requirement. In its absence, the board had to make the best possible assessment and could not be faulted simply for operating without a formal appraisal system. The Court found no evidence of mala fides, political interference, abuse of discretion or irrationality in the board’s decisions.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners had not established that the promotion decisions were arbitrary, capricious or irrational. There was no violation of their fundamental right to equality and equal protection under Article 12(1). The application was dismissed, and the appointments/promotions of the 7th–12th respondents stood undisturbed.
principles_established: Promotion and equality: For a violation of Article 12(1) in promotion cases, it is not enough to show dissatisfaction with the outcome; the decision-making process must be shown to be arbitrary, irrational, capricious or tainted by mala fides or irrelevant considerations.

Criteria and subjectivity: Selection for senior posts may legitimately include subjective elements (e.g., performance, communication skills, managerial ability) as long as the criteria are relevant, clearly defined, and applied in good faith without arbitrariness.

Weightage discretion: The allocation of weight between seniority and merit-related factors is primarily a matter for the decision-maker’s discretion. For posts with greater responsibilities, stronger emphasis on merit, performance and ability is justified, and giving seniority a modest direct weight is not inherently unreasonable, especially where it is also reflected indirectly through experience.

Absence of formal appraisal scheme: Although an annual performance appraisal system is very desirable and may become standard in industrial relations practice, its absence does not automatically invalidate a promotion decision if performance, experience and managerial ability are otherwise reasonably assessed.

Prior disclosure of criteria: It is desirable but not mandatory that criteria and weightage be disclosed to candidates in advance; failure to do so will only be fatal where it leads to unfairness, irrationality or discrimination on the facts of the case.

Judicial deference in promotion decisions: Courts will not re-mark candidates or substitute their own view of appropriate weightage and scores for that of a competent interview board in the absence of evidence of bad faith, abuse of power or manifest unreasonableness.

case_title: Gunaratne and Others v. Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and Others (1996)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation’s Board resolution summarily terminating the petitioners’ dealership agreement and cancelling their statutory authority under section 5E of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation Act, and appointing a new dealer, constituted executive/administrative action which violated the petitioners’ right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution; and whether fundamental rights review can apply only at the ‘threshold stage’ of a contract or also during its subsistence.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, four partners operating the Kottawa Lanka Filling Station, held a dealership agreement with the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) signed by them on 23.03.1994 and by CPC on 26.10.1994, together with statutory authority under section 5E of the CPC Act to sell, supply and distribute Lanka Two Star petrol, diesel and lubricants. Prior to this, the 1st petitioner individually had held a similar dealership for many years at the same station. By letter dated 04.01.1996, signed by the CPC Marketing Manager (9th respondent), CPC summarily terminated the dealership agreement and cancelled the authority, and on the same day took over possession and handed the station to the 11th respondent as the new dealer, pursuant to a Board resolution. The letter referred to five earlier warning letters (1981, 1984, 1986, 1988 and 1995) and cited clause 12B of the agreement and section 5H(4) of the Act. The petitioners argued that: (a) the termination was arbitrary, based mainly on old incidents long predating the partnership agreement and involving only the 1st petitioner; (b) the 2nd–4th petitioners were being penalised for events which occurred before they became partners; (c) the most recent incident in 1995 (a defective pump and trainee pumper error) had already been investigated, the pumper dismissed, and the matter finally disposed of by a warning; (d) there were no valid fresh grounds to reopen it or to justify termination; (e) the CPC Marketing Manual prescribed a procedure for selecting new dealers (multiple applications, area-level evaluation, full Board paper comparing candidates) which had not been followed in appointing the 11th respondent; and (f) the Board had acted without giving the petitioners any hearing or notice, and without properly informing itself of the true factual position, thereby acting arbitrarily and in violation of Article 12(1). They sought relief for infringement of their fundamental rights arising from the termination and cancellation.
respondent_argument: On behalf of CPC (1st respondent) and its Chairman and Directors (2nd–8th respondents), it was contended that: (1) the Board’s decision to terminate the dealership and cancel the authority was a commercial decision in the exercise of contractual rights under a concluded contract and therefore did not constitute ‘executive or administrative action’ within Article 126; at most, only the initial award of the dealership could be subject to fundamental rights review at the ‘threshold stage’; (2) clause 12B of the dealership agreement and section 5H(4) of the CPC Act conferred extremely wide powers on the Board, including termination without notice and without assigning reasons, in the Board’s absolute discretion; (3) the termination was justified by the dealer’s past conduct, including the five warning letters cited (from 1981, 1984, 1986, 1988 and 1995) and other alleged instances of misconduct/inefficiency both before and after the 1994 agreement, such as pumps delivering short and dishonoured cheques; (4) the partnership was between the original dealer (1st petitioner) and his family members and they could not escape the consequences of his earlier conduct; and (5) the Board resolution lawfully combined termination of the existing dealership and appointment of the 11th respondent. The 11th respondent, for his part, argued that he had applied for a dealership in or about August 1995, been interviewed, and that CPC officials had investigated his suitability. He further submitted that the petitioners had neither pleaded that his appointment was wrongful nor sought any specific relief against his dealership as required by Rule 44(1)(d) of the Supreme Court Rules, and therefore no order should be made affecting his appointment.
interpretation_summary: The Court first examined whether the impugned Board resolution was ‘executive or administrative action’ reviewable under Article 126. It held that the supply and distribution of petroleum products by CPC is a governmental function, performed as agent of the State under statute (sections 5B, 5E, 5F of the CPC Act), and that the grant and cancellation of dealership authority is a statutory power, not a purely private commercial matter. The dealership agreement is intimately linked with the statutory authority under section 5E (and referable to section 5F), so decisions to enter into, continue or terminate such dealerships constitute executive/administrative action. Rejecting the ‘threshold stage’ argument, the Court held that Article 12’s equality guarantee applies not only when a contract is initially awarded but throughout its subsistence: the State cannot indirectly do, by termination, what it cannot directly do at the award stage (e.g. discriminate on political, racial or religious grounds). The principle of equality in Article 12 is rooted in the Rule of Law and prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory action; there is no carve-out for post-contract acts or for particular types of contracts. The Court distinguished Roberts v. Ratnayake, noting that the present case involves powers exercised under statute, and adopted a broader view that Article 12 applies to arbitrary actions generally, not only where particular statutory protections are engaged. Having found that the Board’s resolution was executive/administrative action, the Court then considered whether it was arbitrary or discriminatory. Although clause 12B and section 5H(4) appear to confer powers to terminate without notice and ‘without assigning any reasons’ and to cancel authority in ‘absolute discretion’, these powers are held in trust for the public and must be exercised reasonably and for proper purposes. Even if reasons need not be stated at the time of termination, when the decision is challenged the burden lies on CPC to justify it with sufficient cause. The Court scrutinised the grounds invoked. It held that neither clause 12B nor section 5H(4) permitted reliance on conduct occurring before the grant of the current dealership/authority (save perhaps for unknown facts later discovered); otherwise, 2nd–4th petitioners would be punished for events when they had no control or responsibility. Therefore, the four older warning letters (1981, 1984, 1986, 1988) could not be used to justify termination of the 1994 partnership dealership. As to post-1994 conduct: (a) incidents where pumps delivered less were primarily attributable to CPC, as the pumps were CPC’s property, CPC was responsible for proper calibration, and dealers were not supposed to tamper with them. Some inspection reports even showed over-delivery. It would have been unreasonable to terminate on this basis, and in any event the Board paper did not rely on these incidents, so they could not retrospectively justify the decision; (b) dishonoured cheques issued in late December 1995 / early January 1996 could not serve as a ground either. The timing suggested that some cheques may have been presented after the forced takeover on 04.01.1996; CPC had promised to pay for stocks taken over (worth about Rs 577,587) but had not done so, and had taken no legal action regarding the cheques. There was no evidence that this issue influenced the Board’s decision; (c) the only incident clearly relied on was that behind the fifth warning letter dated 29.06.1995, where a pump sometimes failed to return to zero and a trainee pumper attempted to dispense fuel improperly. The defect had been promptly reported to CPC; the pumper was dismissed; and CPC had expressly decided not to take disciplinary action but only to warn, stating that future irregularities would be reported to the Board. The Court held that, given CPC’s responsibility for maintaining its own pumps, this single incident, already dealt with, was insufficient to justify termination. The Board had not been informed that four of the five warnings predated the current partnership and the involvement of 2nd–4th petitioners, and that the remaining incident had been concluded. The Directors had not sworn that they would have terminated solely on that single incident or without any reason. On this basis, the Court concluded that the Board’s decision to summarily terminate the agreement and cancel the authority lacked a rational foundation and was arbitrary. Regarding the structure of the Board resolution, the Court treated it as containing two limbs: (1) termination of the existing dealership and cancellation of the authority; (2) appointment of the 11th respondent as the new dealer with fresh authority. While the two limbs were distinct and severable, the first limb itself (agreement + authority) was not severable because the two were inextricably linked. The first limb was therefore invalid in its entirety for violating Article 12(1). As to the second limb, the Court noted that the marketing manual procedure for selecting new dealers had not been followed and that there was no clear evidence as to how the 11th respondent was chosen. However, since the petitioners had not pleaded that the 11th respondent’s appointment was unlawful nor prayed for any specific relief against his dealership, and because he had not been put clearly on notice that his appointment was in jeopardy, the Court held it would not be just and equitable to disturb his dealership in these proceedings. Instead, it confined relief to the unlawful termination and cancellation affecting the petitioners and compensated them for the resulting loss.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the Board’s resolution terminating the petitioners’ dealership agreement and cancelling their statutory authority constituted executive/administrative action and that, in doing so arbitrarily and without proper grounds, the 1st–8th respondents had violated the petitioners’ fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1). The termination and cancellation (the first limb of the resolution) were declared invalid as against the petitioners. However, the Court declined to make any order affecting the appointment of the 11th respondent as the new dealer, due to the absence of proper pleadings and prayer. The Court awarded the petitioners (collectively) Rs. 75,000 as compensation and costs for the infringement and, recognising that a lawful three-month termination with notice would have yielded further profits, directed the 1st respondent, at its option, either (a) to grant the petitioners, within six months, a dealership in respect of the same filling station or another mutually acceptable station, or (b) to pay them an additional Rs. 500,000 as compensation for lost profits.
principles_established: Executive/administrative character of statutory contracts: Where a public corporation exercises statutory powers to grant and cancel authorities (e.g. exclusive statutory rights to sell and distribute petroleum) and enters into closely linked contracts (dealership agreements) for that purpose, its decisions to grant, continue or terminate such arrangements constitute ‘executive or administrative action’ subject to fundamental rights review, and are not purely private commercial decisions.

No ‘threshold only’ limitation: Fundamental rights constraints under Article 12 apply not only at the initial or ‘threshold’ stage of awarding a contract, licence or dealership, but also throughout its subsistence. The State cannot evade equality obligations by using termination or cancellation after award to achieve discriminatory or arbitrary outcomes it could not justify at the award stage.

Article 12 and the Rule of Law: Article 12 embodies a broad principle of equality before the law as part of the Rule of Law underpinning the Constitution. It prohibits arbitrary, capricious or discriminatory action even where a power is framed in terms of ‘absolute discretion’ or ‘without assigning any reasons’, especially where that power is exercised under statute.

Limits on wide termination powers: Contractual clauses and statutory provisions which allow termination ‘without notice’ or ‘without assigning any reasons’ and cancellation of authority in ‘absolute discretion’ cannot be read as conferring unfettered, arbitrary power. Even if reasons need not be stated initially, valid reasons must exist and can be scrutinised by the Court; reliance on stale, irrelevant, or previously concluded matters, or on facts predating the current contractual relationship, is impermissible where it unfairly prejudices new parties.

Temporal relevance of misconduct: In assessing whether misconduct justifies termination of a later partnership or contract, acts occurring prior to the grant of the current agreement/authority cannot generally be used against parties who were not then responsible or in control, except possibly where such facts were unknown at the time of grant and later discovered.

Duty to maintain fairness in commercial-type public dealings: Even where the State or a public corporation is engaged in commercial activities (e.g. running filling stations), its decisions, particularly those grounded in statutory monopolies and public functions, must meet standards of fairness and rationality; powers are held in trust for the public and cannot be exercised for improper or arbitrary reasons.

Severability in relief: Where a single resolution combines both an unlawful termination/cancellation and a distinct appointment of a new party, the unlawful limb can be invalidated while leaving the appointment intact, especially where the latter has not been specifically challenged in pleadings and disturbing it would be unjust to the newly appointed party.

Remedial flexibility: In fundamental rights jurisdiction, the Court may craft just and equitable remedies that are not limited to simple declarations, including monetary compensation reflecting lost profits and structural orders such as directing the grant of a new dealership or, in the alternative, lump-sum compensation.

case_title: Gunaratne and Others v. Sri Lanka Telecom and Others (1992)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the new schemes of recruitment and promotion introduced by Sri Lanka Telecom, which granted preferential treatment to graduate clerks, violated the right to equality before the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, all non-graduate clerks employed by Sri Lanka Telecom, claimed that the newly adopted schemes of recruitment and promotion unfairly discriminated against them by granting preferential treatment to graduate clerks, regardless of whether their degrees were relevant to the duties of the higher posts. They argued that such classification was arbitrary, unreasonable, and violated their right to equality under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the new schemes were formulated to enhance efficiency in the corporation and to address the grievances of under-employed graduates in public service. They argued that educational qualifications were a legitimate criterion for promotion and that the changes were necessary for the corporation’s evolving needs.
interpretation_summary: The Supreme Court held that while public corporations have the discretion to revise schemes of recruitment to meet service needs, such revisions must not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality. The preferential treatment accorded to graduate clerks in the new schemes was not based on an intelligible differentia that bore a rational connection to the objective of ensuring efficient service. The Court found the classification unreasonable because it gave advantage to graduate clerks (including those with irrelevant external degrees) while disregarding the legitimate expectations of experienced non-graduate clerks. The schemes were also found to prioritize social objectives—addressing underemployment among graduates—over the functional efficiency of the telecommunications service, which was an improper basis for internal promotion criteria.
outcome: The Court declared the preferential treatment given to graduate clerks under the new recruitment schemes (P11A and P11B) void for violating Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered Sri Lanka Telecom to bear costs of Rs. 5,500 and allowed for the possibility of new, constitutionally compliant schemes to be introduced in the future.
principles_established: A recruitment or promotion scheme must be founded on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the objective of the service.
Preferential treatment in employment cannot be justified by social or political considerations unrelated to the efficient functioning of the institution.
An inherently discriminatory scheme may be challenged immediately upon its adoption, without waiting for discriminatory implementation.
Educational qualifications must be relevant to the duties of the post to justify preferential treatment under Article 12(1).
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 70/92, decided on 24 August 1992

case_title: Jayanetti v. The Land Reform Commission and Others (1984)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the Land Reform Commission’s decision to alienate land to an ineligible applicant while rejecting the petitioner’s application constituted unequal treatment and a violation of the fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the Land Reform Commission unfairly rejected his application to purchase 50 acres of Mount Pearl Estate while approving the same land for Mrs. Dassanayake, a public corporation employee who was legally disqualified under section 23 of the Land Reform Law. He claimed this amounted to discriminatory and arbitrary administrative action in violation of Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the Minister and the Land Reform Commission acted lawfully within the framework of the Land Reform Law, that the petitioner’s application lacked merit, and that any procedural irregularities did not amount to a violation of fundamental rights. They further argued that the petition was out of time and that additional parties could not be added beyond the statutory limit under Rule 65(1)(b) of the Supreme Court Rules.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the Land Reform Commission was an instrumentality of the State and that its acts constituted ‘executive or administrative action’ under Article 126. The failure to follow mandatory legal requirements—including Gazette publication under section 26, adherence to eligibility criteria under section 23, and fair consideration of the petitioner’s application—amounted to unequal treatment. The Court ruled that the preferential alienation of land to a disqualified person (a State Corporation employee) while rejecting the petitioner’s valid application violated Article 12(1). The Court also clarified that the two-month time limit for fundamental rights applications is directory, not mandatory, and that necessary parties may be added to ensure a fair hearing. Further, it affirmed that ‘law’ in Article 12(1) includes both legislative and administrative action, and that Article 126 provides the sole and expeditious remedy for fundamental rights violations.
outcome: The Court declared that the alienation of the land to Mrs. Dassanayake was null and void for violating the petitioner’s right to equality under Article 12(1). It held that the transfer deed and related proceedings were invalid and directed the Land Reform Commission to take appropriate lawful action regarding the land. No costs were awarded.
principles_established: The Land Reform Commission is an agency or instrumentality of the State, and its actions constitute executive or administrative action under Article 126.
Article 12(1) protects against unequal treatment arising from both legislative and administrative acts.
Procedural rules are subordinate to constitutional guarantees; justice requires flexibility in adding parties and managing timelines.
The statutory requirement for Gazette publication of alienations is mandatory to ensure fairness and equality.
Preferential or politically influenced treatment in administrative decisions violates the principle of equality before the law.

case_title: Jayasinghe v. The Attorney General and Others (1994)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the prolonged and unexplained delay of about 16 years in commencing and concluding disciplinary proceedings against an interdicted co-operative society employee, who was kept without salary, amounted to a denial of the equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether such disciplinary action of a co-operative society is "executive or administrative action" within the meaning of Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a storekeeper of the 2nd respondent co-operative society, was interdicted without pay on 14.10.1977 over alleged shortages in several stores, but no charge sheet was served on him for more than 14 years, until 1.1.1992, and the disciplinary inquiry was completed only in 1994, after he had come before the Supreme Court. He claimed that this inordinate and unexplained delay, while he remained interdicted without salary and could not take other employment, deprived him of the legal safeguards given by the Co-operative Employees' Commission Act and Regulations and thus denied him the equal protection of the law guaranteed by Article 12(1). He also alleged political victimisation, but that aspect was ultimately not pursued under Article 12(2).
respondent_argument: The 2nd respondent raised a preliminary objection that the application was out of time under Article 126(2). It was also contended that the delays were linked to criminal proceedings and arbitration, and that the disciplinary process of the co-operative society did not amount to "executive or administrative" action within Article 126. The respondents further argued, relying on earlier case law, that the petitioner had not proved unequal treatment because he had not produced evidence of other employees in similar situations who had been treated differently, and therefore the requirement of showing denial of equal protection had not been satisfied.
interpretation_summary:
The Court first rejected the preliminary objection on time bar, holding that it was not clear when prolonged delay turns into a denial of equal protection and that the infringement could be treated as continuing, or at least as imminent when the petitioner came to Court. The allegation of political victimisation under Article 12(2) was not examined because Articles 12(2) and 126 do not apply retrospectively to acts done before the 1978 Constitution. The Court then held that, although many functions of a co-operative society are contractual or commercial, its disciplinary powers over employees are controlled by statute, regulations and the Co-operative Employees' Commission, and are therefore in the nature of "administrative action" within Article 126.

On the scope of Article 12(1), the Court stated that equal protection of the law is not confined only to liberty in criminal matters; it also extends to the protection of livelihood. The Co-operative Employees' Commission Act and its General Regulations give employees legal safeguards such as being served with charges, a fair inquiry with a proper procedure, and a right of appeal. These legal safeguards are part of the "protection of the law" in relation to livelihood. The Court emphasised that justice delayed is justice denied, and similarly, protection delayed is protection denied. A delay of 14 years to serve a charge sheet and 16 years to complete the disciplinary inquiry was far beyond anything that could be considered reasonable, especially where the employee was interdicted without pay and could not easily take other employment. This amounted to a denial of one of the key protections that the law gave him: that disciplinary proceedings which could deprive him of his livelihood should be completed without inordinate delay.

On equal protection, the Court held that, although normally a petitioner must show that he was treated less favourably than others similarly situated, this is not an inflexible rule. In extreme situations the Court can take judicial notice of what ordinarily happens. It is not normal for a charge sheet to be delayed for more than 10 years or for a disciplinary inquiry to last over 15 years, and previous cases showed that even in delayed matters charge sheets were issued within months or a few years. On that basis, the Court concluded that the petitioner had been denied equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). Liability for shortages and the ultimate validity of his dismissal were left to be decided in the separate criminal, arbitral and writ proceedings.
outcome: The Supreme Court declared that the petitioner's fundamental right to the equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) had been infringed by the 2nd respondent co-operative society due to the inordinate and unexplained delay in the disciplinary proceedings while he was interdicted without pay. The Court awarded the petitioner Rs. 100,000 as compensation and Rs. 5,000 as costs, payable by the 2nd respondent. It expressly stated that questions regarding the petitioner's liability for shortages and the justification of his dismissal were to be determined in other pending proceedings and would not affect the relief granted in this fundamental rights application.
principles_established: Disciplinary action by a co-operative society against its employees, including interdiction, framing of charges, holding of inquiries and dismissal, is "administrative action" within the meaning of Article 126 when it is governed by statute, regulations and the Co-operative Employees' Commission.

The guarantee of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) is not confined to the protection of personal liberty; it also extends to the protection of livelihood where the law provides safeguards for employment and disciplinary procedures.

Prolonged and unexplained delay in commencing and concluding disciplinary proceedings against an interdicted employee, especially when interdiction is without pay, can amount to a denial of the protection of the law and thus a violation of Article 12(1). Protection delayed can be protection denied.

In assessing whether there is denial of equal protection, it is not always necessary to produce evidence of specific comparable cases; in extreme and obvious situations, courts may rely on judicial notice of what ordinarily happens in similar disciplinary processes.

Regulatory schemes and statutory safeguards, such as those in the Co-operative Employees' Commission Act and Regulations, imply that disciplinary inquiries should be completed within a reasonable time measured in months rather than years, and failure to do so is inconsistent with those safeguards.
Fundamental rights remedies under Article 126 can be granted independently of the final outcome of related criminal, arbitral or civil proceedings on the same underlying facts.

case_title: Lanka Jathika Sarvodaya Shramadana Sangamaya v. Heengama, Director General of Customs and Others (1993)
judges: G. P. S. De Silva C.J.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the refusal by the Director General of Customs to mitigate the forfeiture of a printing press and accessories under section 163 of the Customs Ordinance, in circumstances where mitigation had been granted to other importers in comparable undervaluation cases, amounted to discriminatory treatment and a violation of the petitioner’s right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a non-governmental organisation, imported a Harris Web V15A printing press and accessories for its printing business. Customs alleged undervaluation, valued the goods at Rs. 18 million (instead of the declared Rs. 11,091,929) and treated them as forfeited under section 52 of the Customs Ordinance. The petitioner applied to the Director General of Customs under section 163 to mitigate the forfeiture and release the machine on payment of duty based on the uplifted value, without prejudice to its right to contest that value in court. This request was refused. The petitioner claimed that, in practice, in cases of undervaluation Customs usually mitigates forfeiture and releases goods on payment of additional duty (and sometimes a penalty), and that in at least 15 comparable cases mitigation had in fact been granted. The refusal in its case was therefore arbitrary and discriminatory, and violated its right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that Customs had correctly valued the machine at Rs. 18 million, relying particularly on expert evidence from the Government Printer and the SGS inspection report, and that the declared value of Rs. 11 million amounted to gross undervaluation. The goods were therefore automatically forfeited by operation of law under section 52, and had been seized as required by section 125. They argued that the Director General’s power to mitigate under section 163 did not apply after seizure, and that only the Minister could restore seized goods under section 164. They further maintained that even if section 163 applied, the Director General had reasonably exercised his discretion by refusing mitigation because the amount of undervaluation and resulting loss of revenue were very high. They denied the existence of any general practice of always mitigating forfeiture in undervaluation cases, and argued that the other importers cited by the petitioner were not similarly circumstanced, so there was no unequal treatment under Article 12(1). They also argued that Article 12(1) guarantees equal protection of the law, not a right to equal violation of the law.
interpretation_summary:
The Court first analysed the customs law framework. It held that, under section 52 as amended, when goods are undervalued in the sense that the declared value is not in accordance with Schedule E (normal open market price, including CIF), the goods become forfeited automatically by operation of law. Section 125 then requires seizure of goods declared to be forfeited. Ordinarily, the owner’s remedy would be to challenge the seizure and forfeiture through proceedings under section 154 of the Ordinance. However, Article 126 of the Constitution now provides an additional remedy in appropriate cases involving fundamental rights.

On the facts, the Court accepted the customs valuation of Rs. 18 million. It relied on the expertise and experience of the Government Printer, the SGS report and surrounding circumstances, and found that the declared value of Rs. 11 million did not reflect the normal price under Schedule E. The sale price to the petitioner had special features (the seller’s desire to move second-hand equipment rather than obtain full market value) and was not a simple open-market transaction where price was the sole consideration. Therefore Customs was justified in rejecting the declared price and treating the goods as undervalued. The forfeiture under section 52 was thus valid and the goods were lawfully forfeited by operation of law. The Court also treated the Director General’s letter refusing to vary the forfeiture as sufficient indication of an intention to permanently deprive the petitioner of the goods, and thus as completing a seizure within the meaning of section 125.

The key issue, however, was the refusal to mitigate the forfeiture. The Court rejected the argument that section 163 did not apply once the goods were seized. The petitioner’s application for mitigation was made before seizure, so it was a valid request under section 163. The Court also rejected the attempt to characterise section 163 as inapplicable to undervalued goods in general, holding that undervalued goods forfeited under section 52 are within the scope of section 163. It therefore presumed that the Director General had validly exercised mitigation powers in other cases cited by the petitioner, where similar undervaluation had occurred and goods had been released upon payment of duty and, where appropriate, a penalty.

The Court then examined the equal protection claim. It accepted that mitigation of forfeiture is a discretionary power to be exercised case by case, but held that discretion must be exercised reasonably, fairly and without discrimination. The mere amount of the undervaluation, viewed in isolation, is not a rational and sufficient basis for refusing mitigation, particularly because the absolute amount will naturally vary depending on the nature and value of the goods. The Court noted that in numerous other undervaluation cases, including instances of significant undervaluation, mitigation had been granted and goods released. In the petitioner’s case, despite the absence of any allegation of fraud and the fact that the goods were a printing press to be used by a social service organisation, the Director General refused mitigation solely on the ground of the amount of undervaluation and the resulting revenue loss.

The Court found that this refusal showed an arbitrary exercise of discretion and a failure to fairly consider the petitioner’s application in light of relevant circumstances. This constituted discrimination in comparison with other similarly situated importers, and thus a denial of the petitioner’s right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). While the Court did not find enough evidence to prove bad faith or collateral political motives, it held that the discriminatory refusal to mitigate was sufficient to vitiate the seizure.

Accordingly, the Court drew a distinction between the validity of the forfeiture (which it upheld) and the legality of the seizure as implemented through the discriminatory refusal to mitigate. It held that although the goods were forfeited by operation of law, the seizure and continued detention were invalid because of discrimination in the exercise of the power under section 163. On that basis, the petitioner was entitled to relief under Article 12(1), including release of the machine on payment of duty on the uplifted value and compensation for the period during which it had paid duty but could not clear the goods.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the printing press and accessories had been lawfully forfeited by operation of law under section 52 of the Customs Ordinance due to undervaluation, and that the customs valuation of Rs. 18 million was justified. However, it found that the Director General of Customs had acted unreasonably and discriminatorily in refusing to mitigate the forfeiture under section 163 when compared with other undervaluation cases in which mitigation had been granted. This discriminatory refusal amounted to a violation of the petitioner’s right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). The Court therefore declared that the petitioner’s Article 12(1) rights had been infringed and ordered the Director General to release the machine and its accessories to the petitioner on payment of duty calculated on the value of Rs. 18 million, without any reservation about later challenging that value. It also awarded compensation of Rs. 662,664.24, representing legal interest for 21 months on the duty already paid on the Bill of Entry of 05.04.1991 during which period the goods were not released, and costs of Rs. 5,500, in favour of the petitioner.
principles_established: Goods declared to be forfeited under provisions such as section 52 of the Customs Ordinance become forfeited automatically by operation of law when the statutory conditions are met, and seizure under section 125 then completes the transfer of effective control to the State.

The value of goods for customs purposes is the normal open market price as defined in Schedule E, which may differ from the actual sale price if that price does not reflect an arm’s-length transaction where price is the sole consideration.

Article 126 of the Constitution provides an additional remedy for owners of seized and forfeited goods in appropriate cases involving fundamental rights, and does not displace the statutory remedy of proceedings under section 154 of the Customs Ordinance.

The Director General of Customs’ power to mitigate forfeiture under section 163 is an exercise of executive or administrative discretion and is therefore subject to constitutional standards of reasonableness, fairness and non-discrimination under Article 12(1).

Discretion in granting or refusing mitigation of forfeiture must be exercised consistently; selective or arbitrary refusal in cases that are materially similar to other cases where mitigation was granted can amount to discrimination and a denial of equal protection of the law.

The sheer amount of undervaluation, taken alone, is not a sufficient or rational basis for refusing mitigation, particularly when other relevant factors such as the nature of the goods, absence of fraud, and the established customs practice point in favour of mitigation.

Where forfeiture itself is valid by operation of law but the subsequent exercise of discretionary powers (such as mitigation) is discriminatory, the seizure and continued detention of goods can be vitiated and relief granted under Article 12(1) without setting aside the statutory forfeiture framework.
