case_title: Brigadier Liyanage v. Chandrananda de Silva, Secretary, Ministry of Defence and Others (1999)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the refusal to promote the petitioner, Brigadier Liyanage, to the rank of Major General, despite his acquittal in the Embilipitiya disappearances case and in spite of a clear recommendation by the Commander of the Army, amounted to unreasonable, arbitrary and discriminatory treatment in violation of the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an Army officer who joined as a cadet in 1968 and rose to the rank of Brigadier in 1995 with an outstanding service record and several gallantry and service medals, claimed that he was unfairly denied promotion to Major General. He was suspended and not considered for promotion while he was an accused in the Embilipitiya disappearances case. During that period he was superseded by two officers who were promoted to Major General on 4 December 1997. After a full trial he was acquitted, and no appeal was filed against his acquittal. The Commander of the Army then recommended that he be promoted to Major General on a supernumerary basis with effect from 4 December 1997, and absorbed into the permanent cadre with effect from 10 February 1999, the date of the High Court judgment. Although he thereafter functioned as Quarter Master General (a post normally held by a Major General), the promotion was not granted. The petitioner alleged that the refusal to promote him, when others above and below him in the chain of command were promoted (and even an officer who was indicted was promoted), was unreasonable, arbitrary and discriminatory, violating Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents accepted that the petitioner had an excellent service record but argued that promotion to the rank of Colonel and above is by selection under Regulation 12 of the Army Officers’ Service Regulations (Regular Force) 1992. They contended that, in addition to past service, promotions at that level must clearly be in the best interest of the Army. They maintained that it was not in the best interest of the Sri Lanka Army to promote the petitioner because he had failed to exercise sufficient control over subordinates involved in the Embilipitiya disappearances, even though he was eventually acquitted by the High Court. They relied on the petitioner’s position in the chain of command and on reports such as the Magistrate’s observations in related habeas corpus proceedings, arguing that these justified withholding promotion. They also attempted to distinguish the petitioner from other officers who had been promoted, on the basis that those officers were not indicted in the case.
interpretation_summary:
The Court noted that the petitioner’s career record was consistently above average, that he had received multiple gallantry and service decorations, and that senior officers had described him as an asset to the Army and to the country. It further observed that, after his acquittal in the Embilipitiya disappearances case and in the absence of any appeal against his acquittal, the Commander of the Army had expressly recommended that he be reinstated and promoted to Major General with backdated seniority and later absorbed into the permanent cadre. The petitioner, in fact, performed the duties of Quarter Master General, a post normally held by a Major General.

The Court considered Regulation 12, which requires that promotions to the rank of Colonel and above be by selection, taking into account both past record and whether promotion is clearly in the best interest of the Army. It accepted that the Army is entitled to exercise a discretion on these matters, but stressed that such discretion must be exercised reasonably and without arbitrariness or discrimination. The respondents relied on the petitioner’s alleged failure to control subordinates in the Embilipitiya incidents. However, the Court observed that the petitioner had been acquitted and that no appeal had been filed against that acquittal, and that there was nothing in the Magistrate’s reports to implicate him in a way that distinguished him from others in the chain of command.

The Court examined the treatment of other officers connected to the same events. Officers above the petitioner in the chain of command, such as the Provincial Commander Brigadier Vajira Wijeratne, were promoted to Major General. Officers below him, including Battery Commanders, were also promoted. Significantly, a Detachment Commander (Capt. K. V. V. Chamarasinghe), who had actually been indicted, was promoted to temporary Major with effect from 2 June 1995. In contrast, the petitioner, who had been acquitted, was denied promotion. The Court held that there was no rational basis for singling out the petitioner for adverse treatment when his legal position, following acquittal, was in no way worse than that of others in the chain of command who had been promoted. The reasons advanced by the respondents did not justify this differential treatment.

The Court therefore concluded that the refusal to promote the petitioner, in the face of a favourable recommendation by the Commander and in light of the promotions granted to others similarly or more blameworthily placed in the chain of command, was unreasonable, irrational, arbitrary and capricious. This amounted to discriminatory treatment and a violation of the petitioner’s fundamental right to the equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the failure to promote the petitioner to the rank of Major General, both with effect from 4 December 1997 on a supernumerary vacancy and with effect from 10 February 1999 in the permanent cadre as recommended by the Commander of the Army, was unreasonable, irrational, arbitrary and discriminatory, and thus violated his fundamental rights under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered that the Commander’s recommendation (letter No. MSB/A.6/1 dated 8 March 1999) be implemented, thereby granting the petitioner the promotions in question. It also directed the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 50,000 as compensation and Rs. 5,000 as costs.
principles_established: Promotion decisions in the armed forces, even where promotion is by selection and based on the "best interests of the Army", are subject to constitutional scrutiny and must not be unreasonable, arbitrary or discriminatory under Article 12(1).

An acquitted officer stands, in the eyes of the law, in no worse position than other officers in the same chain of command who have not been indicted or who have been promoted; relying on vague notions of blameworthiness contrary to the acquittal can amount to arbitrary discrimination.

When other officers above and below a person in the chain of command, including an officer who was actually indicted, are promoted, but the acquitted officer is singled out and denied promotion, such selective adverse treatment is prima facie arbitrary and violates equal protection.

Recommendations of the Commander of the Army, based on service record and the outcome of criminal proceedings, are an important factor in assessing whether refusal of promotion is rational; unexplained departure from such recommendations may indicate arbitrariness.
Article 12(1) protects individuals against discriminatory exercise of administrative discretion in service matters, including promotions, not merely against unequal application of formal rules.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 506/99 (F.R.), decided on 25 November 1999

case_title: Palihawadana v. Attorney General and Two Others (1979)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.
Provides the right to petition the Supreme Court for infringement or imminent infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the Job Bank Scheme, which allowed Members of Parliament to select 1,000 unemployed persons per electorate for employment registration, violated the petitioner’s fundamental rights to equality and non-discrimination under Articles 12(1) and 12(2) by giving unfettered and arbitrary discretion to MPs and by refusing the petitioner an application form.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a 24-year-old unemployed resident of the Hewaheta electorate and a member of the Lanka Sama Samaja Party, claimed that he was denied a Job Bank registration form because of his political affiliation. He argued that the scheme vested arbitrary power in Members of Parliament to choose 1,000 unemployed persons out of many thousands, without guidelines, and that this denied him equality of opportunity for State employment and discriminated against him on political grounds.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioner did not satisfy the eligibility criteria under the Job Bank Scheme. An affidavit from the Grama Sevaka stated that the petitioner’s family had substantial income and property, including salaried parents, pension eligibility, land, and a valuable house. The MP stated that he had already distributed all 1,000 forms allotted to him before the petitioner applied. The State further argued that there was no evidence that the petitioner was refused a form due to political opinion.
interpretation_summary: The Court analysed Article 12 and emphasized that reasonable classification is permitted but arbitrary selection is not. While the eligibility criteria of the Job Bank Scheme were considered valid, the Court held that the scheme’s provision allowing MPs unfettered discretion to select 1,000 persons from the eligible class was unconstitutional because it created inherent discrimination. However, the Court concluded that this unconstitutional portion could be severed from the valid part of the scheme. The petitioner nevertheless had no locus standi because he did not fall within the eligible class of persons as defined by the scheme; his family income and assets placed him outside the criterion of economic disadvantage. Therefore, no fundamental right of the petitioner had been infringed. The Court also observed that although the exclusion of SLFP MPs from receiving forms was discriminatory, it did not affect the petitioner’s case.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that although the part of the Job Bank Scheme granting arbitrary selection power to MPs was unconstitutional, the petitioner was not eligible under the scheme’s criteria and therefore suffered no infringement of his own rights. The application was dismissed without costs.
principles_established: Article 12 permits reasonable classification but prohibits arbitrary selection and class legislation.
A statutory or administrative scheme may be partly invalid; unconstitutional parts may be severed if the remainder is workable.
To invoke Article 126, the petitioner must show that *his own* fundamental rights were infringed; a person outside the affected class has no locus standi.
Equality of opportunity for State employment does not mean a right to obtain employment, only access to fair consideration.
Vesting unfettered discretion in political actors, without guidelines, creates inherent risks of discrimination and violates the equality guarantee.

case_title: Perera and Another v. Cyril Ranatunga, Secretary Defence and Others (1992)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioners, who were senior Authorised Officers in the Department of Immigration and Emigration, were unlawfully denied promotion to Senior Authorised Officer due to an arbitrary and discriminatory promotional scheme and subjective assessment criteria, contrary to their fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, both long-serving Authorised Officers with nearly 19 years of service and no adverse entries in their records, claimed they were unfairly overlooked for promotion in both 1990 and 1991. They argued that the promotional scheme was not based on any published or rational criteria. They contended that the interview board used subjective, undisclosed, and arbitrary methods, including vague scoring systems and heavy reliance on detections alone. Despite being more senior, better qualified academically, and having unblemished service, the petitioners were superseded by several junior officers with fewer years of service and weaker qualifications. They argued that this selective treatment was discriminatory and violated Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents stated that promotions were made on the basis of 'seniority and merit' and that the interview board, consisting of senior officers familiar with the candidates' work, conducted a proper assessment. They argued that the selected officers had superior overall merit, particularly work performance in terms of detections. The Controller claimed that personality, work, attendance, commendations, knowledge of the law, and ability to make decisions were all considered during the interview. They further contended that the petitioners were not entitled to promotion merely by seniority and that the board's judgment should not be interfered with.
interpretation_summary: The Court found several substantial defects in the promotional scheme. First, the criteria used at the interview failed to include core elements normally relevant to public service performance, such as efficiency, conduct, and conscientiousness. Second, the most heavily weighted factor—work performance—was restricted solely to detections over a 5-year period, without considering whether officers had equal opportunity for detections. Third, seniority was given only 15% weight, which the Court held to be unreasonably low in a scheme described as one based on 'seniority and merit', particularly for a promotion in the lower tiers of the service where chances for advancement were limited. Fourth, the Board’s procedure was arbitrary, with interviews lasting only a few minutes, making meaningful evaluation unlikely. The Court also noted that the criteria and scheme were not disclosed in advance, depriving candidates of equal opportunity. There was no material from personal files, supervising officers, or any objective assessments to justify the selection of juniors over seniors. The Court held that the scheme had been influenced by subjective considerations and lacked rational justification, resulting in unequal treatment.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Article 12(1) had been infringed. The Court set aside the promotions of the 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th respondents—junior officers who had been promoted over the petitioners—while allowing the promotions of the four most senior officers to stand since they were not challenged. The Court directed the authorities to formulate a proper promotion scheme consistent with Article 12 and make fresh appointments accordingly. Each petitioner was awarded Rs. 2,500 in costs.
principles_established: A promotional scheme must not rely on subjective or undisclosed criteria; all relevant criteria must be publicised in advance to ensure equal opportunity.
In a scheme based on 'seniority and merit', seniority must be given substantial weight unless there is clear justification for prioritising merit.
Work performance must be assessed on a rational basis; relying solely on one indicator, such as detections, without considering opportunity or job context, is discriminatory.
Promotional decisions must be based on objective, verifiable materials such as personal files and supervisory reports; absence of such evidence may indicate arbitrariness.
Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary and unguided discretion in public service promotions; subjective criteria that produce unpredictable or unjustifiable results violate equal protection.
The right to equality of opportunity in public employment is implicit in Article 12 of the Sri Lankan Constitution.

case_title: Priyangani v. Nanayakkara and Others (1996)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s sudden transfer back to a difficult school, after completing the required period of difficult service and being formally transferred to another school, violated her fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) by arbitrarily identifying her as an excess teacher contrary to the established transfer guidelines.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a primary school teacher, served at Kottucachchiya M.V. (KMV), a school classified as a difficult school. After completing five years there, she obtained a transfer in February 1995 to Anamaduwa Adarsha Kanishta Vidyalaya (AAKV), near her husband’s home. On 29 June 1995 she received a letter dated 13 June 1995 from the 2nd respondent, Director of Education, Puttalam Zone, transferring her back to KMV with immediate effect and without travelling expenses. She claimed this was arbitrary and contrary to the Transfer Circular of 18 March 1995 and subsequent circulars, which required that teachers who had already completed difficult service should not be identified as excess. She argued that designating her as an excess teacher and sending her back to the difficult school violated Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that although KMV was technically a difficult school, it was not difficult for the petitioner because during her service there she had lived in her parental home nearby. They further claimed that KMV had been removed from the difficult-school list by January 1994, so her previous service should not count as difficult service. They relied on paragraph 2 of the Transfer Circular, which gave the Provincial Director and the Zonal Director power to transfer teachers on the exigencies of the service, and argued that the impugned transfer was such a transfer. They also contended that paragraphs 7 and 8 of the Transfer Circular, which set out guidelines for identifying excess teachers and exempting those with difficult service, were only non-binding guidelines and that failure to follow them did not amount to a violation of fundamental rights.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that there was no legal basis to treat KMV as anything other than a difficult school during the petitioner’s five-year service there. There was no rule that a school ceased to be difficult for a teacher merely because her parents’ house was close by, and no documentary proof that KMV had been removed from the difficult-school list in 1994. On the evidence, KMV was a difficult school throughout the relevant period. The Court noted that the Transfer Circular and the later circulars on the selection and transfer of excess teachers had laid down specific criteria and guidelines. Teachers who had completed the required period of difficult service were not to be named as excess teachers. The primary teachers at AAKV formed a class, and within that class a rational, rule-based process was required to decide who was excess. Whether paragraphs 7 and 8 were strictly mandatory or only guidelines did not matter for fundamental rights analysis: under Article 12, discretionary powers must be exercised fairly, reasonably, and for the purposes for which they are given. Public powers are held in trust and cannot be used arbitrarily, at the whim of officials. By selecting the petitioner as an excess teacher despite her being exempt under the guidelines, and by not applying those guidelines to others in the same class, the authorities acted arbitrarily and unreasonably. The 5th respondent, as Principal, failed to follow the criteria he was expressly instructed to apply; the 2nd and 1st respondents merely adopted his decision without independent examination of the facts. The whole process was therefore flawed and resulted in unequal treatment.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) had been violated by the 1st, 2nd, and 5th respondents. The transfer order dated 13 June 1995, sending her back to Kottucachchiya M.V., was quashed. The petitioner was allowed to resume work at Anamaduwa Adarsha Kanishta Vidyalaya. The Court ordered the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 15,000 as compensation, and directed the 1st, 2nd, and 5th respondents personally to pay her a total of Rs. 6,000 as costs (Rs. 2,000 each).
principles_established: Discretionary powers in public administration are never absolute; they are held in trust to be exercised reasonably, for proper purposes, and subject to the Rule of Law.
Even where transfer criteria are described as guidelines rather than mandatory rules, arbitrary departure from them in selecting individuals from a class can violate Article 12(1).

Teachers who have completed the required period of service in difficult schools form a protected group under rational transfer schemes and should not be singled out as excess in disregard of established criteria.

Equal protection requires that when a class of employees is subject to a selection process (such as identifying excess staff), the process must follow clear, pre-established principles to ensure fair play and avoid arbitrary choice.

Administrative powers in the education sector, including transfer powers, must ultimately be exercised in a manner that promotes the best interests of the child and the integrity of the education system, not for convenience or personal preference of officials.
precedents_cited: SC Application No. 339A/95, SCM 29.03.1996 (companion case on arbitrary transfer of a teacher with difficult-service experience)
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 3398/95, decided on 30 August 1996

case_title: Samarasinghe v. Air Lanka Ltd. and Others (1994)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) was violated when Air Lanka failed to appoint him as International Relations Manager, despite a proper internal recruitment process and recommendation in his favour, and instead secretly appointed the 13th respondent outside the established recruitment procedure and without the required experience.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner was Senior International Relations Executive (Grade E V) of Air Lanka. In late 1992, at his request, his post was proposed to be upgraded to International Relations Manager (Grade M1). A Staff Vacancy Notice was issued for internal candidates only, requiring five years’ service at Air Lanka (two years in Senior Executive grade). The petitioner applied, was interviewed by a high-level panel including the Consultant (his head of department), and was recommended for appointment. The Board of Directors, however, deferred his appointment without giving reasons. When he protested, he was told later that the Board was considering appointing the 13th respondent instead. The 13th respondent was then appointed to that post in May 1993, without any public or internal advertisement for external candidates, and without following the normal recruitment procedure. The petitioner alleged that this amounted to unequal and discriminatory treatment, especially since he had been the only internal candidate, had been recommended, and had a legitimate expectation of promotion to the newly upgraded post.
respondent_argument: The former Board of Directors and management contended that Air Lanka’s acts were lawful and that the decision not to promote the petitioner did not violate Article 12(1). They claimed the petitioner was not yet suitable for management responsibilities, citing alleged deficiencies such as lack of competence and confidence, inability to respond quickly and pragmatically, and carelessness or irresponsibility. They argued that, based on discussions with senior managers familiar with the department, there was consensus that someone from outside the International Relations Department should be brought in as Manager and that the petitioner was not ready. The 13th respondent argued that he was appointed on merit: he was an Attorney-at-Law with a Master’s degree in Air and Space Law from McGill University, and had been interviewed by the Chairman, Consultant and others. It was also argued that the petitioner lacked the full five years’ service at Air Lanka required by the internal vacancy notice, whereas the 13th respondent possessed specialised academic qualifications in aviation-related law and organisation.
interpretation_summary: The Court first affirmed, following Rajaratne v. Air Lanka Ltd., that Air Lanka’s actions constitute "executive or administrative action" and are reviewable under Articles 17 and 126. It then examined the sequence of events. The post of International Relations Manager had effectively been created by upgrading the petitioner’s own post. A valid internal recruitment process was initiated, consistent with Air Lanka’s policy that vacancies should be filled, as far as possible, by internal candidates. The petitioner was the only internal applicant, and a properly constituted panel of senior officials (including the Consultant who supervised him) interviewed and recommended him. The Board’s later claim that he was unsuitable was undermined by the absence of any contemporaneous record of poor performance, warnings, or adverse comments. On the contrary, the petitioner had been promoted earlier, had earned increments on time, and had repeatedly been nominated to attend airline and bilateral meetings, indicating confidence in his abilities. The Court found that the criticisms of incompetence and irresponsibility were ex post facto justifications, raised only after litigation began, and were unsupported by documentary evidence. In contrast, it emerged (from documents filed by the new Board) that from as early as 1991–1992, senior management had been informally grooming the 13th respondent for a management position in Air Lanka, even before he applied. His eventual ‘application’ in March 1993 came after telephone and in-person discussions with the Chairman and the Consultant, and he was then interviewed and appointed on a two-year contract without any advertisement of the vacancy. Critically, while the petitioner’s recommendation was rejected partly due to an alleged shortfall of one year’s service, the 13th respondent had no airline experience at all and did not satisfy Air Lanka’s own stated requirements for a Manager M1 (five years’ managerial experience for an external recruit). The Court stressed that equality under Article 12(1) applies from recruitment through to promotion: schemes of recruitment and promotion must exist, and more importantly, their implementation must be free from caprice, bias or prejudice. Favouritism and the "evil eye" towards a disfavoured employee are incompatible with equality. Executive actions must be honest, open and transparent. Here, the process was opaque and manipulated: an internal candidate who met the core criteria and had been recommended was bypassed in favour of a favoured outsider, selected by private negotiation and secretive process, for reasons unrelated to the declared objective of appointing the best qualified person. The petitioner thus had a legitimate expectation of appointment to the upgraded post, and his non-appointment, coupled with the irregular appointment of the 13th respondent, amounted to unwarranted and invidious discrimination.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) had been violated. The Court declared the 13th respondent’s appointment as International Relations Manager invalid, since it had been made outside the recognised recruitment procedure, without the required experience, and in a manner dependent on the violation of the petitioner’s constitutional rights. It directed that the 13th respondent’s appointment be terminated forthwith. However, the Court did not directly appoint the petitioner to the post. Instead, it ordered Air Lanka (the 1st respondent) and the current Board (6th–11th respondents) to fill the resulting vacancy in accordance with its policy of preferring internal candidates and in terms of its promotion/recruitment procedure (P7), within three months. The petitioner’s earlier application was to be treated as a valid application for the post, allowing him to add further material, and the Court directed that any negative opinions expressed about him by the former Board or officials during these proceedings must be entirely disregarded in the fresh selection. As relief, the Court awarded the petitioner Rs. 50,000 as a solatium for the violation of his fundamental rights and Rs. 5,000 as costs, both payable by Air Lanka.
principles_established: Article 12(1) equality applies throughout a public-sector career, from recruitment up to promotions and beyond; recruitment and promotion processes must be founded on proper schemes and implemented without caprice, bias, prejudice or hidden favouritism.

Where a public entity has adopted clear recruitment and promotion procedures and an internal preference policy, arbitrary departure from these in order to favour an outsider over a qualified internal candidate can amount to invidious discrimination and a violation of Article 12(1).

Allegations of incompetence or unsuitability used to justify unequal treatment must be supported by contemporaneous records and proper disciplinary or evaluative steps; unsupported, post-hoc criticisms cannot justify discriminatory decisions.

Appointments to important posts in public or state-linked entities must be carried out with honesty, openness and transparency; appointments made by private negotiation and secrecy, bypassing established procedures and qualifications, are inconsistent with the Rule of Law and equality.

Legitimate expectation can arise where a post is created by upgrading an employee’s existing post, a formal process is conducted, and a duly constituted panel recommends that employee; arbitrary rejection of that recommendation, coupled with secret selection of another, infringes equality.

Courts may, in fundamental rights jurisdiction, invalidate an irregular appointment made in violation of equality rights and direct that a fresh, lawful recruitment process be conducted, rather than directly substituting their own choice of appointee.
Air Lanka’s actions, as a state-controlled corporation, constitute executive or administrative action and are therefore subject to fundamental rights review.
precedents_cited: Rajaratne v. Air Lanka Ltd. (on Air Lanka’s acts being executive/administrative action reviewable under Articles 17 and 126)
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 275/93, judgment dated 02 June 1994

case_title: Tennakoon, Assistant Superintendent of Police v. T. P. F. de Silva, Inspector General of Police and Others (1996)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
The powers of appointment, transfer, dismissal and disciplinary control of public officers are subject to the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

legal_issue: Whether the transfer of the petitioner, an Assistant Superintendent of Police, to Anuradhapura—without reasons, without a vacancy, and based on vague allegations arising from political interference—constituted an arbitrary and unreasonable exercise of power in violation of the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an Assistant Superintendent of Police, had served ten months in Kayts (an operational area) and had thereafter been transferred to Kurunegala and then to Matale, where he was attached to the Dambulla Division. On 20 May 1995 he was abruptly transferred to Anuradhapura by the Inspector General of Police without any reason being given, and despite the fact that there was no vacancy for his grade at Anuradhapura. He alleged that the transfer was instigated by the OIC of Galewela Police Station, against whom he had initiated inquiries for serious misconduct including assault, bribery and rape, and who had then conspired with the 3rd respondent, the Member of Parliament for Dambulla. The MP had complained that the petitioner was conducting his duties with political bias due to family ties with the UNP. The petitioner asserted that he had only performed his duties lawfully and that the transfer was retaliatory, arbitrary, unsupported by facts, and motivated by political interference. He claimed that no inquiry was held, his appeals to the IGP received no response, and the transfer was meant to stifle his investigations into police misconduct.
respondent_argument: The Inspector General of Police stated that although the 3rd respondent had made complaints, the IGP was not personally aware of them at the time of the transfer. He denied acting on political pressure and instead asserted that there were problems in the working relationship between the petitioner and the 3rd respondent, which he learned of through discussions with the Senior Superintendent of Police, Matale. He emphasized that the transfer was not punitive or disciplinary, but necessary to avoid a situation that might become prejudicial to the exercise of police functions. The respondents argued that the petitioner, being in a transferable service, had no fundamental right to remain in one post and that transfers in circumstances of strained relationships between officers and elected representatives were common administrative practice.
interpretation_summary: Justice Fernando noted that Article 55(5) makes clear that the IGP’s transfer powers remain reviewable under Article 12(1). The Court would not substitute its judgment for the IGP’s, but it must examine whether the discretion was exercised reasonably and without arbitrariness. The Court found that the allegations against the petitioner—claiming political bias and poor working relations—were wholly unsupported by facts. The petitioner had provided detailed reports showing he had been investigating four serious offences committed by the OIC/Galewela, including assault, bribery and rape. These reports were not contradicted by the DIG or SSP, Matale, who filed no affidavits. The IGP admitted he was unaware of these facts and knew only a vague allegation of “lack of harmony” conveyed by the SSP. The Court held that the IGP had not formed an independent opinion based on facts but had simply adopted the unverified conclusions of subordinates. The IGP failed to state what actual material supported his belief in poor working relations. The Court emphasised that lack of working relationship with an MP is not a valid ground for transfer unless the officer is culpable for the breakdown and facts support such a conclusion. Allowing transfers on such vague grounds would undermine police independence and encourage improper political influence. The Court reaffirmed that administrative authorities must provide reasons for decisions, as a matter of natural justice and transparency. The failure to investigate allegations, failure to respond to the petitioner’s appeals, reliance on unverified subordinate opinions, and avoidance of factual assessment made the transfer arbitrary, unreasonable and discriminatory.
outcome: By majority (Fernando J. and Wijetunga J.), the Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) was infringed by the 1st respondent, the Inspector General of Police. The Court declined to quash the transfer order, as the petitioner did not insist on reinstatement, but it directed the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 40,000 as compensation and costs. Justice Anandacoomaraswamy dissented, holding that the transfer was made on exigencies of service and did not violate the petitioner’s rights.
principles_established: Article 55(5) makes the powers of appointment, transfer, dismissal and disciplinary control of public officers subject to fundamental rights review.
Transfers of public officers cannot be justified by vague assertions such as 'lack of harmony' or 'interests of the service'; administrative discretion must be exercised based on facts.
Executive authorities cannot rely on unsupported subordinate opinions; they must independently verify facts before exercising powers affecting rights.
Political interference or complaints by elected representatives cannot justify transfers unless supported by objective material and compatible with the norms of equality.
Failure to give reasons for a transfer can indicate arbitrariness; transparency is part of administrative justice.

Working relationship issues cannot justify transferring an officer if the officer is not culpable for any breakdown; otherwise, improper pressure by outsiders would undermine administrative integrity.
A public officer in a transferable service does not lose protection from arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory transfers under Article 12(1).

case_title: Tennakoon v. Piyadigama and Others (1995)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

legal_issue: Whether the compulsory and premature retirement of the petitioner, following the suppression of his post of Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) in the Ministry of Labour, and the failure to offer him reversion or alternative employment, amounted to unequal and discriminatory treatment in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a public officer since 1961, had served as a teacher, press officer and eventually as Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) in several ministries, including the Ministry of Labour and later the Ministry of Public Administration. In 1992 he reverted to the Ministry of Labour as Senior Assistant Secretary (Information). On 15.09.1994 the 1st respondent informed him that his services would be terminated with effect from 30.09.1994 because the Minister intended to appoint another officer to his post. Later, a Cabinet decision of 12.10.1994 authorised suppression of his post and that of Assistant Secretary (Trade Unions), granting incumbents the option to revert to their previous post or retire. The petitioner complains that he was not informed of this option; instead, on 26.10.1994 he was told he would be retired on the ground that his post was abolished. When he learnt of the Cabinet decision and exercised his option on 27.10.1994 to revert to his previous post in the Ministry of Public Administration, he was told that that post too had been abolished and its substitute post of Co-ordinating Officer (Information) had been filled. He further alleged that other officers whose posts were suppressed, such as Assistant Secretary (Trade Unions) W.A. Somasiri, were given the option and found alternative employment, and that posts of Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) continued to exist and were even newly filled in other ministries after the Cabinet decision. He claimed that his compulsory premature retirement at age 52 was arbitrary, mala fide, discriminatory and for collateral purposes, violating his right to equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The 1st respondent, Secretary to the Ministry of Labour and Vocational Training, admitted the sequence of events but maintained that the petitioner was not similarly circumstanced to other officers. He argued that the suppression of the post of Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) in the Ministry of Labour followed the Cabinet decision, and therefore the petitioner had to be retired. The respondents contended that other officers who continued as Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) in other ministries, or who were found alternative posts (such as W.A. Somasiri), were differently placed and that there was no obligation to provide the petitioner with alternative employment. They denied mala fides and maintained that the decision to retire the petitioner flowed from the lawful suppression of his post.
interpretation_summary: Justice Kulatunga held that the petitioner and the other officers holding similar grades were in a like situation, as public officers who normally serve until the prescribed retirement age. Although the petitioner’s post in the Ministry of Labour was suppressed, other posts of Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) continued to exist in several ministries, and appointments to that post were even made after the Cabinet decision. Further, the Cabinet decision clearly granted affected officers an option to revert to their previous posts or to retire. The 1st respondent fully communicated that option to Assistant Secretary (Trade Unions) W.A. Somasiri—who then reverted to a suitable post in the Department of Labour—but deliberately failed to disclose the same option to the petitioner. When the petitioner discovered the existence of the option and exercised it, the administration responded by closing off all avenues of reversion and refusing to explore alternative employment, despite the existence of comparable posts elsewhere. The Court emphasized that, although changes of government may require re-arranging positions and providing personal staff for Ministers, officials like the 1st respondent must ensure that such changes are carried out lawfully, in accordance with Cabinet/government decisions, and without causing serious prejudice to individual officers. In this case, the petitioner was singled out: he was not informed of his option, his attempt to revert was blocked, and no effort was made to find him alternative employment, while others similarly affected were treated more favourably. This amounted to selective discrimination without a rational basis and thus violated Article 12(1).
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s compulsory and premature retirement was null and void as it violated his fundamental rights under Article 12(1). The Court declared the impugned retirement invalid and of no force or effect. As the specific post in the Ministry of Labour had been abolished, the Court directed the 1st and 2nd respondents and the State to appoint the petitioner to another post of Senior Assistant Secretary (Information) in the Public Service or to any other comparable post. The Court further directed the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 60,000 as compensation (representing minimum loss of earnings since his purported retirement) and ordered the 1st respondent to pay Rs. 5,000 as costs.
principles_established: Public officers whose posts are suppressed must be treated equally and fairly; where a general option (e.g. to revert or retire) is granted by Cabinet decision, it must be offered uniformly to all affected officers.
Selective disclosure of options and selective provision of alternative employment, without rational justification, constitutes unlawful discrimination contrary to Article 12(1).

When reorganising ministries and creating personal staff for Ministers following a change of government, administrative authorities must implement such changes lawfully and in conformity with established decisions, ensuring that individual public officers are not arbitrarily or prematurely deprived of their career and retirement expectations.
The suppression of a post does not justify compulsory premature retirement if equivalent or comparable posts exist in the service and other similarly placed officers are retained or accommodated.

Officials responsible for implementing Cabinet and government decisions must avoid selective discrimination and must take reasonable steps to find suitable alternative employment for displaced officers.
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 275/94, decided on 26 June 1995

case_id: Wickrematunga v. Anuruddha Ratwatte and Others, S.C. Application No. F.R. 228/96
case_title: Wickrematunga v. Anurudda Ratwatte and Others

clauses.text:
No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds:
Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office:
Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

legal_issue: Whether the termination of the petitioner's petroleum dealership by the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation amounted to discriminatory, arbitrary, and unconstitutional executive/administrative action violating Articles 12(2) and 14(1)(g).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his dealership was unlawfully and arbitrarily terminated without any valid reason, and that the action was motivated by political discrimination due to his association with the opposition political party.
respondent_argument: The Ceylon Petroleum Corporation argued that the agreement was terminated due to misconduct, lapses, dishonoured cheques, and violations of the dealership agreement. They further contended that the matter was contractual and private, not ‘executive or administrative action’, and therefore outside fundamental rights jurisdiction.
interpretation_summary: The Court found that the allegations of misconduct were unsupported, vague, and not backed by evidence. The Corporation had acted arbitrarily, relying on unfounded assertions, and the termination process showed pre-determination and political motivation. The Court held that the Corporation is a government instrumentality engaged in a public function and therefore subject to constitutional obligations. The discretion to terminate without notice was not unfettered; public authorities must act reasonably and in good faith even when acting through contracts.
outcome: The Court held that the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation violated Articles 12(2) and 14(1)(g). The termination was declared unconstitutional and of no force or effect. The Corporation was ordered to reinstate the petitioner as dealer and pay Rs. 100,000 as solatium and Rs. 25,000 as costs. No violation was found against the Minister (1st respondent).
principles_established: Public corporations are subject to constitutional restraints when performing public functions.
Even contractual acts of public bodies must adhere to Article 12 and cannot be arbitrary or discriminatory.
Unfettered discretion does not exist for public authorities; they must act fairly, reasonably, and in good faith.
Termination of a contract by a public authority can amount to executive or administrative action reviewable under fundamental rights.
Political discrimination constitutes a violation of Article 12(2).

case_title: Wijesinghe v. Attorney General and Others (1979)

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds:
Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office:
Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s removal from the post of Sub Postmistress, following a Cabinet decision based on the findings of the Political Victimization Committee, amounted to a violation of her fundamental rights to equality and non-discrimination under Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that she was removed from her post as Sub Postmistress of Ellagawa without charges, without being heard, and solely to make way for another candidate, Indra Ranjini, on political grounds. She argued that the Cabinet, acting on the report of the Political Victimization Committee which never heard her, arbitrarily terminated her services, thereby violating the guarantees of equal protection and non-discrimination.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the Cabinet acted lawfully under Article 55(1), which allows dismissal of public officers who hold office at pleasure. They contended that the petitioner’s appointment was itself politically influenced and that the Government was merely rectifying earlier political victimization. They further submitted that no discrimination occurred under Article 12(2) because the petitioner was not targeted due to her political opinions but was removed because her initial appointment was improper.
interpretation_summary: The Court acknowledged that the proceedings of the Political Victimization Committee were gravely flawed, as the petitioner was never heard and findings were made on ex parte, largely hearsay evidence. The Committee failed to observe basic principles of natural justice. However, the Court distinguished between ordinary rights and fundamental rights, emphasising that not every administrative injustice or illegality constitutes a fundamental rights violation. A mere breach of law or miscarriage of justice is not equivalent to a violation of Article 12 unless there is intentional, purposeful, or hostile discrimination. The Court held that the Cabinet, relying on its constitutional authority to appoint and dismiss public officers who hold office at pleasure, lawfully exercised its power unless discriminatory intent was proven. As the petitioner failed to show that she was singled out for differential treatment based on political opinion or other prohibited grounds, the Court concluded that, though the outcome was harsh and unjust, it did not amount to a violation of a fundamental right.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application. The petitioner failed to establish a violation of Articles 12(1) or 12(2). The Court held that her removal was within the Cabinet’s constitutional authority under Article 55(1) and that the irregularities in the Committee process, though regrettable, did not constitute unconstitutional discrimination. No costs were ordered against the petitioner.
principles_established: A breach of ordinary law or administrative unfairness does not automatically constitute a violation of a fundamental right under Article 12.
To prove a violation of Article 12(2), there must be evidence of intentional, purposeful, or hostile discrimination.
Public officers holding office 'at pleasure' under Article 55(1) may be lawfully dismissed unless discriminatory grounds are proven.
Findings of committees or inquiries that do not follow natural justice may be invalid, but such invalidity alone does not establish a fundamental rights contravention.
Equal protection is violated only where similarly situated persons are intentionally treated differently; mere error, negligence, or breach of rules is insufficient.

case_title: Faiz v. Attorney-General and Others (1993)

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s arrest, detention, assault, and denial of equal protection—carried out with the participation of police officers and political figures—constituted violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2), and whether private individuals can be held liable when acting in concert with the executive.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a Wildlife Ranger, claimed that after arresting offenders for illegal timber felling, he was threatened and assaulted by political figures (5th–7th respondents), further attacked inside the police station, unlawfully arrested without reasons, unlawfully detained, and denied equal protection because police refused to record his complaint and instead favoured the politicians.
respondent_argument: Police respondents argued that the petitioner was lawfully arrested based on the 6th respondent’s complaint and that the assault was unexpected, with reasonable preventive action taken. Political respondents denied any assault at the police station and claimed the petitioner was intoxicated and the incident was a minor scuffle. They argued no nexus existed between them and the police to create liability under Article 126.
interpretation_summary: The Court accepted the petitioner’s version as more credible, supported by the fact that the suspects he arrested later pleaded guilty to illicit felling. Police failed to record his complaint, failed to investigate under Section 109 CPC, arrested him without explanation, and remanded him despite knowing he was the complainant. They showed hostility and partiality to the political respondents, while taking no action against them despite a serious assault inside the police station. The Court held that police inaction and acquiescence transformed the private individuals’ acts into 'executive or administrative action.' Thus, even non-executive respondents became liable due to instigation, influence, and participation. Fernando J. explained that purely private acts become 'executive' when done with the authority, approval, or connivance of the executive.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s rights under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) were violated (Goonewardena J. dissenting only on Article 13(2)). Compensation totalling Rs. 50,000 and costs of Rs. 5,000 were awarded against the State and respondents 2–7.
principles_established: Police must record complaints and act under Section 109 CPC; failure to do so can amount to a denial of equal protection.
Cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment under Article 11 includes assaults inside police custody, even if caused by private persons acting with police acquiescence.
Equal protection (Article 12(1)) is violated when police take prompt action against one party but ignore serious offences by politically powerful offenders.
Private individuals can be held liable under Article 126 when their acts are enabled, approved, instigated, or condoned by executive or administrative officers.
An unlawful arrest without explanation violates Article 13(1); failure to release a person unlawfully arrested engages liability under Articles 13(1), 13(2), and 12(1).
Denial of equal protection includes both affirmative discrimination and culpable official inaction.
Executive or administrative action includes not only acts of State officers but also acts of private persons done under executive authority or influence.

case_title: Mahanama Tilakaratne v. Bandula Wickramasinghe, Senior Superintendent of Police and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of a High Court Judge (the petitioner) by senior police officers, after the arrest warrant had been cancelled and bail granted, violated Articles 13(1) and 13(2) due to unlawful arrest, misuse of judicial process, and failure to comply with statutory procedures for issuing and executing warrants.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a High Court Judge, claimed that he was unlawfully arrested at his home despite having surrendered to court, had the warrant cancelled, and was released on bail. He argued that police officers ignored court orders, relied on a non-existent or invalid warrant, and unlawfully detained him overnight, violating Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
respondent_argument: The 1st and 3rd respondents argued that they acted on instructions from superiors and based on the Attorney-General’s alleged approval. They claimed the arrest was carried out under normal law due to serious allegations of attempted murder and unlawful assembly. They further claimed they lacked knowledge of the warrant’s cancellation. The Attorney-General (4th respondent) denied giving any such instructions.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the entire process was marred by serious procedural violations. Warrants under section 124 require judicial scrutiny, including evidence recorded on oath, which did not occur. Even if the warrant were valid, it was directed specifically to SI Rodrigo and therefore could not be executed by the 1st respondent without endorsement under section 52(3). The 1st respondent's justification that he acted on the Attorney-General’s orders was rejected because the Attorney-General expressly denied involvement. The Court found that the 1st and 3rd respondents deliberately ignored the Kesbewa Magistrate's order recalling the warrant and releasing the petitioner on bail. Their conduct before the Chief Magistrate, Colombo, showed an attempt to mislead the court with fabricated claims of 'unrest' in Kesbewa. The Court emphasized that issuing a warrant is a judicial act requiring independent judgment, not something granted merely because the suspect is a High Court Judge. Arrests on the instructions of superiors without independent grounds under section 32(1)(b) are unlawful. Thus, the arrest and detention were not according to procedure established by law.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were violated by the 1st and 3rd respondents. The 1st and 3rd respondents were ordered to personally pay Rs. 50,000 each, while the State was ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 compensation and Rs. 50,000 as costs, totalling Rs. 350,000 to the petitioner.
principles_established: A Magistrate must record evidence on oath before issuing a warrant under section 124; warrants cannot be issued merely because investigators request them.
The purpose of court process under section 124 is to secure appearance before court—not to secure presence at police stations.
A named warrant cannot be executed by any other officer unless endorsed under section 52(3).
Arresting a suspect under section 32(1)(b) requires reasonable suspicion or credible information; blind obedience to superiors’ orders does not satisfy the constitutional requirement.
Police cannot ignore or defy a Magistrate’s order cancelling a warrant; doing so violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
Misleading a Magistrate, concealing court orders, or fabricating grounds (such as alleged 'unrest') amounts to unconstitutional executive action.
Detention without lawful authority, even for a few hours, can infringe Article 13(2).

case_title: Mahinda Rajapaksa v. Kudahetti and Others

clauses.text: Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the temporary detention and seizure of documents from the petitioner at the Katunayake Airport violated his rights under Articles 14(1)(a) (freedom of speech) and 13(1) (freedom from arbitrary arrest).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a Member of Parliament, claimed he was arrested and detained illegally at the airport when police seized documents relating to disappearances which he intended to take to a UN Working Group meeting in Geneva. He argued this prevented him from presenting his case and violated his freedom of speech and freedom from arrest.
respondent_argument: The 1st respondent (Assistant Superintendent of Police) argued he examined the petitioner's bags because there was credible information that the petitioner was carrying fabricated documents prejudicial to national security under Regulation 33. He maintained that the petitioner was not arrested, was free to contact a lawyer, and voluntarily handed over the documents before leaving freely for Geneva.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the petitioner failed to establish a violation of Article 14(1)(a) because the documents seized were reports on individual disappearance cases, which were not relevant to the Working Group’s meeting. The Working Group had requested general observations for its annual report, not individual case files, and even those were due several weeks before the meeting. There was no evidence that the petitioner was due to address the meeting, nor that he actually spoke. The Court found that the withheld documents were unnecessary for the Geneva meeting, and the petitioner could have submitted them later since almost all documents were returned within a month. Regarding Article 13(1), the Court held that there was no arrest. Although the petitioner was delayed, it did not amount to being placed in the custody or under the coercive control of law enforcement. He was free to refuse the search, speak to a lawyer, choose whether to surrender the documents, refuse to make a statement, and finally proceed abroad as scheduled. There was no confinement, coercion, or control comparable to arrests recognised in earlier cases such as Namasivayam and Piyasiri. Therefore, neither Article 14(1)(a) nor Article 13(1) was violated.
outcome: Application dismissed. The Court held that neither the right to free speech nor the right to freedom from arbitrary arrest was infringed.
principles_established: Freedom of speech must be assessed in context; not all documents are necessary for a speaker to exercise expressive rights.
Material irrelevant to the purpose of a meeting cannot be used to argue that freedom of speech was impaired.
Not every delay, detention, or search constitutes an arrest under Article 13(1).
Arrest requires submission to custody or coercive control indicating deprivation of liberty.
A person who is free to refuse, negotiate, or walk away is not considered arrested.
Searches or temporary interference with travel do not amount to arrest unless there is clear detention or coercion.

case_title: Sirisena and Others v. Earnest Perera and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be produced before the nearest competent judge according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) were violated by their illegal arrest, detention, and alleged mistreatment by police officers investigating a fatal motor accident.
petitioner_claim: The 1st and 2nd petitioners, both carpenters, claimed that they were illegally arrested, detained from 19 to 22 April 1990, and assaulted by police to force them to implicate a businessman’s son in a fatal accident. The 3rd, 4th and 5th petitioners claimed they were also unlawfully arrested on 21 April at the Coroner’s Court and detained until evening.
respondent_argument: The police denied any arrest or detention, claiming the petitioners voluntarily attended for questioning. They argued the petitioners were merely instructed to assist investigations into the accident and that no torture or illegal detention occurred.
interpretation_summary: The Court rejected the police version as unreliable due to missing investigation notes, contradictory affidavits, and the inherent improbability of their explanation. It accepted that the 1st and 2nd petitioners were continuously detained from 19 to 22 April, and that the 3rd to 5th petitioners were detained on 21 April. However, the Court found insufficient medical or corroborative evidence to establish torture under Article 11. The Court reaffirmed that Article 13(1) protects against any arbitrary deprivation of liberty, not only arrests connected to suspicion of an offence. An ‘arrest’ occurs whenever a person’s liberty to leave is removed, whether or not an offence is alleged. The deprivation of liberty for the purpose of extracting statements was therefore an infringement of Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
outcome: Fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were held to be violated. No violation of Article 11 was proved. Compensation was ordered against both the State and the offending police officers. The Inspector General of Police was directed to conduct an internal inquiry.
principles_established: Arrest under Article 13 does not depend on an allegation of an offence; it depends on whether liberty is restricted.
A person is arrested when deprived of freedom of movement, regardless of whether the arrest is ‘valid’ under criminal procedure.
Police cannot detain persons merely for investigative convenience.
State liability and personal liability of public officers may coexist in fundamental rights violations.
Arbitrary detention for extracting statements violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
Article 11 requires clear, cogent evidence of torture; exaggerated or unsupported claims cannot succeed.

case_title: Thavarasa and Two Others v. Gunasekera and Others (Consolidated Applications)

clauses.text: No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for the arrest.
Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be produced before the nearest competent judge according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the three petitioners—supporters of UNP candidate Anura Bastian—were unlawful and in violation of their fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2), in connection with alleged election-related offences, obstruction, intimidation of police officers, and an alleged attempted shooting.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners claimed they were not pasting posters but arrived after receiving a call that their supporters were being assaulted. They said they approached the police only to inquire and protest, but were unlawfully arrested, assaulted, and detained. They denied any obstruction, denied owning or brandishing a firearm (except acknowledging a licensed pistol kept in a van), and argued that the subsequent allegation of an attempted shooting was fabricated to justify their arrest and refusal of police bail. They stated that the 49 other persons involved were given police bail, and that their continued detention until 11 a.m. was unnecessary and violated Article 13(2).
respondent_argument: The 1st and 2nd respondent police officers stated that they found nearly 50 persons, including the petitioners, illegally pasting posters on a public road, constituting an election offence under section 74 of the Parliamentary Elections Act. They said the petitioners were organisers and leaders who verbally abused, threatened, and obstructed them. One petitioner, Ramanathan, allegedly drew a pistol from his waist and attempted to shoot the HQI, prompting immediate arrest. They argued the arrests were lawful, as the offenders were caught red-handed committing a cognisable offence. They further contended that police bail need not be granted under section 116(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which is discretionary, and that the petitioners were rightly produced before the Magistrate. The respondents attacked the credibility of CID inquiries that later contradicted their version, calling the CID intervention suspicious and politically influenced.
interpretation_summary: The Court accepted the police version that the petitioners were among a large group pasting posters illegally at midnight and that the police were acting under section 74 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, which empowers arrest without warrant. Since the petitioners were caught in flagrante delicto, the police were not required to explain the reason for arrest under Article 13(1). The Court found that the petitioners’ claims of arriving after the police were improbable, considering the evidence of coordinated campaign activities and helpers working at the location. It also held that the petitioners' aggressive language amounted to obstruction and intimidation under sections 183 and 486 of the Penal Code. Regarding Article 13(2), the Court held that detention until 11 a.m. was justified, as section 116(1) CPC gives police discretion not to grant bail and to produce suspects before a Magistrate. The CID’s second B report, which claimed the attempted murder charge was unsupported, was viewed with suspicion and considered unreliable. The Court held the contemporaneous entries of the 1st respondent to be credible and rejected allegations of fabrication. Therefore, no violation of Articles 13(1) or 13(2) was established.
outcome: All three applications were dismissed. The Court held that there was no infringement of the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) or 13(2). Each petitioner was ordered to deposit Rs. 70,000 as costs, with Rs. 10,000 payable to the State and Rs. 100,000 each awarded to the 1st and 2nd respondents.
principles_established: A police officer need not state the reason for arrest when the suspect is caught red-handed committing a cognisable offence.
Section 116(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code is discretionary, not mandatory; police may refuse police bail and produce suspects before a Magistrate depending on circumstances.
Verbal threats, intimidation, and obstructive conduct by political supporters during an arrest can amount to offences under sections 183 and 486 of the Penal Code.
Article 13(1) protects against unlawful arrest, but when arrest is lawful under a statute such as the Parliamentary Elections Act, no violation arises.
Article 13(2) is violated only by arbitrary detention; lawful detention pending production before a Magistrate does not constitute a breach.
CID inquiries that are irregular, politically influenced, or poorly supported may be disregarded by the Court.

case_title: Vinayagamoorthy (on behalf of Wimalenthiran) v. Army Commander and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of Wimalenthiran by the Army and later the CID were lawful under Emergency Regulations 17, 18, and 19, and whether his fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were violated.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that Wimalenthiran was arrested on 2 October 1993 from a lodge at Old Moor Street, blindfolded, and secretly detained for over two months in a house behind the Indian High Commission. He was denied the reasons for his arrest, never handed over to the nearest police station, and kept in unauthorized detention locations contrary to Emergency Regulations. He was produced before a Magistrate only on 23 April 1994, 142 days after arrest. He denied involvement with the LTTE or any crime and stated that his arrest was based purely on suspicion without legal justification.
respondent_argument: The respondents claimed the arrest took place on 23 October 1993 at an Army checkpoint at Kotahena based on reasonable suspicion of LTTE involvement. They argued that he was informed of the reason for arrest, detained at Panagoda Army Camp under a valid Regulation 19 order, then under Regulation 17 detention orders, and later transferred to CID lawfully. They asserted that subsequent investigations showed his involvement in the LTTE network linked to the assassination of President Premadasa. They relied heavily on detention orders and alleged confessions.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the respondents failed to prove any reasonable grounds of suspicion at the time of arrest. The arrest appeared to be based on vague, general suspicion, hoping later evidence might justify it. This violated the requirement under Regulation 18(1), making the arrest unconstitutional under Article 13(1). The Court also found that the correct arrest date was 2 October—not 23 October—which exposed multiple violations: the detainee was not handed over to the nearest police station within 24 hours; he was detained at Panagoda Camp, which at that time was not an authorized detention centre under Regulation 19(4); he was not produced before a Magistrate within the required 48 hours or within seven days; and the Secretary of Defence had issued detention orders mechanically without showing personal satisfaction as required by Regulation 17(1). None of the mandatory safeguards for preventing abuse or disappearance—such as notification to relatives, Magistrate visits, and Human Rights Task Force reporting—were complied with. The CID and Army also failed to justify the delay or produce credible material supporting the Secretary’s ‘satisfaction’. The Court rejected the respondents’ version and accepted the petitioner’s chronology corroborated by Amnesty International reports.
outcome: The Court declared that the arrest violated Article 13(1) and the detention violated Article 13(2). The Court ordered the State to pay Rs. 25,000 as compensation and Rs. 5,000 as costs to Wimalenthiran.
principles_established: Arrest must be justified at the moment it occurs; later discoveries cannot cure an unlawful arrest.
A suspicion must be objectively reasonable; vague or speculative suspicion is insufficient.
Emergency Regulation 18 requires handing the arrested person to the nearest police station within 24 hours when arrested outside the Northern and Eastern Provinces.
Detention is valid only in places officially authorized and published in the Gazette under Regulation 19(4).
The Secretary of Defence must be personally satisfied with clear material before issuing Regulation 17 detention orders; he cannot act mechanically.
Failure to comply with procedural safeguards—Magistrate visits, HRTF notification, and informing relatives—violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
Preventive detention must comply strictly with procedural safeguards to prevent disappearance and abuse.

case_title: Wicremabandu v. Herath and Others
judges: H. A. G. de Silva J.

clauses.text: Freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest; right to be informed of reason for arrest.
Right to be produced before a judge; protection against unlawful detention.
No punishment except by court after conviction.
Permits restrictions on Article 13 rights in the interests of national security and public order.
Existing written law valid despite inconsistency with fundamental rights.
Right to invoke fundamental rights jurisdiction.

legal_issue: Whether Regulation 17 of the Emergency Regulations was ultra vires the Public Security Ordinance and/or the 1978 Constitution, and the extent of the Court’s power to review detention orders made under it.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed his arrest and 15-month detention under Regulation 17 were illegal, unconstitutional, and violated Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), and 13(4). He alleged he was not informed of the reason for arrest, not produced before a judge, and subjected to harsh detention conditions. He also initially claimed political motivation but later withdrew this allegation.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued the detention was lawful under Regulation 17, made in good faith during a grave security emergency. They claimed the petitioner had long-standing involvement with the JVP, including during the 1971 insurgency and after its proscription, and was suspected of advising and supporting violent activities. They maintained that preventive detention was permitted under Article 15(7) and Section 5(2)(a) of the Public Security Ordinance.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that preventive detention is not 'punishment' under Article 13(4). Although Regulation 17 restricts Article 13 rights, it is permitted under Article 15(7) during a public emergency. Most of Regulation 17 is constitutional except Regulation 17(9), which unlawfully removed the right to make representations. The Court further held that judicial review is not ousted by Section 8 of the Public Security Ordinance or Regulation 17(10). Even when the Secretary’s discretion is subjective, courts can review for reasonableness, good faith, and proper grounds. While initial detention was justified, continued detention after the JVP was de-proscribed on 10 May 1988 was unreasonable and therefore unlawful.
outcome: Regulation 17 upheld except Regulation 17(9), which was declared ultra vires. The petitioner’s detention after 10 May 1988 was held unlawful as it was not justified. The Court ordered the State to pay Rs. 15,000 in compensation and Rs. 1,500 in costs.
principles_established: Preventive detention is not 'punishment' under Article 13(4).
Restrictions on Article 13 rights are valid under Article 15(7) if they relate to national security or public order.
A regulation that removes the right to make representations (Reg. 17(9)) is unconstitutional.
Emergency Regulations cannot override the Constitution (Article 155(2)).
Courts retain judicial review powers despite ouster clauses.
Subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is reviewable for reasonableness, good faith, and proper grounds.
Detention must be reassessed monthly; continued detention without fresh grounds is unlawful.
