case_title: Abeywardene v. Inspector General of Police and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection of the law.
No citizen shall be discriminated against on grounds such as political opinion.
Freedom to engage in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
Fundamental rights may be restricted by law in the interests of national security, public order, public health or morality.

legal_issue: Whether the seizure of jackpot machines under Emergency Regulations violated the petitioner's rights to equality (Articles 12(1) and 12(2)) and the freedom to engage in a lawful business (Article 14(1)(g)).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the State illegally targeted and seized his jackpot machines under the Emergency Regulations, violating his right to equal protection and discriminating against him while permitting State-run lotteries. He further claimed the Regulations were politically motivated and that his lawful business was destroyed.
respondent_argument: The State argued that the Regulations were made lawfully under the Public Security Ordinance to preserve public order and national security. Jackpot centres had become linked to crime, narcotics, terrorism, and vice. The differentiation between State lotteries and private jackpot operators was rational and permissible. Since jackpots were unlawful after the Emergency Regulations, the petitioner could not claim protection under Article 14(1)(g).
interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(1) permits reasonable classification. Distinguishing between State lotteries and private jackpot operators did not violate equality because the objectives of the Regulations—public security and public order—were legitimate. State lotteries did not contribute to criminal activity, whereas jackpot machines had become centres of illegal activity. The Regulations were valid exercises of power under the Public Security Ordinance. Emergencies are judged by the President’s subjective satisfaction, and courts cannot question the policy unless bad faith is proven. The petitioner failed to show discrimination, political victimisation, or improper purpose. Since jackpots were illegal under the Emergency Regulations, the petitioner had no protection under Article 14(1)(g).
outcome: The application was dismissed. The Court held that no violation of Articles 12(1), 12(2), or 14(1)(g) occurred. No costs were awarded.
principles_established: Equal protection allows reasonable classification if based on intelligible differentia linked to a legitimate objective.
State lotteries and private gaming operations are not similarly situated; differentiation is permissible.
Emergency Regulations made under the Public Security Ordinance are valid if they appear necessary or expedient to the President.
Courts cannot review the President’s subjective satisfaction in proclaiming an emergency unless bad faith is alleged and proved.
A person cannot claim a fundamental right to engage in an unlawful business.
Equal protection guarantees equal protection of the law, not equal violation of the law.

case_title: Amaratunga v. Sirimal and Others (Jana Ghosha Case)

clauses.text: Freedom of speech and expression, including peaceful criticism of the Government.

legal_issue: Whether disrupting the Jana Ghosha protest and preventing the petitioner from beating his drum amounted to a violation of his freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an SLFP member participating in the nationwide Jana Ghosha protest, beat a drum to express dissent. Police officers ordered him to stop, broke his drum with a rice pounder, and assaulted him. He claimed his right to peaceful political expression was unlawfully suppressed.
respondent_argument: The police argued that a large crowd was behaving violently, shouted slogans urging rioting, and formed a cordon blocking the road. They claimed they acted under Section 78(1) of the Police Ordinance to prevent a breach of the peace, and used tear gas and batons only after warnings.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that the police acted not because they feared violence or a breach of the peace, but simply because anti-government slogans were being shouted. There was no evidence of violence in the contemporaneous police notes, and the crowd was only expressing political dissent. The petitioner's drumming and clapping were forms of 'speech and expression'. Criticism of the Government is a core part of democratic life and is fully protected under Article 14(1)(a). Since the police acted without any lawful reason to stop the protest, the petitioner's fundamental right was violated.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's freedom of speech and expression was violated. The State was ordered to pay Rs. 50,000 as compensation.
principles_established: Peaceful political dissent, including loud or noisy protest, is protected speech.
Criticism of the Government is per se a permissible exercise of Article 14(1)(a).
Police can disperse a gathering only if there is a reasonable apprehension of a breach of the peace.
Drumming, clapping, and other symbolic actions constitute protected expression.
"Stifling peaceful dissent today leads to violent upheaval tomorrow" – emphasising the constitutional duty to protect free expression.

case_title: Deshapriya and Another v. Municipal Council, Nuwara Eliya and Others

clauses.text: Freedom of speech and expression, including publication.
Equal protection of the law; prohibits discrimination based on political opinion (relevant to context).

legal_issue: Whether the Mayoress’s seizure of 450 copies of the newspaper ‘Yukthiya’ amounted to an infringement of the petitioners’ freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, the Editor and Proprietor of 'Yukthiya', alleged that the Mayoress of Nuwara Eliya seized four bundles (450 copies) of the newspaper from the Lake House stall, preventing distribution in the Nuwara Eliya area. They said the seizure was politically motivated because the paper contained anti-government content.
respondent_argument: The 2nd respondent denied seizing the newspapers. She claimed she visited the stall only to inspect sanitation conditions during a routine town inspection. She said she merely instructed the stall worker to clean the premises and that the accusation was false and politically motivated.
interpretation_summary: The Court examined conflicting affidavits and held, on a balance of probabilities, that the 2nd respondent did seize the 450 copies. Her conduct was under colour of office because she acted as Mayoress in a stall owned by the Municipal Council. The motive was political: she attempted to suppress an anti-government newspaper and even threatened the cancellation of the Lake House agency. The Court explained that freedom of speech includes the right to publish and distribute newspapers. Suppression of distribution—even in a small area—constitutes an infringement. Political motivation aggravates the violation, as it undermines democracy by discouraging dissent. The Mayoress also attempted to use the influence of Lake House (75% government-owned) to reinforce suppression, further aggravating the violation.
outcome: The Court held that the petitioners’ freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a) was violated. The 2nd respondent (Mayoress) was personally ordered to pay Rs. 100,000 in compensation and Rs. 10,000 in costs.
principles_established: Freedom of speech includes the right to publish and distribute newspapers.
Suppression of anti-government publication, even in a limited area or small number of copies, constitutes an infringement of Article 14(1)(a).
Executive action includes acts done 'under colour of office', even if officials misuse public authority for political ends.
Political motive makes the violation more serious, especially when state-controlled media power (e.g., Lake House) is used or threatened.
Democracy requires encouraging—not suppressing—dissent and criticism of the government.

case_title: Fernando v. The Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation and Others

clauses.text: Freedom of speech and expression, including publication.
Freedom of thought (discussed as the possible basis for a general right to receive information, but not decided in this case).

legal_issue: Whether the sudden stoppage of the SLBC Non-Formal Education Programme (NFEP) infringed the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, including publication, under Article 14(1)(a), especially in his capacity as a participatory listener.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a retired teacher, trade unionist, and election-monitoring activist, regularly listened to and participated in SLBC’s Non-Formal Education Programme (NFEP) by taking part in discussions and asking live questions on topics such as human rights, current affairs and ethnic issues. On 6 February 1995, during the ‘Kamkaru Prajawa’ programme which discussed a labour dispute and included a live phone interview with Minister C. V. Gooneratne, the programme was suddenly cut off and music was broadcast instead. Thereafter, the NFEP was effectively stopped or reduced to a mere pretence. The petitioner alleged that this arbitrary stoppage violated his freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
respondent_argument: The SLBC (1st respondent) and its Chairman (2nd respondent) argued that stopping the NFEP was justified for several reasons: (1) some programmes were no longer educational or relevant to non-formal education (including ‘Pasu Vimasuma’, ‘Puvath Adahorawa’, ‘Subharathi’ and the ‘Kamkaru Prajawa’ programme); (2) the content allegedly exposed SLBC and its management to potential civil and criminal defamation; (3) staff were using the NFEP to criticise SLBC management and to seek public support, which was said to be inappropriate and an internal matter; and (4) public complaints showed discontent with NFEP. They also suggested the issue was one of programme restructuring and management policy and that the petitioner, as a listener, had no independent fundamental-right claim.
interpretation_summary:
The Court first found that NFEP was a serious, structured, regular educational service with wide listener participation, not a casual set of programmes. It accepted that the petitioner had actively participated as a listener-speaker. The Court examined the reasons given for stopping NFEP and held that all four grounds lacked merit. Discussion of the peace talks, government media policy, labour disputes and criticism of SLBC management were legitimate matters of public interest and non-formal education. Nothing shown from the cited broadcasts was defamatory; telephone contributions were screened; any problems could have been dealt with by guidance or replacing particular programmes, not by killing the entire NFEP. The sudden stoppage, especially immediately after critical programmes, showed undue haste and lack of bona fides.

On the legal side, the Court explained that Article 14(1)(a) must not be interpreted narrowly. It covers all forms of expression and can work together with other rights like equality. It may also include implied rights necessary to make freedom of speech meaningful, such as the right to obtain and record information through interviews, recordings, publications and similar methods, and arguably a privilege to protect sources where needed. However, Fernando J. expressed doubt that Article 14(1)(a) goes so far as to protect a general right to information ‘simpliciter’ for mere private curiosity. The Court reviewed foreign and local cases on whether listeners or readers have rights, and distinguished between (a) a general right to receive information (which it did not finally accept under Article 14(1)(a)), and (b) the specific position of someone who uses a broadcast to communicate his own views.

The Court held that the petitioner was not just a passive listener but a ‘participatory listener’ who used NFEP as a platform to express his ideas and ask questions. Stopping NFEP arbitrarily prevented his further participation and therefore directly interfered with his own exercise of freedom of speech and expression. Even if the producers themselves did not come to court, the petitioner’s Article 14(1)(a) right as a participatory contributor had been infringed by the 1st and 2nd respondents.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the sudden stoppage of the NFEP was arbitrary and unjustified. It declared that the 1st respondent (SLBC) and 2nd respondent (Chairman) had infringed the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 14(1)(a). Considering that the 1995 NFEP schedule had already expired and that the legal question was a first-time issue, the Court did not order resumption of the programme. Instead, it ordered the 1st respondent to pay the petitioner Rs. 15,000 as compensation and Rs. 5,000 as costs.
principles_established: Article 14(1)(a) should be interpreted broadly; it covers every form of expression and may require recognising implied rights necessary to make free speech effective (such as obtaining and recording information).

There is a distinction between a general right to receive information ‘simpliciter’ (which the Court doubted existed under Article 14(1)(a)) and the specific rights of a person who uses a medium to express his own views.

A ‘participatory listener’ who actively contributes to a broadcast (through questions, discussions, etc.) exercises his own freedom of speech; arbitrary removal of that platform can infringe his Article 14(1)(a) rights.
State broadcasting frequencies are a public resource; state broadcasters like SLBC carry a heightened obligation to respect and facilitate public discussion, especially on matters of public interest.

Criticism of public institutions, including the broadcaster itself and government policies, is a legitimate part of media freedom and cannot be suppressed merely because it is uncomfortable or politically inconvenient.
Administrative or management reasons cannot be used as a pretext for arbitrarily silencing programmes that encourage critical, informed public debate consistent with stated government media policy.

case_title: Karunathilaka and Another v. Dayananda Dissanayake, Commissioner of Elections and Others
judges: G. P. S. de Silva, C.J.

clauses.text: Right to equality and equal protection of the law.
Freedom of speech and expression, which the Court held includes the act of voting.

legal_issue: Whether the cancellation of the Provincial Council election date through an Emergency Regulation, and the subsequent failure to fix a new date, violated the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a).
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, registered voters, alleged that their rights were violated when: (1) the date of poll for five Provincial Councils (fixed for 28.08.1998) was cancelled through an Emergency Regulation issued on 04.08.1998; (2) postal voting scheduled for 04.08.1998 was unlawfully and arbitrarily suspended on 03.08.1998 without reasons; and (3) the Commissioner of Elections failed to fix a fresh date of poll under Section 22(6). They argued that the delay in holding elections infringed their equality rights and their freedom of expression — since the act of voting is a form of political expression.
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the Emergency Proclamation and Regulation were validly made under the Public Security Ordinance and therefore compelled the Commissioner to refrain from continuing the electoral process. They contended that the postponement affected all five Provincial Councils equally and therefore did not constitute discrimination. They also argued that Article 14(1)(a) does not cover the right to vote, and that under Article 35 the President’s actions could not be reviewed.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 35 (Presidential immunity) does not bar judicial review of executive action where the President's act is relied upon by another official to justify their conduct. The Court further held that section 8 of the Public Security Ordinance does not oust the Court’s constitutional jurisdiction under Article 126. The impugned Emergency Regulation was found invalid because it was not truly an emergency regulation within section 5 — it merely acted as an order suspending statutory notices, without any security-related justification. The Court held that the suspension of postal voting on 03.08.1998 was unlawful, arbitrary, not bona fide, and likely done with foreknowledge of the impending Emergency Regulation. The Commissioner had full power under section 22(6) to fix a new date of poll irrespective of whether the Regulation was valid, but failed to do so. This failure resulted in discriminatory treatment because elections for the North Western Provincial Council (dissolved later) were allowed to proceed while the earlier five were indefinitely delayed. Regarding Article 14(1)(a), the Court held that voting is a protected form of political expression. Casting a vote is a silent but powerful expression of political preference and therefore falls within the freedom of speech and expression.
outcome: The Court declared that the 1st to 13th respondents violated the petitioners’ rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a). The Court ordered the Commissioner of Elections to fix: (a) new dates for issuing postal ballot papers within two weeks, and (b) new dates of poll within three months. Costs of Rs. 30,000 were awarded to the petitioners. No compensation was awarded because it had not been requested.
principles_established: Presidential immunity under Article 35 does not shield acts from judicial review; it only bars proceedings against the President personally.
The Supreme Court retains jurisdiction under Article 126 to review emergency regulations despite section 8 of the PSO.
Emergency regulations must be legislative in character and must fall within the purposes of section 5 of the PSO; arbitrary cancellation of election dates is invalid.
Voting is a form of political expression protected by Article 14(1)(a).
The Commissioner of Elections has a constitutional duty of independence and must act to ensure elections occur lawfully and without undue delay.
Section 22(6) must be interpreted broadly: any emergency or unforeseen circumstance—lawful or unlawful—permits fixing a new date of poll.
Indefinite postponement of elections and preferential treatment of voters in different provinces violate Article 12(1).

case_title: Bernard Soysa and Two Others v. The Attorney-General and Two Others

clauses.text: Freedom of speech and expression.
Freedom of peaceful assembly.

legal_issue: Whether the police violated the petitioners’ fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly by dispersing a Satyagraha held at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, leaders of recognized political parties, claimed that they gathered with about 300 supporters to hold a peaceful Satyagraha and picket on 15 December 1990. They alleged that the police unlawfully assaulted and dispersed them in the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa, thereby violating their rights under Article 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b). They insisted that the Maha Maluwa was a public place where no permission was required.
respondent_argument: The police argued that the Maha Maluwa belonged to the Dalada Maligawa and was under the authority of the Diyawadana Nilame, and therefore not open for political demonstrations without permission. They asserted that the petitioners and supporters behaved in an unruly manner, shouted slogans, disturbed the religious atmosphere, and refused police instructions to disperse. They also stated that the Diyawadana Nilame specifically requested police intervention due to disturbance.
interpretation_summary: The Court held that although the public had physical access to the Maha Maluwa for religious worship and leisure, such access did not amount to a legal right to use it for political events. Political demonstrations or Satyagrahas in such a religious precinct required express permission of the Diyawadana Nilame. The Court emphasized that freedom of speech and assembly is subject to restrictions for public order. The gathering, even if intended as peaceful, became disruptive in a sensitive religious environment. Under Sections 95 and 97 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and Section 56 of the Police Ordinance, the police were entitled to disperse assemblies likely to disturb public peace. The Court found that the police acted bona fide to preserve order and prevent disturbance near a sacred religious site.
outcome: Application dismissed. The Court held that the petitioners had no right to conduct a Satyagraha in the Maha Maluwa without permission, the assembly was not peaceful, and the police lawfully dispersed the gathering. No fundamental rights under Article 14(1)(a) or 14(1)(b) were infringed.
principles_established: Public access to a religious premises does not create a right to conduct political demonstrations there.
Freedom of speech and assembly is subject to restrictions necessary for maintaining public order.
Police are legally empowered to disperse gatherings likely to disturb public peace, especially near religious sites.
Express permission is required to hold political events in sensitive religious precincts.
Prior use of a location for demonstrations does not create a prescriptive right to hold similar events in the future.
precedents_cited: Whitney v. California (1927) 274 U.S. 357
Schenck v. U.S. (1949) 249 U.S. 47
Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators’ Association (1983) 460 U.S. 37
Railway Board v. Niranjan Singh (1969) 1 SCC 502
source: Supreme Court judgment, pages 56–67.

case_title: Victor Ivon v. Sarath N. Silva, Attorney General and Another

clauses.text: Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law.
Freedom of speech and expression, including publication.
Freedom to engage in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

legal_issue: Whether the Attorney General, in deciding to indict the petitioner for criminal defamation, exercised his statutory discretion arbitrarily, for collateral purposes, or in a discriminatory manner, thereby infringing the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(g).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Editor of the ‘Ravaya’ newspaper, argued that the Attorney General (AG) and/or his officers had indiscriminately and arbitrarily indicted him for several offences of criminal defamation in the High Court. He claimed this was done without proper assessment of the facts, for collateral purposes, and in disregard of constitutional protections of journalists. He relied on a pattern of prosecutions (six indictments in all, including two new ones in 1998) and ‘Ravaya’ articles critical of the AG’s Department, to allege bias and victimisation. He contended that these decisions violated his right to equality (Art. 12(1)), his freedom of speech and expression including publication as a journalist (Art. 14(1)(a)), and his freedom to engage in his lawful profession as an editor (Art. 14(1)(g)).
respondent_argument: The Attorney General, represented by counsel, maintained that the decisions to grant sanction and to indict for criminal defamation were made within the lawful statutory discretion conferred by the Code of Criminal Procedure and were based on the evidence in each complaint. They emphasized that the AG had also refused or declined to act on nine other complaints of criminal defamation against the petitioner, showing that he was not targeting the ‘Ravaya’ editor. The respondents contended that the indictments in issue – particularly those involving alleged defamation of the Inspector General of Police and a former Minister of Fisheries – raised matters of public interest (such as public confidence in law enforcement and in the conduct of a Ministry) and therefore justified State-led prosecutions. They denied any arbitrary or discriminatory exercise of power and argued that the High Court was the proper forum to challenge the indictments, not by way of a fundamental rights application.
interpretation_summary:
The Court first analysed the nature of the Attorney General’s discretion in criminal defamation cases. Under Sections 135 and 393 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the AG has: (i) discretion to grant or refuse sanction for prosecution (without which no private or police prosecution can commence), and (ii) discretion either to allow a summary trial or to direct non-summary proceedings and/or file an indictment in the High Court. Fernando J. held that this is a statutory discretion amounting to ‘executive or administrative action’, not legislative or judicial action, and hence is in principle subject to review under Article 126 when a fundamental right is alleged to be infringed. The Court stressed that the AG’s discretion is neither absolute nor unfettered. It may be abused, for example, if exercised without investigation, on plainly insufficient evidence, or on constitutionally impermissible grounds such as political bias or unequal treatment of similar offenders or complainants. The Court illustrated with hypotheticals: granting sanction based on a single unreliable witness with no investigation, or selectively granting sanction only against members of one political party. Such uses of discretion could violate equality (Articles 12(1) or 12(2)) and be reviewable.

However, the Court also emphasised that the AG’s power to file an indictment is held in trust for the public and must be exercised in the public interest, not merely to benefit an individual complainant. The State should bear the burden of criminal prosecution only where there is some distinct public interest (for example, allegations likely to disrupt racial or religious harmony, undermine international relations, or seriously erode public confidence in law and order or justice).

On the jurisdiction point, the Court held that the existence of pending High Court indictments does not oust the Supreme Court’s fundamental rights jurisdiction. The High Court cannot review the antecedent decision to indict for conformity with fundamental rights. Nonetheless, the Supreme Court will exercise its power with caution where parallel proceedings are pending.

Applying these principles, the Court examined the particular indictments. In the case alleging defamation of the Inspector General of Police, there was an actual complaint by the IGP, and the impugned article alleged interference with an investigation into sexual abuse of children. State counsel had before them denials by the IGP, suspects and investigating officer, but the petitioner provided no material to substantiate his serious allegations. The Court accepted that this could affect public confidence in law enforcement and therefore justified an indictment in the public interest. In the case involving the former Minister of Fisheries, there were specific allegations of serious corruption. Although there were later official reports relevant to one allegation, these had not been before the AG at the time; the lapse lay in investigation rather than in the AG’s decision. Even if one allegation might be true, there was no material at all supporting two other specific allegations, so prosecution on at least those aspects could not be called arbitrary. The Court also noted that earlier indictments had been withdrawn in circumstances not suggesting abuse, and that during the same period the AG had refused to act on nine other complaints against the petitioner.

The Court rejected the argument that newspaper editors or journalists should enjoy a higher threshold against prosecution or special immunity. The freedom of the press is part of the general freedom of speech and expression enjoyed by ‘everyone alike’, and while the press may play a vital role in exposing corruption, that does not entitle it to defame without responsibility. Ultimately, the Court found no prima facie evidence that the AG’s decisions to indict in these two cases were arbitrary, discriminatory, or aimed at suppressing the petitioner’s expression or profession.
outcome: Leave to proceed refused. The Supreme Court held that although the Attorney General’s discretion to sanction and to indict for criminal defamation is reviewable under the fundamental rights jurisdiction, the petitioner failed to establish a prima facie case that this discretion had been exercised arbitrarily, discriminatorily, or for a collateral purpose in the two indictments in question. No violation of Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) or 14(1)(g) was disclosed on the material before the Court.
principles_established: The Attorney General’s power to grant sanction for prosecution and to file an indictment is a discretionary power amounting to executive or administrative action and is, in principle, reviewable under Article 126 where a fundamental right is alleged to be infringed.

That discretion is neither absolute nor unfettered. It must not be exercised on plainly insufficient evidence, without proper investigation, or on impermissible grounds such as political bias or unequal treatment of similarly situated persons.

The mere fact that High Court proceedings are pending on an indictment does not bar the Supreme Court from exercising its fundamental rights jurisdiction, although the Court will proceed with caution in such situations.

The State’s decision to conduct a criminal defamation prosecution at public expense should be based on a distinct public interest (e.g. serious impact on public confidence or public order), not simply on private vindication of reputation.

Press freedom is not a separate fundamental right but falls within the general guarantee of freedom of speech and expression; journalists and editors enjoy the same protection as other citizens but also the same responsibilities and exposure to criminal law.

Errors or omissions in investigation or prosecution do not, by themselves, prove arbitrariness or a fundamental rights violation; there must be evidence of improper motive, discrimination, or manifest unreasonableness.
source: Supreme Court judgment, pages 340–350.

case_title: Mrs. W. M. K. De Silva v. Chairman, Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

legal_issue: Whether the treatment of the petitioner by the Chairman and the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, after she gave evidence to a Presidential Commission, amounted to (i) torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment contrary to Article 11, and/or (ii) a violation of her freedom to engage in a lawful occupation under Article 14(1)(g), and/or (iii) a denial of equality and equal protection under Article 12(1).
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Secretary to the Board and Personal Assistant to the Chairman of the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, gave a statement in February 1987 to the CID Unit of a Special Presidential Commission regarding an irregular rebate on a urea supply contract. She alleged that, because she refused to take responsibility for an ‘omission’ in the minutes and because she testified against the Chairman, he and the Board turned against her: she was sent on compulsory leave, and when recalled with effect from 01.01.1988 she was not given her former duties or cubicle, was given no work, was made to sit in a verandah on a broken chair at a broken table, at times was locked out, and was publicly humiliated and isolated in front of colleagues. She claimed that this course of conduct between 01.01.1988 and 19.01.1988 amounted to mental torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in violation of Article 11 and that she was effectively denied continuity of employment and her freedom to be engaged in her chosen occupation in violation of Article 14(1)(g). She also alleged unequal treatment under Article 12(1), especially in the preference shown to another officer (Noel Fernando) for the post of Secretary to the Board.
respondent_argument: The respondents (Chairman and Corporation) contended that the petitioner's treatment, though she may be dissatisfied, did not reach the level of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 11. They argued that any grievances she had were in the realm of contractual and labour rights, not fundamental rights, and that the Corporation, being a trading body engaged in importing, mixing and selling fertilizer in competition with other entities, was not engaging in 'executive or administrative action' in the relevant dealings with her. They denied any unlawful discrimination under Article 12(1) and maintained that she had no fundamental right to a particular post or to be assigned particular duties under Article 14(1)(g).
interpretation_summary:
On the facts, the Court accepted that there had been a serious breakdown in the relationship between the petitioner and the Chairman, largely arising from an irregular price reduction on a urea contract and a disputed Board ‘decision’ of 29.11.1985. The petitioner refused to sign any document taking responsibility for an ‘omission’ in the minutes and later gave evidence about the rebate to a Presidential Commission. Thereafter she was placed on compulsory leave, later recalled, but given no work and subjected to degrading treatment (made to sit outside on a verandah, with a broken chair and table, and at times locked out). Jameel J. held that this conduct undoubtedly amounted to a grossly unfair labour practice and a breach of contractual expectations, but fell short of the high threshold required for ‘torture’ or ‘cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment’ under Article 11. The acts were not ‘torture’ or ‘punishment’ in the constitutional sense and lacked the severity of mental or physical coercion or viciousness demanded by Article 11.

Amerasinghe J. gave an important general interpretation of Article 11. He held that Article 11 is not limited to physical violence: it covers both physical and mental pain or suffering. He adopted international materials (e.g. the UN Declaration on the Protection of All Persons from Being Subjected to Torture) and local case law to state that Article 11 prohibits any act by which severe physical or mental pain or suffering is intentionally inflicted by a public official, acting in an executive or administrative capacity or under colour of office, for purposes such as obtaining a confession or information, imposing a penalty for an offence or breach of a rule, or intimidating or coercing the person (or a third party) to do or refrain from doing something the official believes ought to be done. He stressed that Article 11 belongs to the group of rights protecting life and personal freedom (alongside Article 13 on arrest, detention and punishment) and is not aimed at disputes about contractual rights at the workplace. Even if the Chairman’s conduct amounted to constructive dismissal or justified repudiation of the contract, that is a matter for labour or civil remedies, not for Article 11. The petitioner failed to show that the humiliation she suffered was imposed for a constitutionally relevant ‘punishment’ purpose or as part of the kind of coercive state action that Article 11 targets.

On Article 14(1)(g), the Court reaffirmed earlier dicta (especially Elmore Perera v. Jayawickrema) that the freedom ‘to engage in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise’ is a general right to pursue work of a chosen kind, not a right to hold a particular job, occupy a particular post, or be employed by a particular employer. Amerasinghe J. explained that Article 14(1)(g) recognises the citizen’s right to use their mental and physical powers in any lawful calling, but does not impose an obligation on any employer to provide a particular kind of work or continued employment; even the question whether there is a contractual right to be given work (as distinct from wages) is a matter of ordinary labour law, not constitutional law. Since the petitioner was not prevented from engaging in any lawful occupation elsewhere, and remained on the payroll, her Article 14(1)(g) right was not infringed, even though she was not assigned duties and may have had a contractual claim.

Regarding Article 12(1), the Court held that not every breach of contract or unfair treatment becomes a violation of equality or equal protection. The petitioner had not proved that she was subjected to unequal or selective treatment in the constitutionally relevant sense (such as discriminatory treatment vis-à-vis similarly situated persons), so no breach of Article 12(1) was made out. Jameel J. also noted that, following Wijeratne v. People’s Bank, the Corporation’s conduct in its trading functions does not amount to ‘executive or administrative action’, which is a threshold requirement for a fundamental rights application under Article 126.

In summary, the Court drew a clear line between serious, purpose-driven, coercive State ill-treatment covered by Article 11 and ordinary (even very unfair) employment disputes; and between the general freedom to choose an occupation under Article 14(1)(g) and any supposed right to a specific job, duties, or workplace.
outcome: Application dismissed. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s treatment, though degrading and amounting to an unfair labour practice, did not constitute torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment under Article 11, did not violate her freedom to engage in a lawful occupation under Article 14(1)(g), and did not amount to unconstitutional discrimination under Article 12(1). The case was dismissed without costs, in view of the special circumstances.
principles_established: Article 11 applies to both physical and mental pain or suffering, but only where severe pain or suffering is intentionally inflicted by or at the instigation of a public official, for specific purposes such as extracting information or confessions, imposing penalties for offences, or coercing or intimidating a person. Not every form of workplace humiliation or unfair treatment meets this standard.

Article 11 is part of the broader group of rights protecting life and personal liberty (alongside protections against arbitrary arrest, detention and punishment). It is not aimed at resolving contractual employment disputes or unfair labour practices, even if such conduct is very harsh.

Ill-treatment, whether physical or mental, must reach a very high degree of severity to qualify as ‘cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment’ under Article 11; mere humiliation, unfairness, or constructive dismissal, without the requisite severity and purpose, does not suffice.

Article 14(1)(g) recognises a general freedom to engage in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise. It does not guarantee a right to hold a specific job, to occupy a particular post, to be employed by a particular employer, or to be assigned particular work.

A breach of contractual or labour rights does not automatically amount to a violation of Article 12(1). To invoke equality or equal protection, a petitioner must show constitutionally relevant discrimination or selective treatment, not just unfairness.

Where a public corporation is acting in its trading or commercial capacity, its conduct may not constitute ‘executive or administrative action’ for the purposes of Article 126; purely contractual employment issues in such bodies will ordinarily fall outside fundamental rights jurisdiction.

case_title: Herath Banda v. Sub Inspector of Police, Wasgiyawatte Police Station and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

legal_issue: Whether, after leave to proceed has been granted on an alleged violation of Article 11 due to a brutal police assault, the petitioner can be permitted to withdraw the fundamental rights application on the ground that he has ‘settled his differences’ with the police officer; and whether, in such circumstances, the Court should nevertheless proceed to determine and declare a violation of Article 11.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that on 28 May 1993 the first respondent, a Sub Inspector of Police, came to his home, ordered him to accompany him to the police station, and when he sought an explanation, addressed him in rude terms, slapped him, dragged him out, and beat him all over his body with a thick stick taken from his garden fence until he lost consciousness. He was taken to Polpitigama Government Hospital, then admitted to Kurunegala Government Hospital and examined by the Judicial Medical Officer, treated for five days, then transferred to Ehetuwewa Government Hospital for two days, and thereafter treated by an Ayurvedic physician. He claimed that as a result of the assault he was bedridden. He sought a declaration that his fundamental right under Article 11 had been violated and claimed Rs. 200,000 as compensation.
respondent_argument: On the hearing date, the respondents were initially absent and unrepresented. Later, the Deputy Solicitor General, appearing to assist the Court, did not argue for withdrawal on the basis of a private settlement. Instead, he submitted, relying on Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax, that an application alleging a violation of fundamental rights is not a purely private dispute which the parties may freely settle or withdraw at will, especially where an alleged violation of Article 11 is concerned. No substantive contradiction of the assault facts was placed before the Court; the question was principally whether the petition could be withdrawn.
interpretation_summary:
After leave to proceed had been granted and a medical examination ordered, the matter was fixed for argument. On 24 August 1993, counsel for the petitioner moved to withdraw the application on the basis that the petitioner had ‘settled his differences with the police officer’. The Court, concerned with the nature of fundamental rights proceedings, adjourned and requested the assistance of the Attorney General on whether such withdrawal should be allowed.

Amerasinghe J., delivering judgment, agreed with the Deputy Solicitor General that applications relating to fundamental rights are not ordinary private matters that parties can dispose of purely by settlement or withdrawal, particularly in relation to Article 11. However, he declined to adopt a rigid rule based on the ‘importance’ of particular rights. He noted that while Article 11 has special distinguishing features (as earlier recognised in Velmurugu), the question of allowing withdrawal must be considered case by case. The Court has an absolute discretion whether to permit withdrawal, and hundreds of fundamental rights applications are in fact withdrawn each term, depending on circumstances.

In this case, the medical material before the Court clearly supported the petitioner’s allegations of a brutal assault by the Sub Inspector. The petition itself stated that attempts had been made to prevent him from seeking redress in Court. Against that background, and given the seriousness of the alleged police ill-treatment and the public character of Article 11, the Court viewed the ‘change of heart’ and request to withdraw with suspicion. It refused the request to withdraw the application, holding that it would not be appropriate to allow the matter to be terminated on the basis of a private ‘settlement’ between victim and alleged violator of a fundamental right.

The Court then proceeded to decide the merits. On the uncontroverted facts and the supporting medical evidence, it held that the petitioner’s right under Article 11 of the Constitution had been violated by the conduct of the first respondent. However, since counsel informed the Court that the petitioner had ‘settled’ his ‘differences’ with the police officer, the Court did not award compensation. Instead, it focused on public accountability and remedial action within the police. It directed the Inspector General of Police to investigate the complaint against the officer, to take such action as deemed appropriate, and to report back to the Court by a specified date, forwarding certified copies of the petition, affidavits and medical reports.

Thus, the judgment emphasises that fundamental rights proceedings serve a public interest in policing State power and cannot always be treated as a private bargaining chip. Even where a petitioner wishes to withdraw after a settlement, the Court may refuse withdrawal, declare a violation, and order follow-up action in the public interest, particularly in serious Article 11 cases involving police brutality.
outcome: Request to withdraw the petition was refused. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 11 had been violated by the brutal assault. No compensation was awarded in light of the petitioner’s reported settlement with the police officer. The Inspector General of Police was directed to investigate the complaint against the officer and to report to the Court on the action taken.
principles_established: Applications regarding fundamental rights are not merely private disputes between individuals; they implicate public interest in the control of State power and the vindication of constitutional guarantees.

Leave to withdraw a fundamental rights application is a matter within the absolute discretion of the Supreme Court. Each case must be assessed on its own circumstances; there is no automatic right to withdraw once leave to proceed has been granted.

The Court will be especially cautious about allowing withdrawal where serious violations such as alleged torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 11 are involved, particularly if there is evidence of pressure or attempts to prevent the petitioner from seeking redress.

Even if a victim ‘settles’ with the alleged violator, the Court may still refuse withdrawal, declare that a fundamental right has been violated, and order institutional action (such as directing the IGP to investigate), shifting focus from purely compensatory relief to systemic accountability.

The seriousness of Article 11 violations, supported by medical evidence, can justify the Court in proceeding ex mero motu to declare a violation and order follow-up measures, regardless of the petitioner’s later change of heart about pursuing the case.
precedents_cited: Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax AIR 1959 SC 149
Velmurugu v. The Attorney General and another (1981) 1 FRD 180
source: Supreme Court judgment, pages 324–326.

case_title: Nalika Kumudini, Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of Malsha Kumari) v. Nihal Mahinda, O.I.C. Hungama Police and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law, and shall not be further held in custody except upon and in terms of the order of such judge.

legal_issue: Whether the 14-year-old girl, Malsha Kumari, was unlawfully arrested and detained and subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment by officers of the Hungama Police (including the OIC), thereby infringing her fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1) and 13(2); whether the application was out of time under Article 126(2); and what effective relief and compensation should be granted.
petitioner_claim: On 5 September 1995, 14-year-old Malsha Kumari was arrested at home by two policemen from Hungama Police, accused of stealing a gold chain, money, rings and other items from a neighbour (Kirthiraja). She says she had only picked up a small red glass box with a chain from the roadside. At home and then at the neighbour’s house she was beaten with sticks, dragged and slapped. At the police station she was beaten with a hose pipe, slapped and trampled by the 1st respondent, the OIC. Later, at the neighbour’s house, her hands were tied behind her back, and she was hung from a kohomba tree with a rope while the OIC and several other officers beat her with a hose pipe and a stick. She sustained injuries to her body, spine, and wrists (encircling marks like bangles) and vomited blood, needed admission to hospital at Tangalla and then Matara, and continued to suffer pain, dizziness and reduced vision. She was not produced before a Magistrate. She and her mother also alleged that afterwards the OIC tried to pressure them with threats and offers of money to withdraw complaints, and used a JP to get the mother’s signature on a document. She sought declarations of violation of Articles 11, 13(1) and 13(2), and compensation of Rs. 200,000.
respondent_argument: The 1st respondent denied arresting or detaining the girl or having her at the police station on that day and denied any assault. He relied on affidavits from the neighbour Kirthiraja, another villager (Hinniappuhamy), and Police Sergeant Sumanapala. Their version was that the neighbour lost his chain on the road, later heard the petitioner had picked something up, and complained to Hungama Police. PS Sumanapala alone went to the petitioner’s house at about 5 p.m., questioned her, and the father slapped her, whereupon she ran and fell into a stone quarry, sustaining minor injuries. She then voluntarily brought the chain from where she had hidden it; the chain was identified and returned to the owner who did not want legal action, so the constable only ‘severely warned’ the girl and recorded her statement. Later cries heard from her house were, they said, due to further beating by the father. The petition was also challenged as time-barred, since, according to the 1st respondent, it could have been filed between 16 September and 16 October 1995 but was filed only on 9 November 1995. The father also filed an affidavit stating that the signature on the original letter of complaint to the human rights organisation was not his, and later the police claimed that the family did not wish to proceed as the officers had apologised and agreed to pay costs.
interpretation_summary:
The application was filed by an Attorney-at-Law on 9 November 1995, based on a letter purportedly from the girl’s father. On 15 November 1995, the Supreme Court excused delay and indicated the minor must be properly represented and admissible evidence filed. On 18 January 1996, counsel sought to withdraw, saying the family no longer wished to proceed because the police had apologised and agreed to pay costs; counsel himself felt this change of attitude was due to pressure. Given the seriousness of the allegations, the hospitalization, and continuing treatment and impaired sight, the Court refused to allow withdrawal and granted leave, emphasising its earlier view that, particularly in torture cases, withdrawal cannot lightly be permitted.

The girl and her mother later came to Colombo and gave detailed instructions to Lawyers for Human Rights and Development, resulting in draft affidavits (X5, X6) describing the arrest, assaults, hanging from the tree, and subsequent medical treatment. Because of threats and intimidation from the 1st respondent and other Hungama police officers, they did not initially sign them. However, in October 1996 they filed sworn affidavits adopting those drafts, and the Court appointed the mother as guardian ad litem. The 1st respondent did not file any reply to these later affidavits, and no complaint of lack of opportunity to respond was made.

Fernando A.C.J. treated the draft affidavits as incorporated into the sworn affidavits and accepted them as evidence, together with the contemporaneous statement given to Tangalla Police on 6 September 1995 and the medical records. The Court noted some minor inconsistencies between the statement and later affidavits (e.g. whether anyone saw her pick up the box), but held such lapses were understandable given the trauma.

By contrast, the Court found serious contradictions and weaknesses in the affidavits and notes of inquiry produced by the 1st respondent. These included unexplained delay in the neighbour’s complaint, lack of detail about the informant who allegedly saw the girl pick up the chain, inconsistent accounts of how and where the chain was recovered, the absence of identifying marks in the original statement despite the later claim that such marks were recorded, and the police claim that the father alone caused the injuries without any follow-up investigation against him. These discrepancies made the police version improbable.

The decisive factor was the unchallenged medical finding that on 6 September 1995 the girl had two-inch-wide injuries encircling both wrists “like a bangle”. This was wholly inconsistent with the story of a fall into a quarry and a few blows from her father, but perfectly consistent with her account of having her hands tied behind her back and being suspended from a tree. The Court therefore rejected the police version and accepted the petitioner’s account that she was arrested without proper basis, detained without production before a Magistrate, and subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment by the 1st respondent and other officers, with the 1st respondent playing a leading role.

On the time-bar objection, the Court reconsidered the issue despite its earlier ex parte order, holding that natural justice required hearing the 1st respondent. It emphasised that the right to file a fundamental rights application within one month itself is a fundamental right under Article 17, but that the one-month period in Article 126(2) must run only during a time when the petitioner is free of any disability caused by the infringement, and genuinely free to take legal steps. Where the same wrongdoer causes a physical or practical incapacity (through injuries, hospitalization, or threats) that prevents filing within a month, the principle lex non cogit ad impossibilia applies: a violator cannot escape liability by incapacitating the victim for more than one month. The petitioner, a minor, remained physically and psychologically affected, vomiting blood and undergoing repeated admissions, and under the shadow of police threats. On those facts, which were uncontroverted, the Court held she filed within one month of being free of the disabling effects of the violations and overruled the time-bar objection.

On the merits, the Court held that the 1st respondent acquiesced in and condoned the unlawful arrest and loss of liberty, was responsible for unjustified detention without production before a Magistrate, and subjected the girl to torture to extract an admission and recover property. Her rights under Articles 11, 13(1) and 13(2) were infringed. The torture was prolonged, its consequences serious, and the 1st respondent later attempted, by threats and by influencing proceedings in MC Hambantota 25528, to deter her from pursuing legal remedies.

As to relief, the Court noted that in many prior cases it had urged the Inspector-General of Police to prevent such violations and had sometimes ordered disciplinary action, but the institutional response had not inspired confidence in the effectiveness of such directions. That persuaded the Court that here monetary compensation was the most appropriate form of effective redress. It ordered the State to pay Rs. 150,000 as compensation (to be placed in a fixed deposit in the National Savings Bank, with monthly interest payable to the mother for the child’s benefit, and the capital accessible to the girl on attaining majority), and ordered the 1st respondent personally to pay Rs. 50,000 in five monthly instalments of Rs. 10,000 (one for immediate welfare, the remaining four also to be deposited for her future). The State was additionally ordered to pay Rs. 5,000 as costs. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to ensure that neither the petitioner nor her family were harassed or interfered with by Hungama Police. The Court also commented critically on the security-for-peace proceedings in MC Hambantota 25528, which appeared to be used to harass the petitioner, and directed the Magistrate’s record to be returned and a copy of its order sent to the Judicial Service Commission.
outcome: Relief granted. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1) and 13(2) had been violated by the 1st respondent and other Hungama police officers. The time-bar objection was overruled. The State was ordered to pay Rs. 150,000 as compensation (to be held in fixed deposit for the minor, with interest to the mother), and the 1st respondent was ordered personally to pay Rs. 50,000 in five monthly instalments, mostly to be similarly deposited. The State was also ordered to pay Rs. 5,000 as costs. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to prevent further harassment of the petitioner and her family.
principles_established: Severe physical ill-treatment, including tying a child’s hands, suspending her from a tree, and beating her to extract an admission, constitutes torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of Article 11.
Arresting a minor without lawful basis, detaining her, and failing to produce her before a Magistrate amounts to violations of Articles 13(1) and 13(2).

The one-month time limit in Article 126(2) runs only during a period in which the victim is free of the disability caused by the violation and is genuinely free to take legal steps; if the wrongdoer’s acts (e.g. injuries, hospitalization, threats) prevent timely filing, they cannot rely on the time bar. The law does not compel impossibilities (lex non cogit ad impossibilia).
Minority is relevant when assessing whether the impact of coercion, injury, or threats has worn off for the purpose of the time-limit analysis.

Fundamental rights petitions, particularly in torture cases, cannot be treated as ordinary private disputes to be withdrawn at will after a ‘settlement’; the Court may refuse withdrawal and continue to adjudicate in the public interest.

Where repeated judicial directions to the police hierarchy to prevent fundamental rights violations have proved ineffective, substantial monetary compensation may be the most appropriate form of effective relief.
The Supreme Court may scrutinize parallel lower-court proceedings (e.g. security-for-peace applications) to ensure they are not being used to harass a fundamental rights petitioner.
A police officer’s personal liability to pay compensation can be ordered in addition to State liability, reinforcing individual accountability for fundamental rights violations.
precedents_cited: Lakshman v. Fernando, S.C. 324/90, S.C. Minutes 29.09.1995
Premadasa v. Officer in Charge of the Hakmana Police, S.C. 127/94, S.C. Minutes 10.03.1995
source: Supreme Court judgment, pages 331–343.

case_title: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture, or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner, while under arrest and in police custody at Panadura Police Station, was subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution, and if so, whether the State is liable to pay compensation even though the exact individual police officers responsible could not be conclusively identified.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner was arrested by Panadura Police on suspicion of stealing side mirrors of motor vehicles. He says he was actually arrested on 9.10.1986 and then kept at Panadura Police Station for five nights without being produced before a Magistrate. During this period he alleges that the 1st to 4th respondents (police officers) repeatedly assaulted him with batons, hung him from a beam by his hands tied with a rope, crushed his penis by placing it in a drawer and closing it, and when he asked for water, forced him to drink water mixed with chilli powder. He claims these acts caused him unbearable pain and suffering, amounting to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11.
respondent_argument: The 1st to 4th respondents denied all allegations. They said the petitioner was not arrested on 9.10.1986 but on 13.10.1986 near the Panadura bus stand by a police party (including the 1st and 4th respondents and two others). They claimed the petitioner dropped his bicycle and ran, was chased and arrested, and only reasonable force was used when he twice tried to escape. They denied any assault or torture and relied strongly on the medical officer’s (Bandaragama MO) report which recorded ‘no external injuries’ when the petitioner was examined on 14.10.1986, and on the fact that the petitioner made no complaint of assault to that MO or to the acting Magistrate when he was first produced. They argued that the later injuries recorded by the prison doctor and the Assistant JMO Colombo could not be linked to police ill-treatment.
interpretation_summary:
At the hearing, petitioner’s counsel ultimately confined the case to the alleged violation of Article 11 alone. There was a factual dispute about the exact date of arrest (9th vs 13th October), but counsel for the petitioner candidly admitted there was no supporting material beyond the petitioner’s own assertion; the entries in the police notes of inquiry (1R5) supported the police version that arrest took place on 13.10.1986. The Court therefore focused on the core question: whether the petitioner was subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment while in custody.

The undisputed sequence was that the petitioner was arrested on 13.10.1986, kept overnight in police custody, and on 14.10.1986 was taken by PC Senaratne first to Panadura Hospital (D.M.O. unavailable), then to Bandaragama Hospital, where the MO examined him at about 8 p.m. and wrote ‘no external injuries’ in his report. That same day the petitioner was produced before the acting Magistrate and remanded to the Fiscal’s custody at Panadura Remand Prison. On 15.10.1986 his attorney moved the Magistrate’s Court seeking a medical report for injuries on the petitioner, and on 16.10.1986 informed the Court that the petitioner had been hung from a beam, beaten, and had his penis slammed in a drawer, drawing the Court’s attention to the way the petitioner walked when called. The Magistrate ordered that he be produced before the JMO Colombo and re-produced in Court.

There was delay in complying with that order. The petitioner was admitted to the prison hospital on 17.10.1986. The prison doctor found pyelitis and two abrasions just above the right wrist and at the back of the left wrist. The JMO Colombo finally examined the petitioner on 24.10.1986, noted three scars (left wrist, right wrist, lower right forearm) and traumatic urethritis due to trauma to the penis, causing pain and difficulty passing urine. The JMO recorded the history given by the petitioner: that he was hung and beaten with clubs and that his penis was crushed in a drawer by the 1st–4th respondents on 13.10.1986. The JMO opined that the scars were consistent with ligature marks from hanging and that the injuries were compatible with the history.

Meanwhile, the Bandaragama MO’s report left all boxes blank and simply stated ‘No external injuries’. When the Magistrate summoned him to explain, he said in Court that he noted ‘no external injuries’ because the petitioner did not complain of any pain or injuries when asked. The Supreme Court, per Atukorale J., was highly critical of this. The Court held that the Bandaragama MO had failed in his duty to conduct an independent, proper examination; it was ‘preposterous’ to expect a suspect in the physical custody of police to openly complain, in the officer’s presence, that his injuries were caused by police assault. The Court rejected the Bandaragama MO’s report as worthless, and described his conduct as showing a gross lack of responsibility and dereliction of duty.

The Court then examined who could have caused the injuries. From the time of arrest on 13.10.1986 until the JMO examination on 24.10.1986, the petitioner was continuously in either police custody or Fiscal/prison custody; the injuries were not self-inflicted, and they were not alleged to have been pre-existing. Even if one assumed that there were no injuries visible on 14.10.1986, the unchallenged presence of characteristic ligature marks and penile trauma by 17–24 October meant they must have been inflicted while the petitioner was in State custody. In the absence of material that prison officers assaulted him, and given the timing and nature of the injuries and the delay in obeying the Magistrate’s order to produce him before the JMO, the Court concluded that the injuries were in fact inflicted while the petitioner was in police custody at Panadura.

The Court gave particular weight to the early, consistent complaints made by the petitioner’s attorney in the Magistrate’s Court on 15 and 16 October, at the first opportunity when the petitioner had access to legal representation and was no longer under direct police control. These complaints matched the history later given to the JMO. The Court found that the petitioner had been subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, by one or more police officers of the Panadura Police Station, while under arrest and detention.

Because there was documentary material (routine books) showing that two of the respondents (e.g. the 2nd respondent) were away from the station on official duty in Anuradhapura from 12–15 October and had not taken part in the arrest, and because the petitioner had not clearly set out the basis of his identification, the Court held that it was unsafe, on the available material, to pinpoint exactly which respondents committed the assaults. Thus, it did not make a specific adverse finding against the individual respondents. But it held that this uncertainty did not affect the petitioner’s right to relief against the State since the police, as an organ of the State, had clearly subjected him to prohibited ill-treatment.

The Court emphasized that Article 11 is absolute, with no restrictions or limitations, and protects every person, including suspected or ‘hard-core’ criminals. It stressed that the police, as an organ of the State, are bound not only to enjoy that right themselves but also to respect, advance and secure it for others, and that courts must jealously protect it so it does not become an illusion. The Court condemned ‘third degree’ methods as ‘barbaric, savage and inhuman’, said they were revolting to human dignity, and warned that such conduct breeds public contempt for the law and erodes confidence in the police.

Accordingly, the Court held that the petitioner had established a violation of Article 11 by executive action and was entitled to compensation under Article 126. Because the exact officers could not safely be identified on the evidence, the Court imposed liability on the State rather than on named individuals. It ordered the Inspector-General of Police to hold a full disciplinary inquiry to identify and punish those responsible, stating that the inability of the Court to make a specific finding against the 1st–4th respondents on the limited material before it should not prevent their being found guilty at a proper inquiry if further material emerges.
outcome: Relief granted. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner had been subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, in violation of Article 11, while in police custody. Although the Court did not identify specific individual respondents as the torturers due to evidential doubts, it held the State liable as the police are an organ of the State. The Court ordered the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 10,000 as compensation and Rs. 1,000 as costs. It also directed the Inspector-General of Police to conduct a full inquiry to identify the officers responsible and to take disciplinary action against them.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute fundamental right with no restrictions or limitations; it protects every person, including criminals, from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

When a person in continuous State custody (police, Fiscal or prison) is found with non-self-inflicted injuries consistent with torture, and there is no plausible innocent explanation, the Court may infer that those injuries were inflicted by State officers while in custody.

Even if exact identification of the particular police officers is doubtful on the available evidence, the State remains liable for torture or ill-treatment inflicted by its police, as the police force is an organ of the State.

Medical officers have a duty to conduct independent examinations of detainees produced by police; blindly relying on the detainee’s silence in the presence of police and issuing a ‘no injuries’ report without proper examination is a dereliction of duty and cannot be used to defeat a credible torture claim.

Early complaints made to a Magistrate or Court, once the detainee has access to legal representation and is out of direct police control, are highly significant in assessing credibility of torture allegations.
Courts must not allow ‘police solidarity’ or concealment to undermine constitutional guarantees; they must jealously guard Article 11 to prevent it from becoming a mere illusion.
Use of ‘third degree methods’ by police is condemned as barbaric, savage and inhuman, undermining public confidence in law enforcement.

Where torture is found but specific individual culprits cannot be judicially identified, courts can still order State compensation and direct the Inspector-General of Police to conduct disciplinary inquiries to identify and punish those officers.
source: Supreme Court judgment, pages 119–127.

case_title: Wickramanayaka v. The State

clauses.text: Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of association.
No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

legal_issue: Whether clauses of the Essential Public Services Bill infringed fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14(1)(g), 14(1)(h), 14(1)(a) read with 14(1)(d), and Article 11 of the Constitution, and whether a Cabinet certificate under Article 84 conclusively determines the constitutionality of a Bill.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner challenged the Essential Public Services Bill, arguing that Clause 2 compelled employees engaged in declared essential services to remain in employment and work under threat of criminal prosecution, thereby violating the freedom to engage in a lawful occupation under Article 14(1)(g). He further claimed that compulsory service violated freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h), that restrictions on speech and encouragement of strikes violated Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(d), and that Clause 4(2), which imposed mandatory forfeiture of property and removal from professional registers, amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment contrary to Article 11. He also argued that the Cabinet certificate implied constitutional inconsistency requiring a referendum.
respondent_argument: The State argued that the Bill imposed reasonable restrictions permitted under Article 15 in the interests of national security, public order, and the general welfare of society. It was submitted that essential services were vital to the life of the community and that the State had a duty to ensure their uninterrupted functioning. The Attorney General further contended that the Cabinet certificate merely indicated the intention to pass the Bill with a special majority and was not conclusive of any constitutional inconsistency.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that Article 14(1)(g) must be read subject to the permissible restrictions under Article 15. The Essential Public Services Bill was intended to operate only in emergency situations and applied to services vital to the maintenance of the life of the community. The Court accepted that limitations on strikes and compulsory service in essential services constituted reasonable restrictions and did not violate Articles 14(1)(g), 14(1)(h), or 14(1)(a) read with 14(1)(d).

However, the Court found that Clause 4(2) of the Bill imposed mandatory forfeiture of property and mandatory removal from professional registers in addition to imprisonment or fines. This cumulative and indiscriminate piling of punishments amounted to excessive and cruel punishment. The Court held that such mandatory penalties violated Article 11 of the Constitution. It emphasized that punishment must be proportionate and that cruelty need not involve physical force to fall within Article 11.

The Court also clarified that a Cabinet certificate under Article 84 is not conclusive of constitutionality and that the Court has a duty to independently examine whether a Bill is inconsistent with the Constitution, particularly entrenched provisions.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that while the restrictions imposed by the Essential Public Services Bill on occupational freedom, movement, speech, and association were constitutionally valid, Clause 4(2) of the Bill was inconsistent with Article 11 due to its mandatory and excessive punishments. The Court determined that the Bill, in its existing form, required approval by a special majority and a referendum unless Clause 4(2) was amended to make the additional punishments discretionary rather than mandatory.
principles_established: Fundamental rights under Article 14 are subject to reasonable restrictions permitted under Article 15 in the interests of national security, public order, and the general welfare of society.
There is no fundamental right to strike, particularly in relation to essential services necessary for the maintenance of the life of the community.
A Cabinet certificate under Article 84 is not conclusive of constitutional validity; the Supreme Court has an independent duty to examine constitutionality.
Punishment that cumulatively and indiscriminately piles penalties may amount to cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment under Article 11.
Cruel or inhuman punishment under Article 11 does not require physical force and includes disproportionate or excessive penalties.
precedents_cited: Leavie Collymore v. Attorney-General (1970) 38 F.J.R. 79
Radhey v. P.M.G. Nagpur AIR 1965 SC 311
All India Bank Employees' Association v. National Industrial Tribunal AIR 1962 SC 171
Raghubar Dayal v. Union of India AIR 1962 SC 263
Gosh v. Joseph AIR 1963 SC 812
Trop v. Dulles 356 U.S. 86
Robinson v. California 370 U.S. 660
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, Wickramanayaka v. The State, S.C. Appeal No. 58/79, decided on 24 September 1979

case_title: Fernando v. Attorney General and Another

clauses.text: Every person is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest of the petitioner during a protest fast and procession violated his fundamental rights under Articles 10, 11, 13(1), and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution, and whether the police acted lawfully in dispersing and arresting participants in an alleged illegal procession.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a medical practitioner, claimed that while participating in a peaceful one-day fast held at church premises to protest the detention of several persons under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, he was unlawfully assaulted, arrested, and detained by police officers. He alleged that the police violated his freedom of thought and conscience, subjected him to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, arrested him without lawful authority or explanation, and infringed his freedom of peaceful assembly and expression.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioner was a participant and organiser of an illegal procession that entered the Horowpatana Road during the period of a declared Referendum. They argued that despite warnings, the procession attempted to proceed, resulting in stone-throwing, injury to a police officer, and damage to police vehicles. The police maintained that they acted within their lawful powers to disperse an illegal procession and to arrest those involved, including the petitioner.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined whether a procession had in fact taken place and whether it was illegal. Relying on independent evidence, including the statement of the parish priest, the Court rejected the petitioner’s version and accepted that the assembled group attempted to leave the church premises in procession, entered the Horowpatana Highway, and was blocked by police.

The Court held that the procession was illegal under Section 45 of the Referendum Act No. 7 of 1981, as a Referendum had been proclaimed and the procession was neither religious nor social in nature. It was also illegal under Section 77 of the Police Ordinance due to failure to give prior notice. The Court ruled that the police had lawful authority to disperse the procession and arrest participants, and that an error in citing the precise legal provision did not invalidate otherwise lawful police action.

The Court found no evidence substantiating allegations of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or violation of freedom of thought and conscience. Regarding Article 13(1), the Court held that informing the petitioner that he was arrested for participation in an illegal procession was sufficient, and that police are not required to cite exact statutory provisions at the time of arrest.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the procession was illegal and that the police acted within their lawful powers in dispersing it and arresting the petitioner. No violation of the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 10, 11, 13(1), or 14(1)(b) was established. The application was dismissed with costs.
principles_established: A gathering that attempts to proceed in procession becomes a procession even if part of it remains within private premises.
Processions conducted during a Referendum period, except those expressly permitted, are illegal under Section 45 of the Referendum Act.
