Police action does not become unlawful merely because the wrong statutory provision is cited, provided lawful authority exists.
For purposes of Article 13(1), it is sufficient if the arrested person is informed in substance of the reason for arrest; exact legal citations are not required.
Allegations of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment must be strictly proved and will not be inferred without clear evidence.
precedents_cited: Vijaya Kumaranatunga v. G.V.P. Samarasinghe (S.C. Application No. 121/82, Minutes of 3-2-1983)
source: Fernando v. Attorney General and Another [1983] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 2 of 1983

case_title: Premalal Perera v. Weerasuriya and Others

clauses.text: Every person is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the freedom to have or to adopt a religion or belief of his choice.

Every citizen is entitled to the freedom, either by himself or in association with others, and either in public or in private, to manifest his religion or belief in worship, observance, practice and teaching.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
The fundamental rights which are by the Constitution declared and recognized shall be respected, secured and advanced by all the organs of government.

legal_issue: Whether a circular requiring a deduction from a government employee’s salary to the National Security Fund unless an objection was expressly communicated infringed the petitioner’s fundamental rights to freedom of thought, conscience and religion under Articles 10 and 14(1)(e), and the right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an employee of the Government Railway Department and a Buddhist, claimed that Circular P2, which authorised deduction of a day’s salary to the National Security Fund unless an objection was expressly made, violated his freedom of thought, conscience and religion. He believed that the Fund would be used to purchase arms and military equipment, which was contrary to Buddhist teachings against violence and the taking of life. He further argued that the requirement to expressly object forced him to disclose his beliefs publicly, exposing him to possible harassment. He also alleged a violation of Article 12(1), claiming unequal treatment because employees of other departments, such as the Health Department, were not required to make similar contributions.
respondent_argument: The respondents accepted that the circular was issued and that the deduction of Rs. 19 was made, but stated that the deduction applied only for January 1985 and that no further deductions were contemplated. They denied any intention to single out or victimise employees who objected. It was argued that the requirement to communicate an objection did not compel any religious act, impose any penalty, or interfere with the petitioner’s ability to practise his religion. The respondents further denied the allegation of unequal treatment and maintained that there was insufficient evidence to establish discrimination under Article 12(1).
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that freedom of thought, conscience and religion under Article 10 is cast in absolute terms and is not subject to post-Constitution restrictions, except to the extent permitted by Article 16(1). Beliefs rooted in religion are protected, and courts are not arbiters of scriptural interpretation. A religious belief need not be logical or acceptable to others to merit protection.

However, the Court found that Circular P2 did not interfere with the full and free exercise of the petitioner’s religion. The requirement to express an objection did not compel the petitioner to affirm a belief contrary to his faith, impose any penalty, or cause any material disadvantage. No sanction or disability attached to refusal to contribute, and once an objection was made, no deduction would occur. The Court distinguished this case from situations where individuals were forced to choose between religious fidelity and serious penalties or loss of livelihood.

On the equality claim under Article 12(1), the Court held that the petitioner had failed to place sufficient material before Court to establish unequal treatment, and therefore no violation was proved.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that Circular P2 did not infringe the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 10 or 14(1)(e), and that no violation of Article 12(1) was established. The application was dismissed, without costs. The respondent’s undertaking to refund the deducted sum of Rs. 19 was noted.
principles_established: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion under Article 10 is absolute, subject only to laws in force at the time the Constitution came into operation.
Courts are not competent to judge the correctness or logic of religious beliefs; sincerity and religious rooting are the relevant considerations.
A regulation neutral on its face may still infringe fundamental rights if its application places a substantial burden on religious exercise.
Requiring an express objection, without penalties or disabilities, does not amount to an infringement of freedom of religion where no substantial burden is imposed.
A claim of unequal treatment under Article 12(1) must be supported by adequate and specific evidence.
precedents_cited: Reynolds v. United States 98 U.S. 145
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette 319 U.S. 624
Braunfeld v. Brown 366 U.S. 599
Sherbert v. Verner 374 U.S. 398
Wisconsin v. Yoder 406 U.S. 205
Thomas v. Review Board of the Indiana Employment Security Division 450 U.S. 707
Gillette v. United States 401 U.S. 437
United States v. Seeger 380 U.S. 163
Welsh v. United States 398 U.S. 333
Elmore Perera v. Montague Jayawickreme [1985] 1 SLR 285
source: Premalal Perera v. Weerasuriya and Others [1985] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 18 of 1985

case_title: Bernard Soysa and Two Others v. Attorney-General and Two Others

clauses.text: Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

legal_issue: Whether the dispersal by the police of a satyagraha and picket held by the petitioners at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa infringed their fundamental rights to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly under Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, who were leaders of recognised political parties, claimed that they organised a satyagraha and picket at the Maha Maluwa in Kandy to protest against economic hardship and alleged violations of democratic and human rights. They asserted that the Maha Maluwa was a public place to which the public had free access, and that no permission was required to conduct a peaceful satyagraha there. They alleged that the police unlawfully and violently disrupted the satyagraha, assaulted participants, caused injuries, seized cameras, and thereby violated their fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the Maha Maluwa is not a public place but property belonging to the Sri Dalada Maligawa and is under the control of the Diyawadana Nilame. They argued that no permission had been obtained to hold a political satyagraha there, and that the gathering became unruly, with shouting of slogans and disturbance to the peaceful religious atmosphere of the Maligawa. The police maintained that they acted lawfully under the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and the Police Ordinance to preserve public order and to disperse an unlawful and non-peaceful assembly at the request of the Maligawa authorities.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the nature of the Maha Maluwa and held that although the public has access to it for purposes of worship, it cannot be treated as a public place for political demonstrations such as a satyagraha. Any access enjoyed by the public was permissive and revocable, and permission to use the premises for one purpose could not imply permission for a fundamentally different purpose.

The Court held that a satyagraha is a political event and that no implied permission could be presumed for holding such an activity within the precincts of the Dalada Maligawa. Express permission from the Diyawadana Nilame was required. The Court further found that the meeting was not peaceful, that the conduct of the participants disturbed the religious atmosphere of the Maligawa, and that the police acted bona fide in dispersing the gathering.

Relying on both Sri Lankan statutory provisions and comparative jurisprudence, the Court emphasised that the exercise of freedom of speech and assembly depends on the place and circumstances, and that restrictions in the interests of public order are constitutionally permissible. The police were therefore entitled to act under Sections 95 and 97 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and Section 56 of the Police Ordinance.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the police action in dispersing the satyagraha and picket at the Maha Maluwa was lawful and justified, and that there was no infringement of the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 14(1)(a) or 14(1)(b). The application was dismissed with costs.
principles_established: Access by the public to premises for religious worship does not confer a right to use such premises for political demonstrations.
A satyagraha is a political event for which no implied permission can be presumed in relation to the precincts of a religious shrine.
The scope of freedom of speech and peaceful assembly depends on the nature of the place and the surrounding circumstances.
Fundamental rights under Article 14 are subject to lawful restrictions imposed in the interests of public order.
Police are entitled to disperse assemblies that are unauthorised or not peaceful under the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and the Police Ordinance.
precedents_cited: Whitney v. California (1927) 274 U.S. 357
Schenck v. United States (1919) 249 U.S. 47
Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators’ Association (1983) 460 U.S. 37
Railway Board v. Niranjan Singh (1969) 1 SCC 502
source: Bernard Soysa and Two Others v. Attorney-General and Two Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 2 of 1991

case_title: Gamini Dissanayake v. M. C. M. Kaleel and Others

clauses.text: Provides jurisdiction to the Supreme Court to determine whether the expulsion of a Member of Parliament from a recognised political party is valid in law.
Provides for the initiation of a resolution for the removal of the President by Members of Parliament.
Freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Freedom of association.

legal_issue: Whether the expulsion of eight Members of Parliament from the United National Party for signing a notice of resolution to impeach the President and for engaging in public agitation without prior internal party discussion was lawful, valid, and consistent with the Constitution, statutory law, and principles of natural justice.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners contended that their expulsion was unlawful as it was based on the exercise of constitutional rights, including signing a resolution under Article 38 and expressing views on constitutional reform. They argued that the Working Committee lacked jurisdiction, that party rules could not override constitutional freedoms, that their expulsion violated the principles of natural justice, and that the decision was tainted by bias and mala fides.
respondent_argument: The respondents maintained that the expulsions were not for signing the impeachment resolution per se, but for grave indiscipline arising from the failure to raise issues internally within the party, betrayal of party discipline, misleading the Cabinet, and publicly undermining the party leadership. They asserted that the Working Committee had validly delegated disciplinary powers and acted bona fide in accordance with the party constitution.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that political parties occupy a constitutionally central position and that Members of Parliament derive their mandate through the party. Party discipline is therefore a legitimate constitutional value. Although an MP is entitled to sign a notice of resolution under Article 38 as a parliamentary act, this does not absolve the MP from obligations voluntarily assumed under party membership.

The Court found that the Working Committee of the UNP had valid jurisdiction to expel members due to a lawful delegation of disciplinary powers by the National Executive Committee. The failure of the petitioners to raise serious allegations internally before launching a public campaign constituted indiscipline. The Court further held that freedom of speech and association under Article 14 may be subject to voluntary restrictions arising from party membership.

The principles of natural justice were not violated, as the Supreme Court proceedings themselves provided an effective hearing, and no prejudice was caused. Allegations of bias and mala fides were rejected as unsubstantiated.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the expulsions of all eight petitioners were valid and lawful. The applications were dismissed, and the petitioners were held to have validly lost their seats in Parliament under Article 99(13)(a).
principles_established: Political parties have constitutional primacy over individual Members of Parliament in relation to party discipline.
Freedom of speech and association may be voluntarily limited by obligations undertaken through party membership.
Signing a presidential impeachment resolution is a parliamentary act, but does not immunise a member from party discipline.
Failure to raise issues internally before public agitation may constitute serious party indiscipline.
Delegation of disciplinary powers within a political party is valid if authorised by the party constitution.
Natural justice is satisfied where no prejudice is caused and the Supreme Court provides a full hearing.
precedents_cited: Wickremabahu v. Herath SC 27/1988
Joseph Perera v. Attorney-General SC 107–109/86
New York Times v. United States (1971)
Dissanayake v. Sri Jayewardenepura University [1986] 2 Sri L.R. 254
source: Gamini Dissanayake v. M. C. M. Kaleel and Others [1993] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. (Special) Nos. 4–11 of 1991

case_title: Jayatillake and Another v. Kaleel and Others

clauses.text: Provides jurisdiction to the Supreme Court to determine the validity of the expulsion of a Member of Parliament from a recognised political party.
Provides for the initiation of a notice of resolution for the removal of the President by Members of Parliament.
Freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

legal_issue: Whether the expulsion of two Members of Parliament from the United National Party, following their conduct relating to the signing, revocation, and continued support of a presidential impeachment resolution and their subsequent conduct, was lawful, valid, and consistent with the Constitution, party constitution, and principles of natural justice.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners contended that their expulsion was unlawful and unconstitutional. They argued that signing the impeachment notice was an exercise of a constitutional right under Article 38(2)(a) and could not attract party discipline. They claimed that the Working Committee lacked disciplinary jurisdiction, that there was a legitimate understanding that no disciplinary action would be taken against members who retracted their signatures, that they were denied a fair hearing in breach of natural justice, and that their freedoms of speech, thought, and conscience were violated.
respondent_argument: The respondents maintained that the expulsions were not based merely on signing the impeachment notice but on a course of deceitful and disloyal conduct. They argued that the petitioners signed and later repudiated the impeachment notice alleging misrepresentation and deceit, but thereafter continued to support it, misled the party and the Speaker, failed to observe party discipline, absented themselves from Parliament during a critical vote, and publicly associated with dissidents campaigning against the party. They asserted that the Working Committee had validly delegated disciplinary powers and that any initial procedural defects were cured by subsequent proceedings.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that while a Member of Parliament has a constitutional right to sign a notice of impeachment, this right must be exercised with independent judgment and responsibility. Signing such a document without knowing its contents constituted a grave misuse of a constitutional power. The petitioners’ later conduct, including revoking their signatures while simultaneously continuing to support the impeachment and disputing the Speaker’s rejection of it, justified an inference of deceit.

The Court found that the Working Committee had validly delegated disciplinary powers. It accepted that the initial proceedings of 6 December 1991 were in breach of the audi alteram partem rule due to inadequate notice and lack of particulars. However, the subsequent opportunity given to the petitioners to submit written observations, which they utilised, cured the procedural defects. In light of the undisputed facts and the seriousness of the misconduct, an oral hearing was unnecessary.

The Court emphasised that freedom of speech and thought of Members of Parliament is constrained by party discipline. An MP cannot use constitutional freedoms to create a parallel party or to conduct a campaign calculated to destroy the party while retaining party membership. Such conduct forfeits the protection of Article 14. The Court rejected claims of promissory estoppel, holding that no promise existed to protect future misconduct. Overall, the expulsions were found to be lawful, fair, and justified.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the expulsions of the petitioners from the United National Party were valid and lawful. The applications were dismissed, and the petitioners were held to have validly lost their party membership and parliamentary seats under Article 99(13)(a).
principles_established: A Member of Parliament has a constitutional right to sign an impeachment notice, but this right must be exercised with informed and independent judgment.
Signing a constitutional document without knowledge of its contents constitutes a misuse of constitutional power.
Freedom of speech and thought of Members of Parliament is subject to the requirements of party discipline.
An MP cannot conduct a campaign to undermine or destroy the party while retaining party membership; the Constitution does not permit a party within a party.
Disciplinary powers may validly be delegated within a political party if authorised by the party constitution.
Initial breaches of natural justice may be cured by subsequent fair procedures if no prejudice is caused and a fair overall hearing is afforded.
No promissory estoppel arises where there is no promise to excuse future misconduct.
precedents_cited: Dissanayake v. Kaleel SC (Special) Nos. 4–11/91
Pakir Mohideen v. Mohamadu Cassim [1900] 4 NLR 299
Ridge v. Baldwin [1964] AC 40
Russell v. Duke of Norfolk [1949] 1 All ER 109
Joseph Perera v. Attorney-General SC 107–109/86
Dissanayake v. Sri Jayewardenepura University [1986] 2 Sri L.R. 264
source: Jayatillake and Another v. Kaleel and Others [1994] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. Applications Nos. 1 & 2 of 1992

case_title: Ven. Ellawala Medananda Thero v. District Secretary, Ampara and Others

clauses.text: Every person is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.

legal_issue: Whether the executive and administrative action taken to alienate approximately 60 acres of land near the Deeghavapi Raja Maha Viharaya to about 500 Muslim families was ultra vires, arbitrary, discriminatory, and in violation of Articles 10, 12(1), and 12(2) of the Constitution, due to failure to comply with the 13th Amendment, the Land Development Ordinance, and the Rule of Law.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, including the Viharadhipathi of the Deeghavapi Raja Maha Viharaya and representatives of Buddhist organisations, alleged that the impugned alienation of land was carried out without any lawful authority, without a fair or transparent process, and in violation of the 13th Amendment and the Land Development Ordinance. They claimed that the settlement of 500 Muslim families in close proximity to a major Buddhist sacred site would prevent expansion of Sinhala Buddhist settlements, discriminate against landless Sinhala and Tamil persons, and infringe freedom of religion. They further alleged that the stated justification of tsunami resettlement was a sham masking a long-standing demand for Muslim settlement in the area.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the beneficiaries were selected under a circular issued by the Secretariat of the President following the 2004 tsunami, that the land was not State land but vested in the Sri Lanka Sugar Corporation, and that neither the 13th Amendment nor the Land Development Ordinance prohibited the alienation. They argued that executive action is valid so long as it is not expressly prohibited by law.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that there was a complete failure to comply with the Land Development Ordinance and the 13th Amendment in relation to the alienation of the land. The State failed to produce any evidence identifying the authority or process by which the land and beneficiaries were selected. The Circular relied upon was not issued under any law, did not specify criteria for land selection, and could not justify administrative action taken several years after the tsunami.

The Court rejected the contention that executive action is valid merely because it is not prohibited by law, holding that such a view is contrary to the Rule of Law and the doctrine of ultra vires. Every act of a public authority must have legal justification, fall within lawful authority, and be authorised by law. State land is held by the executive in trust for the People and may be alienated only as permitted by law.

The Court further found that the justification of resettling 500 tsunami victims was factually unsustainable, as contemporaneous official correspondence established that only about 50 families required resettlement. The demand to allocate land to 500 Muslim families predated the tsunami by several years. The impugned alienation was therefore not bona fide and was discriminatory. The petitioners established violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 10 of the Constitution.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the impugned alienation of land was illegal, ultra vires, arbitrary, and discriminatory, and violated the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 10, 12(1), and 12(2) of the Constitution. The application was allowed, the alienation was restrained, and the State was ordered to pay Rs. 150,000 as costs to the petitioners.
principles_established: State land is held by the executive in trust for the People and may be alienated only in accordance with law.
Executive or administrative action must have legal justification, fall within lawful authority, and be authorised by law; action is not valid merely because it is not prohibited.
The doctrine of ultra vires is a core component of the Rule of Law in Sri Lankan public law.
Executive circulars not issued under statutory authority cannot justify alienation of State land.
Arbitrary and non-transparent allocation of State land amounts to a violation of equality and non-discrimination under Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
Administrative action affecting religious sensitivity and historic religious sites must strictly comply with constitutional and statutory safeguards.
precedents_cited: Liyanage v. Gampaha Urban Council [1991] 1 Sri L.R. 1
source: Ven. Ellawala Medananda Thero v. District Secretary, Ampara and Others [2009] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. F.R. Application No. 178 of 2008

case_title: Thadchanamoorthi and Others v. Attorney-General and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Provides the procedure and time limits for invoking the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

legal_issue: Whether the alleged assaults and ill-treatment of the petitioners by police officers amounted to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution, and whether such acts constituted infringement by executive or administrative action within the meaning of Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that while in police custody they were subjected to severe physical assaults, including beatings with batons, fists and shoed feet, being hung up by their wrists, and other forms of brutal treatment, for the purpose of extracting confessions to serious criminal offences. They claimed that such treatment amounted to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and ill-treatment. They contended that any force used was reasonable and necessary in the course of arrest when the petitioners resisted custody or attempted to escape. They further argued that the injuries recorded were minor and inconsistent with the grave allegations made. The Attorney-General also raised a preliminary objection that one application was filed out of time under Article 126(2), and that the acts complained of did not constitute infringement by executive or administrative action.
interpretation_summary:
The Court first held that Application No. 68/80 was filed outside the one-month time limit prescribed by Article 126(2) and that no adequate explanation for the delay was provided. That application was therefore rejected.

In relation to Application No. 63/80, the Court emphasised that the burden of proof lies on the petitioner to establish a violation of Article 11. On an examination of the medical evidence, the Court found that the injuries sustained were minor in nature and did not support the serious allegations of torture described in the petition. There was considerable doubt as to how and when the injuries were sustained, and it was possible that they occurred during lawful arrest when reasonable force was used.

The Court also examined whether the alleged acts amounted to infringement by executive or administrative action. Drawing on comparative jurisprudence, including the decision of the European Court of Human Rights in Ireland v. United Kingdom, the Court explained that State responsibility for torture may arise where there is an ‘administrative practice’ involving repetition of acts and official tolerance. However, the existence of an ongoing police inquiry into the complaints strongly negated any inference of such an administrative practice in Sri Lanka.

Accordingly, the Court held that the petitioners failed to establish a violation of Article 11 by executive or administrative action.
outcome: The Supreme Court rejected Application No. 68/80 as being out of time and dismissed Application No. 63/80 on the merits, holding that no violation of Article 11 was established. The applications were dismissed, and the respondents were awarded costs.
principles_established: An application under Article 126 must be filed within one month of the alleged infringement, unless an adequate explanation for delay is provided.
The burden of proving torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 11 lies on the petitioner.
Minor injuries, where their origin is doubtful, are insufficient to establish torture or ill-treatment.
For State responsibility to arise, acts of torture must amount to an ‘administrative practice’ involving repetition and official tolerance.
The existence of an ongoing and bona fide police inquiry into alleged ill-treatment negatives the inference of an administrative practice.
Not every unlawful act by a public officer constitutes executive or administrative action for the purposes of Article 126.
precedents_cited: Ireland v. United Kingdom (European Court of Human Rights)
Greek Case (European Commission of Human Rights)
source: Thadchanamoorthi and Others v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. Nos. 63 and 68 of 1980

case_title: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the alleged torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment inflicted on the petitioner by Army personnel after his arrest, allegedly at the instigation of a police officer, constituted an infringement of Article 11 by executive or administrative action so as to attract State liability under Article 126 of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an elected member of the Amparai District Development Council, alleged that he was illegally arrested by the 2nd respondent, a police officer acting as a coordinating officer during communal disturbances, without being informed of the reasons for arrest. He claimed that the 2nd respondent instructed Army and Police personnel to take him and do as they wished, following which he was subjected to severe torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment by Army personnel while in custody. He further alleged that attempts were made to suppress his complaints when his statement was recorded and that threats were made against his life.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and instigation. The 2nd respondent admitted arresting the petitioner but denied ordering or encouraging any ill-treatment. The Attorney-General raised a preliminary objection that the acts complained of did not amount to infringement by executive or administrative action within Article 126, contending that individual criminal acts of officers, if any, did not attract State liability unless authorised or supported by the State. It was also argued that the petitioner failed to prove that the injuries were sustained while in lawful custody or at the instigation of the 2nd respondent.
interpretation_summary:
The majority of the Court held that although Article 11 occupies a preferred and entrenched position in the Constitution, the burden lay on the petitioner to establish, on a high degree of probability proportionate to the seriousness of the allegation, that torture had occurred and that it was attributable to executive or administrative action. On the facts, the Court found significant inconsistencies and a lack of corroboration.

The petitioner had multiple opportunities to complain to responsible authorities, including the Magistrate, the District Medical Officer, the Judicial Medical Officer, and in a detailed later police statement, but failed to implicate the 2nd respondent at those stages. The Magistrate’s report expressly contradicted the petitioner’s claim of difficulty in walking or visible injury at the time of production. The medical and documentary evidence did not support the allegation that injuries were inflicted at the instigation of the 2nd respondent.

The majority further held that State liability under Article 126 may arise where there is an authorisation, encouragement, benefit to the State, or an ‘administrative practice’ involving repetition and official tolerance. On the facts, the alleged acts, even if they had occurred, were characterised as individual and personal acts of aberration, not attributable to an administrative practice or State policy.

In powerful dissenting judgments, Sharvananda J. and Ratwatte J. took the view that abuse of coercive power by a public officer acting under colour of office constitutes executive action, and that the State should be strictly liable where such power is misused to violate Article 11. They emphasised that Article 11 is non-derogable and that constitutional remedies must be given a liberal interpretation to prevent impunity.
outcome: By a majority, the Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner failed to prove that the alleged torture and ill-treatment occurred at the instigation of the 2nd respondent or that it amounted to infringement by executive or administrative action under Article 126. Costs were awarded to the 2nd respondent.
principles_established: The standard of proof in Article 11 cases is the civil standard of preponderance of probability, but the degree of probability required increases with the seriousness of the allegation.
Article 11 is an entrenched and non-derogable fundamental right applicable to all persons without exception.
State liability under Article 126 is not vicarious tort liability but a distinct public law liability.

Acts of torture by subordinate officers attract State liability only if they are authorised, encouraged, done for the benefit of the State, or constitute an ‘administrative practice’ involving repetition and official tolerance.
Failure to complain at the earliest reasonable opportunity may seriously undermine allegations of torture.
Dissent: Abuse of coercive power by a public officer acting under colour of office constitutes executive action, regardless of authorisation.
precedents_cited: Maharaja v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago [1979] AC 385 (PC)
Thornhill v. Attorney-General [1980] 2 WLR 510 (PC)
Ex parte Commonwealth of Virginia 100 US 339
Ireland v. United Kingdom (European Court of Human Rights, 1978)
Thadchanamoorthi v. Attorney-General (S.C. 63/80)
source: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. No. 74 of 1981

case_title: The Associated Newspapers of Ceylon Ltd. v. Jayasinghe

clauses.text: Provides that the language of courts and tribunals shall be Sinhala and that pleadings, proceedings, judgments, orders and records shall be in Sinhala.

legal_issue: Whether applications for relief made to Labour Tribunals under section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act during the operation of the 1972 Constitution were null and void because they were made in English instead of Sinhala, and whether a Labour Tribunal may award back wages in addition to compensation in lieu of reinstatement.
petitioner_claim: The employer contended that the applications made by the employees to the Labour Tribunal were invalid and should have been rejected in limine because they were filed in English, contrary to Article 11(1) of the 1972 Constitution which required pleadings before Labour Tribunals to be in Sinhala. The employer also challenged the awards of compensation and back wages granted by the Labour Tribunal.
respondent_argument: The employees argued that an application for relief under section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act was not a ‘pleading’ within the meaning of Article 11(1) of the 1972 Constitution, and that no prejudice had been caused by the proceedings being conducted in English. They further contended that back wages could be awarded in addition to compensation where termination was found to be unjustified.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that the word ‘pleadings’ in Article 11(1) of the 1972 Constitution does not include an application for relief or redress under section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act. Such an application is required by law to be signed by the applicant personally, and the applicant cannot reasonably be expected to take responsibility for its contents if compelled to file it in a language with which he is not conversant.

The Court further held that Article 11(1) did not preclude applications being made to Labour Tribunals in English. The responsibility lay on the Tribunal to cause a Sinhala translation to be made for the record. In the absence of prejudice, non-compliance with the language requirement amounted only to an irregularity and was not fatal to the proceedings.

On the question of relief, the Court held that when a Tribunal awards compensation in lieu of reinstatement, it is not entitled to make a separate award of back wages. Back wages are one of the factors to be taken into account in assessing compensation, and awarding both would result in duplication.
outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeal. The appeals by both the employer and the employees were dismissed. The award of compensation in lieu of reinstatement was upheld, and the deletion of the separate awards of back wages was confirmed. No costs were awarded.
principles_established: An application for relief under section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act is not a ‘pleading’ within the meaning of Article 11(1) of the 1972 Constitution.
Article 11(1) of the 1972 Constitution does not invalidate applications made in English to Labour Tribunals where no prejudice is caused.
Failure to comply with constitutional language requirements, in the absence of prejudice, results in an irregularity and not a nullity.
When compensation is awarded in lieu of reinstatement, back wages must be taken into account as a factor in computing compensation and cannot be awarded separately.
The assessment of compensation for unjust termination must depend on the circumstances of each case and aims to approximate the monetary equivalent of the loss suffered.
precedents_cited: Dixon v. Calcraft (1892) 1 Q.B. 458
Nelungaloo Pty Ltd. v. The Commonwealth (1947–1948) 75 C.L.R. 495
source: The Associated Newspapers of Ceylon Ltd. v. Jayasinghe [1982] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Appeals Nos. 10/81 and 13/81

case_title: Gunawardena v. Perera and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the petitioner during a protest demonstration amounted to an infringement of Article 13(1) of the Constitution, whether she was subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11, and whether the impugned acts constituted executive or administrative action attracting State liability under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Mrs. Vivienne Gunawardena, a veteran politician, alleged that while she was inside the Kollupitiya Police Station seeking the release of a press photographer, the Officer-in-Charge arrested her without lawful basis, assaulted her by throwing her to the ground, kicking her, and placing his foot on her leg, and detained her without informing her of the reasons for arrest. She claimed these acts violated her fundamental rights under Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied that the 1st respondent assaulted or arrested the petitioner inside the Police Station. They contended that the petitioner had been lawfully arrested earlier on Galle Road by a Sub-Inspector for participating in an illegal procession conducted without authority and for obstructing a police officer in the execution of his duties. They further argued that any force used was minimal and lawful, and that the State could not be held liable unless the impugned acts were authorised or adopted by it.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that the petitioner failed to establish, by proof to the high degree of probability required, that she was subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment by the 1st respondent. Accordingly, no violation of Article 11 was proved.

On the issue of arrest, the Court found that the petitioner had not proved that she was arrested by the 1st respondent inside the Police Station. However, the Sub-Inspector admitted arresting her on Galle Road. The Court examined the legality of that arrest and held that conducting a procession without prior notice under section 77(1) of the Police Ordinance was a non-cognizable offence for which arrest without a warrant was not permissible. The absence of a permit did not render the procession illegal, and there was no state of emergency at the time.

Accordingly, the order to disperse was unlawful, and the arrest could not be justified under section 32(1)(f) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The arrest therefore violated Article 13(1).

On State liability, the Court held that acts done by a police officer under colour of office in the exercise of coercive powers constitute executive action, whether or not the State expressly authorised or later adopted such acts. Since the Sub-Inspector’s conduct was executive action, the State was liable for the infringement.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s arrest was unlawful and violated Article 13(1) of the Constitution. The allegation of violation of Article 11 was rejected. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 2,500 as compensation. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: The burden of proof in fundamental rights applications is on the petitioner, and the standard is a preponderance of probabilities with a degree commensurate to the seriousness of the allegation.
Failure to prove cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment to a high degree of probability defeats a claim under Article 11.
Contravention of section 77(1) of the Police Ordinance is a non-cognizable offence and does not justify arrest without a warrant.
The absence of a permit does not make a procession illegal; only prior notice is required under the Police Ordinance.
An arrest based on an unlawful order to disperse is not according to procedure established by law and violates Article 13(1).
Acts committed by police officers under colour of office constitute executive action, attracting State liability even if not expressly authorised.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Maharaj v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago (No. 2) [1979] A.C. 385
Thornhill v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago [1980] 2 W.L.R. 510
Mariyadas Raj v. Attorney-General and Another (S.C. No. 130/82)
source: Gunawardena v. Perera and Others [1983] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 20 of 1983

case_title: Kapugeekiyana v. Hettiarachchi and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an attorney-at-law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest, detention, interrogation, and conduct of the respondents violated the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), 13(3), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution, including illegal detention beyond 24 hours, torture or cruel treatment, interference with access to counsel, and denial of the freedom to engage in a lawful profession.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a suspect in a murder case, alleged that CID officers entered his residence without a search warrant, arrested him without a warrant or lawful procedure, and detained him incommunicado on the 4th floor of the CID for several days without producing him before a Magistrate. He claimed that during this period he was subjected to harassment, assault, torture, and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. He further alleged interference with his right to communicate freely with his attorney-at-law, and that the seizure of his professional documents and his detention prevented him from engaging in his lawful occupation.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and illegal detention, asserting that the petitioner was lawfully arrested based on information obtained during investigations into a contract killing. They maintained that the arrest took place later than alleged by the petitioner, that the detention was lawful, that no torture or cruel treatment was inflicted, and that the petitioner’s professional activities were lawfully curtailed due to the necessities of criminal investigation.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that even a suspect on the gravest criminal charges is entitled to the full protection of fundamental rights. Applying the civil standard of proof articulated in Velmurugu v. Attorney-General, the Court examined extensive documentary and affidavit evidence to determine the date of arrest and duration of detention.

The Court found that the petitioner had in fact been arrested on 13 June 1984 and illegally detained on the 4th floor of the CID until 17 June 1984 without being produced before a Magistrate, in violation of Article 13(2) read with sections 36 and 37 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. However, the Court held that the arrest itself was not shown to be unlawful, and that there was insufficient proof that the petitioner had not been informed of the reason for his arrest, rejecting the Article 13(1) claim.

The allegations of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 11 were not established due to lack of corroborative medical or independent evidence. The Court strongly criticised the conduct of the first respondent in attempting to inspect a written communication between the petitioner and his counsel, affirming that communications between lawyer and client are privileged, but held that no actual denial of a fair trial occurred.

The Court further held that temporary inability to engage in one’s profession due to lawful criminal investigation or detention does not, by itself, constitute a violation of Article 14(1)(g).
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 13(2) had been violated due to illegal detention beyond 24 hours without judicial oversight. Claims under Articles 11, 13(1), 13(3), and 14(1)(g) were rejected. The first and second respondents were ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 10,000 as compensation and costs.
principles_established: Even a person accused of the gravest criminal offences is entitled to the full protection of fundamental rights.
The standard of proof in fundamental rights applications is the civil standard, with the degree of probability increasing with the gravity of the allegation.
Detention beyond 24 hours without production before a Magistrate violates Article 13(2) and sections 36 and 37 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
Allegations of torture under Article 11 require credible and corroborated evidence.
Communications between counsel and client are privileged and any attempt to interfere with them is reprehensible.
Temporary curtailment of professional activity due to lawful criminal investigation or detention does not necessarily violate Article 14(1)(g).
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General (S.C. Application No. 74/81)
source: Kapugeekiyana v. Hettiarachchi and Others [1984] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. No. 80 of 1984

case_title: Peter Leo Fernando v. The Attorney-General and Two Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement of a fundamental right by executive or administrative action.
The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine questions relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the detention of the petitioner for several hours in a Magistrate’s Court cell pursuant to an order made by a Magistrate, without compliance with mandatory provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, amounted to an infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action within the meaning of Articles 17 and 126, and whether a Judge or the State could be held liable for such judicial acts.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, who was seated in the well of the Magistrate’s Court of Attanagalla as a member of the public, alleged that the Magistrate ordered his detention in the court cell for about four hours on the basis of an unverified allegation made by counsel in an unrelated case. He claimed that the order was made without informing him of any charge, without examination of the complainant, and in violation of the mandatory procedure under sections 136, 139 and 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. He alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2) and 14(1)(b), and sought compensation under Article 126.
respondent_argument: The Magistrate contended that the order of detention was made in the bona fide exercise of judicial authority under section 136(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, on the belief that an offence of criminal intimidation had been committed within the court’s jurisdiction. It was argued that even if the order was procedurally erroneous, it remained a judicial act protected by judicial immunity and did not constitute executive or administrative action. The State and prison officer contended that no liability arose from acts done in good faith pursuant to a judicial order.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that the Magistrate had clearly misapplied sections 136, 139 and 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The petitioner was improperly detained without examination of the complainant on oath, without recording such examination, and without issuing summons or warrant as required by law. Nevertheless, there was no evidence of mala fides or absence of good faith on the part of the Magistrate.

The Court emphasised that judicial acts, even when unlawful or erroneous, do not become executive or administrative acts merely because they are wrong. Judicial power is exercised independently under Article 4(c) of the Constitution, and judicial officers are not subject to executive or ministerial control. Accordingly, acts done by a Judge in the exercise or purported exercise of judicial functions fall outside the scope of Article 126.

The Court reaffirmed the doctrine of judicial immunity under both common law and Roman-Dutch law. Every Judge, whether of a superior or inferior court, enjoys immunity from civil and criminal liability for acts done judicially and in good faith. The State is likewise not liable under Article 126 or under the Crown (Liability in Delict) Act for judicial acts or for acts done by officers executing judicial orders in good faith.

The proper remedy for judicial error lies in appeal or revision, not in fundamental rights proceedings under Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the impugned detention resulted from a judicial act and not from executive or administrative action. Accordingly, no relief was available under Article 126. The application was dismissed without costs.
principles_established: Judicial acts, even if unlawful or procedurally erroneous, do not constitute executive or administrative action within the meaning of Articles 17 and 126.
Judges enjoy absolute immunity from civil and criminal liability for acts done in the exercise or purported exercise of judicial functions, provided they act in good faith.
The State is not liable for judicial acts or for acts done by officers executing judicial orders in good faith.
Errors committed by judges must be corrected through appeal or revision and not through fundamental rights applications.
Article 126 provides a public law remedy only against executive or administrative action and does not extend to judicial action.
precedents_cited: Sirros v. Moore [1975] 1 Q.B. 118
Maharaj v. Attorney-General of Trinidad and Tobago (No. 2) [1979] A.C. 385
A.K. Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Others
Perera v. University Grants Commission
Wijetunga v. Insurance Corporation of Sri Lanka
Naresh S. Murajikar v. State of Maharashtra AIR 1967 SC 1
source: Peter Leo Fernando v. Attorney-General and Two Others [1985] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 31 of 1985

case_title: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment while in police custody, in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution, and whether the State is liable to pay compensation even where there is doubt regarding the precise identification of the police officers responsible.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that after being arrested by police officers attached to the Panadura Police Station on suspicion of theft, he was detained in custody and subjected to severe torture. He claimed that he was beaten with batons, hung from a beam with his hands tied, had his penis crushed by being placed in a drawer, and was forced to drink water mixed with chilli powder. He asserted that these acts constituted torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of Article 11.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied that the petitioner was subjected to torture or cruel treatment. They disputed the date and circumstances of arrest and contended that any force used was only such as was reasonably necessary at the time of arrest. They relied heavily on the report of the Medical Officer, Bandaragama, which stated that the petitioner had no external injuries, and argued that the petitioner had failed to complain of torture at the earliest opportunity.
interpretation_summary:
The Court confined its analysis to Article 11. It held that the presence of injuries on the petitioner was conclusively established by the reports of the prison doctor and the Additional Judicial Medical Officer (A.J.M.O.), Colombo. The A.J.M.O. found scars on both wrists and the forearm, as well as traumatic urethritis, and expressed the opinion that the injuries were consistent with ligature marks and trauma caused in the manner described by the petitioner.

The Court rejected the report of the Medical Officer, Bandaragama, describing it as valueless and unacceptable because he had not carried out an independent examination and had expected the petitioner to complain of police assault in the presence of police officers. The Court observed that such an expectation was wholly unrealistic and amounted to a dereliction of duty.

Although the Court found it unsafe to make a specific finding against any one of the four named police officers due to doubts regarding identification, it held that the petitioner had clearly established that he was subjected to torture and cruel treatment while in custody of the police or fiscal officers. The police force being an organ of the State, such conduct constituted executive or administrative action.

Article 11 was described as an absolute and non-derogable right, admitting of no restrictions whatsoever. The Court emphasised its constitutional duty to jealously protect this right and condemned third-degree methods adopted by police officers as barbaric, savage and inhuman.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner had established a violation of Article 11 of the Constitution by executive action. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 10,000 as compensation and Rs. 1,000 as costs. The Inspector-General of Police was further directed to conduct a full inquiry to identify the officers responsible and to take disciplinary action against them.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute and non-derogable fundamental right, applicable to every person irrespective of guilt or innocence.
Torture or cruel treatment inflicted by police officers constitutes executive or administrative action.
The State is liable to pay compensation for torture even where the precise identification of the individual police officers responsible is uncertain.
Medical reports must be assessed critically; a report made without an independent examination is of no evidentiary value.

Failure of a detainee to complain of torture at the earliest opportunity does not necessarily discredit the allegation, particularly where the detainee was in police custody without access to legal assistance.
Courts have a duty to strongly condemn and deter the use of third-degree methods by law enforcement authorities.
source: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 186 of 1986

case_title: Fernando v. Attorney General and Others (1983)

clauses.text: Every person is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

legal_issue: Whether the actions of the police in dispersing the gathering at St. Anthony’s Church, arresting the petitioner, and using force amounted to violations of the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 10, 11, 13(1), and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution, and whether the police acted without legal authority.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, Dr. S. N. Fernando, a registered medical practitioner attached to the Base Hospital, Vavuniya, claimed that while he was participating in a peaceful one-day fast and assembly at the premises of St. Anthony’s Church to protest against the detention of several persons under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, the police unlawfully entered the church premises, baton-charged the participants, assaulted him, arrested him without informing him of the reasons for arrest, and subjected him to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. He alleged that his freedom of thought and conscience, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of speech were violated, and that the arrest and use of force were illegal.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioner and others were part of an illegal procession that entered the Horowpatana Road during the period of a declared Referendum, in contravention of Section 45 of the Referendum Act No. 7 of 1981 and Sections 77(1) and 77(3) of the Police Ordinance. They stated that despite police warnings, the procession attempted to proceed, resulting in violence, stone throwing, injury to a police officer, and damage to police vehicles. The police maintained that they acted lawfully to disperse an illegal procession and to arrest those involved, including the petitioner.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined whether a procession in fact took place and whether it entered the Horowpatana Highway. Relying on the statement of the Parish Priest of St. Anthony’s Church and contemporaneous police records, the Court rejected the petitioner’s version and accepted that the gathering attempted to leave the church premises in procession, that part of the procession entered the highway, and that it was blocked by the police. The Court held that the procession was illegal under Section 45 of the Referendum Act, as a Referendum had been proclaimed and the procession did not fall within the permitted exceptions. The procession was also illegal due to failure to give notice under Section 77(1) of the Police Ordinance.

The Court further held that the police had the legal authority to disperse the illegal procession and to arrest participants. The fact that the police may initially have relied on incorrect Emergency Regulations did not render their actions unlawful, as the procession was in fact illegal under other valid statutory provisions. The allegations relating to violations of freedom of thought and conscience, cruel and degrading treatment, and failure to inform the petitioner of the reason for arrest were either not substantiated or not pursued. Informing the petitioner that he was being arrested for participation in an illegal procession was held to be sufficient compliance with Article 13(1).
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the procession was illegal, that the police had the power to act in the manner they did, and that no violation of the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 10, 11, 13(1), or 14(1)(b) of the Constitution was established. The petition was dismissed with costs.
principles_established: A gathering that attempts to proceed as a procession during the period of a declared Referendum, in violation of Section 45 of the Referendum Act, constitutes an illegal procession.
Failure to give notice of a procession under Section 77(1) of the Police Ordinance renders such procession illegal under Section 77(3).
The police are entitled to disperse an illegal procession and arrest participants using lawful powers conferred by statute.
An arrest is not rendered unlawful merely because the police relied on an incorrect statutory provision, provided there exists valid legal authority justifying the action.
Police officers are not required to cite precise statutory provisions at the time of arrest, so long as the person arrested is informed of the substance of the reason for arrest.
precedents_cited: Vijaya Kumaranatunga v. G. V. P. Samarasinghe (1983)
source: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 2 of 1983, decided on 16 March 1983

case_title: Namasivayam v. Gunawardena
judges: H. A. G. de Silva J.

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement of a fundamental right by executive or administrative action.
The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine questions relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.
The expiry or revocation of a Proclamation of Emergency shall not affect anything lawfully done or any liability incurred while it was in operation.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s arrest without being informed of the reasons violated Article 13(1), whether he was subjected to torture in violation of Article 11, whether his detention under Emergency Regulations remained lawful after the lapse of the regulations, and whether the application under Article 126 was barred by the one-month limitation period.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that while travelling in a bus on 28 July 1986 he was arrested by the 3rd respondent without being informed of the reasons. He claimed that he was taken to a security personnel camp, repeatedly assaulted, forced to make statements dictated by the police, denied access to his lawyer, and unlawfully detained for a prolonged period under successive detention orders. He alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and illegal detention. The 3rd respondent claimed that on 28 July 1986 the petitioner was only requested to accompany him for questioning and was released thereafter, and that a lawful arrest was effected later on 4 August 1986 under the Emergency Regulations. The respondents also raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed out of time under Article 126(2).
interpretation_summary:
The Court first addressed the preliminary objection on limitation. It held that Article 126(2) must be given a generous and purposive interpretation. Where a petitioner is continuously detained and denied free access to lawyers and the Court, the one-month period should be calculated from the time he is free from such restraint. Otherwise, the constitutional remedy under Article 126 would become illusory. Accordingly, the delayed application was entertained.

On the allegation of torture, the Court held that the petitioner’s claim was not corroborated by medical evidence and therefore a violation of Article 11 was not established.

On arrest, the Court held that when the 3rd respondent compelled the petitioner to accompany him to the police station on 28 July 1986, the petitioner was in law arrested. As the petitioner was not informed of the reason for his arrest and no reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence was established, Article 13(1) was violated.

On detention, the Court held that although the Emergency Regulations under which the detention order was made had lapsed, Regulation 19(2), Article 155(5) of the Constitution, and section 4(a) and (b) of the Public Security Ordinance preserved the validity of detention orders and liabilities incurred during the currency of the Emergency. Therefore, the detention was not unlawful on that ground.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 13(1) was violated by his unlawful arrest without being informed of the reasons. No violation of Articles 11 or 13(2) was established. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 3,000 as compensation. Parties were directed to bear their own costs.
principles_established: Article 126(2) must be interpreted liberally so as not to render the constitutional remedy illusory, particularly where a petitioner is continuously detained without access to legal assistance.
Compelling a person to accompany a police officer to a police station against his will constitutes an arrest in law.
Failure to inform an arrestee of the reasons for arrest violates Article 13(1) of the Constitution.
Allegations of torture under Article 11 must be supported by credible medical or corroborative evidence.
Detention orders made under Emergency Regulations remain valid despite the lapse of the Emergency, by virtue of Article 155(5) of the Constitution and section 4 of the Public Security Ordinance.
source: Namasivayam v. Gunawardena [1989] 1 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 166 of 1986

case_title: Veeradas v. Controller of Immigration and Emigration and Others
judges: H. A. G. de Silva J.

clauses.text: Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka and to return to Sri Lanka.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the refusal by the Controller of Immigration and Emigration to issue a passport to the petitioner, without providing reasons and without affording a fair opportunity to be heard, amounted to an arbitrary and unreasonable exercise of administrative discretion violating Articles 14(1)(g) and 14(1)(h) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a Sri Lankan citizen who had previously worked overseas, applied for a passport in order to travel abroad for employment. His application was rejected by the Controller of Immigration and Emigration without any reasons being given. The petitioner claimed that the refusal prevented him from engaging in his lawful occupation abroad and from travelling outside Sri Lanka, thereby violating his fundamental rights under Articles 14(1)(g) and 14(1)(h). He further alleged that the refusal was arbitrary, lacked procedural fairness, and was not based on any lawful ground.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the issuance of passports is a matter of administrative discretion vested in the Controller of Immigration and Emigration under the Immigrants and Emigrants Act. They argued that the Controller was entitled to refuse a passport in the interests of national security and public order, and that it was not necessary to disclose the reasons for refusal in every case.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that although the issuance of passports involves administrative discretion, such discretion must be exercised reasonably, in good faith, and in conformity with fundamental rights. The right to travel abroad is closely connected to the freedom to engage in a lawful occupation, especially where overseas employment is concerned.

The Court emphasised that unfettered discretion is unknown to constitutional law. Where an administrative decision adversely affects a fundamental right, the authority concerned must act fairly and must disclose at least the substance of the reasons for the decision, unless disclosure is lawfully excluded on compelling grounds such as national security.

In the present case, the respondents failed to place any material before Court justifying the refusal of a passport. No reasons were given to the petitioner, and no opportunity was afforded to him to answer any adverse allegations. The Court held that such a refusal was arbitrary and unreasonable, and therefore unconstitutional.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the refusal to issue a passport to the petitioner violated his fundamental rights under Articles 14(1)(g) and 14(1)(h) of the Constitution. The respondents were directed to issue the petitioner a passport forthwith. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: The right to travel abroad is closely linked to the freedom to engage in a lawful occupation, particularly where overseas employment is involved.
Administrative discretion affecting fundamental rights must be exercised reasonably, fairly, and in good faith.
Unfettered or absolute discretion is incompatible with constitutional governance.
Where a fundamental right is adversely affected, the administrative authority must disclose reasons unless lawfully excluded on compelling grounds.
Failure to provide reasons or an opportunity to be heard renders an administrative decision arbitrary and unconstitutional.
precedents_cited: Fernando v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority [1987] 1 Sri L.R. 329
Ridge v. Baldwin [1964] AC 40
source: Veeradas v. Controller of Immigration and Emigration and Others [1989] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 353 of 1987

case_title: Wijayasiriwardene v. Kumara, Inspector of Police and Two Others
judges: H. A. G. de Silva J.

clauses.text: No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the petitioner by police officers without reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence, without informing him of the reasons for arrest, and without producing him before a Magistrate within the prescribed time violated Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested by police officers without a warrant and without reasonable suspicion of any cognizable offence. He claimed that he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest, was detained at the police station for an extended period, and was not produced before a Magistrate within the time required by law. He asserted that these acts constituted violations of his fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioner was arrested on reasonable suspicion in connection with a criminal investigation and that the detention was necessary for the purpose of inquiry. They maintained that the arrest was lawful and that any delay in producing the petitioner before a Magistrate was justified by practical difficulties arising in the course of police duties.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that the power of arrest without a warrant must be exercised strictly in accordance with the law and only where reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence exists. Mere suspicion, curiosity, or desire to question a person does not justify arrest.

The Court found that the respondents failed to establish the existence of reasonable grounds for arresting the petitioner. There was no evidence that the petitioner had committed or was reasonably suspected of having committed a cognizable offence at the time of arrest. The failure to inform the petitioner of the reasons for his arrest constituted a clear violation of Article 13(1).

The Court further held that detention beyond the permissible period without producing the petitioner before a Magistrate violated Article 13(2) and the mandatory provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. Acts done by police officers in the exercise of arrest and detention powers constitute executive action, attracting State liability under Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 5,000 as compensation. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Arrest without a warrant must be based on reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence.
Police officers are under a constitutional duty to inform an arrested person of the reasons for arrest.
Detention without production before a Magistrate within the prescribed time violates Article 13(2).
Arrest for the mere purpose of questioning or inquiry is unlawful.
Acts of arrest and detention by police officers constitute executive action, giving rise to State liability under Article 126.
precedents_cited: Gunawardena v. Perera and Others [1983] 1 Sri L.R.
Namasivayam v. Gunawardena [1989] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Wijayasiriwardene v. Kumara, Inspector of Police and Two Others [1989] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 155 of 1987

case_title: Mrs. W. M. K. de Silva v. Chairman, Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation
judges: H. A. G. de Silva J.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the termination of the petitioner’s employment by the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, without assigning reasons and without affording a fair hearing, amounted to arbitrary and discriminatory executive action violating Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner was employed by the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation and had served continuously for several years. She claimed that her services were abruptly terminated by the Chairman of the Corporation without any reasons being given, without an inquiry, and without an opportunity to be heard. She alleged that similarly placed employees were retained in service, and that her termination was arbitrary, unreasonable, and discriminatory. She further contended that the termination deprived her of her livelihood and violated her right to engage in a lawful occupation.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioner was a temporary employee whose services could be terminated in accordance with the terms of her appointment. They argued that the decision to terminate her employment was an administrative decision taken in the interests of efficiency and reorganisation, and that no fundamental right was infringed. They denied any discrimination or arbitrariness and maintained that no reasons were required to be given.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that even where an employee is described as temporary, the employer, if it is a public corporation, is an instrumentality of the State and is bound by constitutional obligations. Administrative decisions affecting the livelihood of an employee must satisfy the test of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness under Article 12(1).

The Court found that the respondents failed to place before Court any material justifying the termination of the petitioner while retaining other similarly situated employees. The absence of reasons, coupled with unequal treatment, rendered the decision arbitrary and discriminatory. The Court further held that the petitioner had a legitimate expectation of being treated fairly, and that abrupt termination without inquiry or explanation violated basic standards of fairness.

Although Article 14(1)(g) does not guarantee a right to public employment, arbitrary termination by a State corporation that deprives a person of her livelihood may amount to an infringement when read together with Article 12(1).
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the termination of the petitioner’s employment violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The respondents were directed to pay the petitioner compensation in a sum of Rs. 15,000. No order was made as to reinstatement.
principles_established: Public corporations are organs of the State and are bound by the equality and non-arbitrariness requirements of Article 12(1).
Even temporary employees of State institutions are entitled to fair and non-discriminatory treatment.
Administrative decisions affecting livelihood must be supported by reasons and must not be arbitrary.
Unequal treatment of similarly placed employees, without justification, amounts to discrimination under Article 12(1).
While there is no fundamental right to public employment, arbitrary deprivation of livelihood by State action may attract constitutional scrutiny.
precedents_cited: Fernando v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority [1987] 1 Sri L.R. 329
Elmore Perera v. Montague Jayawickrema [1985] 1 Sri L.R. 285
source: Mrs. W. M. K. de Silva v. Chairman, Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation [1989] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 341 of 1987

case_title: Gamlath v. Neville Silva and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.
