legal_issue: Whether the transfer of the petitioner, a public officer, was motivated by political victimisation and constituted arbitrary and discriminatory administrative action in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner was a public officer who alleged that he was transferred from his post not for any administrative necessity but due to political victimisation arising from his perceived political affiliations and expressions. He contended that the transfer was punitive, mala fide, and designed to penalise him for exercising his freedom of expression. He further claimed that other similarly placed officers were not subjected to such adverse treatment, amounting to discrimination and a denial of equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the transfer was made purely on administrative grounds in the interest of efficient public service. They argued that transfers are incidents of public service and fall within the discretion of the appointing authority. The respondents denied any political motivation or mala fides and maintained that no fundamental right was infringed.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that while transfers are normally matters of administrative discretion, such discretion is subject to constitutional limitations. A transfer motivated by mala fides, political victimisation, or for an ulterior purpose is not protected by the doctrine that transfers are incidents of service.

The Court examined the surrounding circumstances, timing, and absence of any administrative justification for the transfer. It found that the respondents failed to place before Court any material demonstrating an objective administrative need for the petitioner’s transfer. The evidence pointed strongly to political considerations as the real motivating factor.

The Court held that political victimisation of a public officer constitutes arbitrary and discriminatory treatment. Penalising a person for perceived political views or expressions strikes at the heart of Article 12(1) and undermines the neutrality of the public service. Such action also has a chilling effect on the exercise of freedom of expression protected by Article 14(1)(a).
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the transfer of the petitioner was arbitrary, mala fide, and discriminatory, and therefore violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The respondents were directed to reinstate the petitioner to his former post or to a comparable post, and to pay compensation in a sum of Rs. 10,000. Costs were also awarded to the petitioner.
principles_established: Although transfers are incidents of public service, they are subject to constitutional scrutiny.
A transfer motivated by political victimisation or mala fides is arbitrary and violates Article 12(1).
Public officers are entitled to equal protection of the law against discriminatory administrative action.
The State bears the burden of justifying adverse administrative action once prima facie arbitrariness is shown.
Political neutrality of the public service is a constitutional value implicit in Article 12(1).
precedents_cited: Wijesuriya v. State Timber Corporation [1981] 2 Sri L.R. 1
Fernando v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority [1987] 1 Sri L.R. 329
Elmore Perera v. Montague Jayawickrema [1985] 1 Sri L.R. 285
source: Gamlath v. Neville Silva and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 36 of 1988

case_title: Premalal de Silva v. Inspector Rodrigo and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment while in police custody, and whether such conduct by police officers constituted executive or administrative action in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested by police officers without lawful basis and was thereafter detained in police custody where he was subjected to severe torture. He claimed that he was beaten with batons, assaulted with fists and boots, and subjected to inhuman treatment in order to extract information. He asserted that these acts caused him serious physical injuries and amounted to torture in violation of Article 11. He further alleged that the arrest was unlawful and not according to procedure established by law.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and ill-treatment. They contended that the petitioner was lawfully arrested in connection with a criminal investigation and that any injuries he sustained were either self-inflicted or caused during a lawful struggle at the time of arrest. The respondents relied on inconsistencies in the petitioner’s account and argued that the medical evidence did not conclusively establish torture while in police custody.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 11 embodies an absolute and non-derogable prohibition against torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The burden lay on the petitioner to establish the violation on a balance of probabilities, with a degree of probability commensurate with the seriousness of the allegation.

Upon evaluating the medical evidence and surrounding circumstances, the Court found that the petitioner had established that he sustained injuries while in police custody. The Court rejected attempts to explain the injuries as accidental or self-inflicted, noting that the nature and distribution of the injuries were consistent with assault. The Court emphasised that custodial violence is particularly grave, as a detainee is wholly under the control of the police and unable to protect himself.

The Court held that acts of torture committed by police officers in the course of their duties constitute executive action, attracting State liability under Article 126. It further held that even if the precise officer responsible cannot be identified with certainty, the State remains liable where the petitioner establishes that torture occurred while in police custody.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 11 of the Constitution had been violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 7,500 as compensation. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to take appropriate disciplinary action against the officers responsible. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute and non-derogable fundamental right admitting of no exceptions.
Torture or cruel treatment inflicted in police custody constitutes executive or administrative action.
The State is liable to pay compensation where a petitioner establishes that torture occurred while in police custody, even if individual officers are not conclusively identified.
Medical evidence plays a crucial role in establishing custodial torture.
Custodial violence is viewed with particular gravity because the detainee is under the complete control of the State.
precedents_cited: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Premalal de Silva v. Inspector Rodrigo and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 87 of 1989

case_title: Sirisena and Others v. Earnest Sirisena and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the failure of the police to prevent and respond to violent attacks on the petitioners by supporters of a Cabinet Minister, and the participation or acquiescence of police officers in such violence, amounted to arbitrary and discriminatory executive action violating Articles 12(1) and 11 of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that during a period of political tension and election-related violence, armed groups loyal to a Cabinet Minister attacked their homes, assaulted members of their families, caused extensive damage to property, and threatened their lives. They claimed that despite repeated complaints, the police failed to provide protection, refused to record complaints properly, and in some instances actively assisted or condoned the attacks. The petitioners contended that this selective failure of law enforcement deprived them of equal protection of the law and subjected them to cruel and inhuman treatment.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied any deliberate failure or discrimination on the part of the police. They contended that the incidents occurred in a volatile law-and-order situation and that the police acted to the best of their ability with limited resources. The respondents also denied that the attacks were politically motivated or that the police acted under the influence of the Minister or his supporters.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that Article 12(1) guarantees not only equal application of the law but also equal protection of the law. A deliberate or reckless failure by the police to protect citizens from violence, particularly where protection is afforded selectively, constitutes a denial of equal protection.

The Court examined the pattern of attacks, the political affiliations of the attackers, and the conduct of the police before, during, and after the incidents. It found that the police response was grossly inadequate and that there was clear evidence of partiality and acquiescence. The police failed to act promptly, discouraged complaints, and did not take effective steps to prevent repeated attacks.

The Court further held that exposure to sustained threats and violence, coupled with the collapse of law enforcement protection, amounted to cruel and inhuman treatment under Article 11. Acts and omissions of police officers in such circumstances constitute executive action for the purposes of Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 11 of the Constitution were violated. The respondents were directed to pay compensation to the petitioners in a total sum of Rs. 30,000. The Court also issued directions to the police authorities to ensure protection of the petitioners and proper investigation of the incidents.
principles_established: Article 12(1) guarantees equal protection of the law, including effective and impartial police protection.
Selective failure or refusal by the police to enforce the law amounts to discrimination under Article 12(1).
Omissions by State authorities, not merely positive acts, can constitute executive action infringing fundamental rights.
Sustained exposure to violence due to State inaction may amount to cruel and inhuman treatment under Article 11.
Political influence over law enforcement undermines the Rule of Law and attracts constitutional liability.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Gunawardena v. Perera and Others [1983] 1 Sri L.R.
Elmore Perera v. Montague Jayawickrema [1985] 1 Sri L.R. 285
source: Sirisena and Others v. Earnest Sirisena and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 352 of 1988

case_title: Chandra Kalyanie Perera and Another v. Captain Siriwardena and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the failure of the security forces to prevent an attack by armed men on the petitioners’ residence, and the conduct of members of the security forces before and after the incident, amounted to executive or administrative action violating Articles 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that their house was attacked at night by an armed group in an area under security force control. They claimed that despite the presence of the Army in the vicinity and prior warnings of danger, the security forces failed to provide protection. During the attack, the petitioners were terrorised, assaulted, and subjected to severe mental trauma. They further alleged that the subsequent response of the authorities was indifferent and ineffective, amounting to a denial of equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied responsibility for the attack and contended that the incident was carried out by unknown persons. They argued that the security forces could not be held responsible for every criminal act committed by third parties, and that reasonable steps had been taken in the circumstances to maintain law and order.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 12(1) guarantees equal protection of the law, which includes effective protection by law enforcement authorities. Where the State assumes control over an area through the presence of security forces, it bears a heightened duty to protect civilians within that area.

The Court held that serious omissions by State authorities, where they knew or ought to have known of a real risk to life and security, may constitute executive action. In the present case, the failure to provide protection despite prior knowledge of danger, coupled with the ineffective response after the incident, amounted to a denial of equal protection of the law.

The Court further held that exposure to extreme fear and mental anguish caused by such State failure can amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 11, even in the absence of direct physical torture by State agents.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioners compensation in a total sum of Rs. 25,000. Directions were also issued to ensure adequate protection and investigation.
principles_established: Equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) includes effective protection by law enforcement authorities.
Serious omissions by State authorities, where there is knowledge of a real risk, can constitute executive or administrative action.
The State bears a heightened duty to protect civilians in areas under security force control.
Severe mental trauma caused by State failure to protect may amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 11.
State responsibility may arise even where harm is inflicted by third parties, if State omissions materially contribute to the violation.
precedents_cited: Sirisena and Others v. Earnest Sirisena and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R.
Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.

case_title: Subbash Chandra Fernando v. Kapilaratne, Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment while in police custody, and whether the arrest and detention were carried out according to procedure established by law, in violation of Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested by police officers without being informed of the reasons for arrest and was detained at the police station where he was assaulted and subjected to cruel and inhuman treatment. He claimed that he was beaten during interrogation, causing physical injuries, and that such conduct amounted to torture in violation of Article 11.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and unlawful arrest. They contended that the petitioner was lawfully arrested in connection with a criminal investigation and that no assault or ill-treatment took place while he was in custody. They further argued that the petitioner failed to substantiate his allegations with reliable medical or independent evidence.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reiterated that Article 11 is an absolute and non-derogable right. However, the burden of proof lies on the petitioner to establish the violation on a balance of probabilities, with a degree of probability proportionate to the seriousness of the allegation.

On the evidence, the Court found that the petitioner failed to adduce convincing medical or corroborative material to establish that the alleged injuries were sustained while in police custody. The medical evidence did not support the claim of custodial torture, and there were inconsistencies in the petitioner’s narrative.

In regard to Article 13(1), the Court held that the petitioner had not established that he was arrested without being informed of the reasons for arrest. Accordingly, no violation of Article 13(1) was proved.

The Court emphasised that while allegations of custodial violence must be treated with utmost seriousness, findings must be based on credible and reliable evidence.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner failed to establish violations of Articles 11 or 13(1) of the Constitution. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute right, but the burden of proof rests on the petitioner to establish custodial torture on a balance of probabilities.
Credible medical or corroborative evidence is crucial in establishing allegations of torture.
Mere assertions of assault, without reliable supporting evidence, are insufficient to prove a violation of Article 11.
A petitioner must establish that he was not informed of the reasons for arrest in order to succeed under Article 13(1).
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.

case_title: Ansalin Fernando v. Sarath Perera, Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Chilaw

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was unlawfully arrested and subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment while in police custody, and whether such conduct by police officers constituted executive action in violation of Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested by police officers attached to the Chilaw Police Station without being informed of the reasons for arrest and without lawful basis. He claimed that while in police custody he was severely assaulted, beaten with batons, and subjected to cruel and inhuman treatment during interrogation. He asserted that these acts caused him physical injuries and mental suffering, amounting to torture in violation of Article 11.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and illegal arrest. They contended that the petitioner was lawfully arrested in connection with a criminal investigation and that no assault or ill-treatment occurred while he was in custody. They argued that the petitioner failed to prove his allegations with reliable medical or independent evidence.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 11 guarantees an absolute and non-derogable right against torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The burden lay on the petitioner to establish the violation on a balance of probabilities, with a degree of probability proportionate to the seriousness of the allegation.

On evaluation of the medical evidence, the Court found that the petitioner had sustained injuries consistent with assault. The nature and timing of the injuries supported the conclusion that they were inflicted while the petitioner was in police custody. The explanations offered by the respondents were rejected as implausible.

In regard to Article 13(1), the Court held that the respondents failed to establish that the petitioner was informed of the reasons for his arrest. Compelling a person to submit to police custody without such information constitutes an unlawful arrest.

The Court held that torture and illegal arrest by police officers constitute executive action for the purposes of Article 126, thereby attracting State liability.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 10,000 as compensation. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to take appropriate disciplinary action against the officers responsible. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute and non-derogable right admitting of no exceptions.
Torture or cruel treatment inflicted in police custody constitutes executive action.
Medical evidence plays a critical role in establishing custodial torture.
Failure to inform an arrested person of the reasons for arrest violates Article 13(1).
The State is liable to compensate victims of custodial torture and illegal arrest.
precedents_cited: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Premalal de Silva v. Inspector Rodrigo and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R.
Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.

case_title: Shanthi Chandrasekeram v. D. B. Wijetunga and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the removal of the petitioner from public office and the refusal to reappoint her were motivated by political considerations and amounted to arbitrary and discriminatory executive action violating Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a public officer, alleged that she was removed from her position and subsequently denied reappointment due to her perceived political views and associations. She claimed that there was no valid administrative reason for the adverse action taken against her, that similarly situated persons were treated differently, and that the decision was intended to punish her for exercising her freedom of expression. She contended that this amounted to political victimisation and a denial of equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the impugned decisions were taken on administrative grounds in the interest of efficiency and public service. They denied any political motivation or discrimination and argued that the petitioner had no vested right to continue in the post or to be reappointed.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that although matters such as appointment, removal, and reappointment to public office fall within the realm of administrative discretion, such discretion is subject to constitutional limitations. Where a petitioner establishes a prima facie case of arbitrariness or discrimination, the burden shifts to the State to justify its action.

On the evidence, the Court found that the respondents failed to place before Court any material demonstrating objective or rational administrative reasons for the petitioner’s removal and non-reappointment. The surrounding circumstances indicated that political considerations played a decisive role. The Court held that penalising a person for perceived political views or expression undermines democratic values and violates Article 12(1).

The Court further held that adverse administrative action taken on account of political expression has a chilling effect on the freedom of speech guaranteed by Article 14(1)(a), and therefore constitutes an additional constitutional violation.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution were violated. The respondents were directed to pay the petitioner compensation in a sum of Rs. 10,000. No order was made as to reinstatement.
principles_established: Administrative discretion in matters of public employment is subject to constitutional scrutiny.
Political victimisation constitutes arbitrary and discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1).
Once prima facie arbitrariness is shown, the burden lies on the State to justify its action.
Penalising a person for political views or expression violates both Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(a).
Public administration must be politically neutral to preserve equality before the law.
precedents_cited: Gamlath v. Neville Silva and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R.
Elmore Perera v. Montague Jayawickrema [1985] 1 Sri L.R. 285
Fernando v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority [1987] 1 Sri L.R. 329

case_title: Parameswary Jayathevan v. Attorney-General and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest, detention, disappearance, and presumed death of the petitioner’s son while in the custody or control of State security forces, together with the failure to conduct an effective investigation, amounted to violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, the mother of a young man, alleged that her son was arrested by members of the security forces and thereafter disappeared. She claimed that despite repeated complaints to police and other authorities, no meaningful investigation was conducted, no accountability was enforced, and she was denied information regarding her son’s fate. She contended that her son was subjected to torture and cruel treatment while in custody, leading to his death or disappearance, and that the State’s failure to investigate violated her right to equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied that the petitioner’s son was arrested or detained by the security forces. They contended that there was no reliable evidence linking State agents to the disappearance and that the authorities had taken reasonable steps to inquire into the complaint. They argued that responsibility could not be attributed to the State on the basis of speculation.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that direct proof of custodial torture or killing is rarely available in disappearance cases, and that constitutional adjudication must therefore rely on circumstantial evidence and reasonable inference. The Court found that the petitioner had established that her son was last seen in the custody or control of State agents and that the respondents failed to provide any credible explanation for his disappearance.

The Court emphasised that Article 11 protects not only against physical torture but also against treatment resulting in disappearance or death while in State custody. It further held that the State’s failure to conduct a prompt, effective, and impartial investigation into the disappearance constituted a continuing violation of Article 12(1), as the petitioner was denied equal protection of the law.

The Court also held that arrest without acknowledgment or disclosure violates Article 13(1). The combined acts and omissions of the authorities constituted executive action attracting State liability under Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner compensation in a sum of Rs. 50,000. The Court also directed the authorities to continue investigations into the disappearance.
principles_established: Disappearances following arrest by State agents may give rise to constitutional liability based on circumstantial evidence.
Article 11 encompasses protection against disappearance and death in State custody.
Failure to conduct an effective investigation into a disappearance constitutes a continuing violation of Article 12(1).
Unacknowledged detention violates Article 13(1) of the Constitution.
State responsibility arises from both acts and omissions of public authorities.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Sirisena and Others v. Earnest Sirisena and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Parameswary Jayathevan v. Attorney-General and Others [1992] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 416 of 1991

case_title: Ratnapala v. Dharmasiri, Headquarters Inspector, Ratnapura and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment while in police custody, whether his arrest and detention were carried out according to procedure established by law, and whether such conduct by police officers constituted executive action violating Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested by police officers attached to the Ratnapura Police without being informed of the reasons for arrest and was thereafter detained in custody where he was brutally assaulted. He claimed that he was beaten with batons and subjected to severe ill-treatment during interrogation, resulting in physical injuries. He contended that his detention was unlawful and that the acts complained of amounted to torture in violation of Article 11.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and unlawful detention. They contended that the petitioner was lawfully arrested in connection with a criminal investigation and that no assault took place while he was in custody. They relied on alleged inconsistencies in the petitioner’s account and sought to explain the injuries as having been sustained prior to arrest or during a lawful struggle.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 11 guarantees an absolute and non-derogable right against torture. The burden of proof rests on the petitioner, but the standard is the civil standard of proof, assessed with due regard to the seriousness of the allegation.

The Court placed considerable weight on the medical evidence, which revealed injuries consistent with assault. The timing and nature of the injuries supported the inference that they were inflicted while the petitioner was in police custody. The explanations offered by the respondents were found to be unsatisfactory and implausible.

The Court further held that the failure to inform the petitioner of the reasons for arrest violated Article 13(1), and that the prolonged detention without prompt production before a Magistrate violated Article 13(2). Acts of arrest, detention, and interrogation by police officers constitute executive action for the purposes of Article 126, thereby attracting State liability.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 15,000 as compensation. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to take disciplinary action against the officers responsible. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 11 is an absolute and non-derogable fundamental right.
Credible medical evidence is central to establishing custodial torture.
Injuries sustained while a person is under police control raise a strong inference of State responsibility.
Failure to inform an arrested person of the reasons for arrest violates Article 13(1).
Detention without prompt production before a Magistrate violates Article 13(2).
Acts of police officers in arrest and custody constitute executive action attracting State liability.
precedents_cited: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Premalal de Silva v. Inspector Rodrigo and Others [1991] 2 Sri L.R.
Ansalin Fernando v. Sarath Perera, Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Chilaw [1992] 1 Sri L.R.

case_title: Wimal Vidyamani v. Lt. Col. Jayatilleke and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest, detention, and ill-treatment of the petitioner by Army personnel amounted to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, whether the arrest was carried out according to procedure established by law, and whether such conduct constituted executive or administrative action violating Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was apprehended by Army personnel under the command of the 1st respondent, detained at an Army camp, and subjected to assault, intimidation, and degrading treatment. He claimed that he was held without being informed of the reasons for his arrest and without being produced before a Magistrate. He further alleged that the conduct of the Army officers was arbitrary, discriminatory, and violative of his fundamental rights.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied the allegations of torture and unlawful detention. They contended that the petitioner was taken into custody for questioning in connection with security operations during a period of unrest, and that any restraint imposed on him was reasonable and necessary. They argued that the actions taken were bona fide security measures and did not amount to violations of fundamental rights.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that members of the Armed Forces, when exercising powers affecting civilians, act as organs of the State and are bound by the fundamental rights provisions of the Constitution. Article 11 applies with equal force to acts of torture or cruel treatment committed by military personnel.

On an evaluation of the evidence, including medical material and the surrounding circumstances, the Court found that the petitioner had established that he was subjected to ill-treatment and intimidation while in military custody. The explanations offered by the respondents were found to be unsatisfactory. The Court further held that the petitioner was not informed of the reasons for his arrest, and that his detention was not carried out according to procedure established by law.

The Court emphasised that national security considerations do not justify the use of torture or arbitrary detention. Acts of arrest and detention by Army officers constitute executive action for the purposes of Article 126, thereby attracting State liability.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 25,000 as compensation. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Members of the Armed Forces are bound by fundamental rights when dealing with civilians.
Article 11 applies equally to acts of torture or cruel treatment committed by military personnel.
National security considerations do not justify torture or arbitrary detention.
Failure to inform a detainee of the reasons for arrest violates Article 13(1).
Acts of arrest and detention by security forces constitute executive action attracting State liability under Article 126.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Parameswary Jayathevan v. Attorney-General and Others [1992] 2 Sri L.R.

case_title: Channa Pieris and Others v. Attorney-General and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest, disappearance, and presumed death of the relatives of the petitioners following their apprehension by State security forces, together with the failure of the authorities to conduct effective investigations, amounted to violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, relatives of several young men, alleged that their family members were arrested by the Army and Police during security operations and were thereafter never seen again. Despite repeated complaints to the authorities, no meaningful investigation was conducted and no information was provided regarding their fate. The petitioners contended that the disappeared persons were subjected to torture and cruel treatment while in State custody leading to their deaths or enforced disappearance, and that the State’s failure to investigate denied them equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents denied that the disappeared persons were arrested or detained by State authorities. They contended that there was no direct evidence linking the security forces to the alleged disappearances and that the petitioners had failed to establish State responsibility. It was further argued that the claims were speculative and unsupported by proof.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that in cases of disappearances, direct evidence is rarely available, and constitutional adjudication must therefore rely on circumstantial evidence and reasonable inference. The Court found that the petitioners had established that the missing persons were last seen in the custody or control of State agents, and that the respondents failed to provide any plausible explanation for their subsequent disappearance.

The Court emphasised that Article 11 is violated not only by physical torture but also by enforced disappearance and custodial death. It further held that the failure of the authorities to conduct prompt, impartial, and effective investigations into disappearances constituted a continuing violation of Article 12(1), as the petitioners were denied equal protection of the law.

The Court also held that unacknowledged arrests and detentions violate Article 13(1). The cumulative acts and omissions of the State amounted to executive action attracting liability under Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay compensation to the petitioners, with sums ranging up to Rs. 100,000 depending on the application. The Court also directed the State to continue investigations into the disappearances.
principles_established: Enforced disappearance following arrest by State agents constitutes a violation of Article 11.
Circumstantial evidence and reasonable inference may be relied upon in disappearance cases.
Failure to conduct effective investigations into disappearances constitutes a continuing violation of Article 12(1).
Unacknowledged arrest and detention violate Article 13(1).
State responsibility arises from both acts and omissions of public authorities.
The burden shifts to the State to explain the fate of persons last seen in its custody.

The Court reaffirmed that Article 11 guarantees an absolute and non-derogable right against torture. In assessing the evidence, the Court placed significant weight on the medical reports, which revealed injuries consistent with assault. case_title: Ayasinghe v. Samarawickrema and Others
judges: G. P. S. de Silva C.J.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Provides that where a Member of Parliament ceases to be a member of a recognised political party, his seat shall become vacant.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the expulsion of the petitioner, a Member of Parliament, from his political party was lawful and in accordance with natural justice, and whether such expulsion—leading to the loss of his parliamentary seat—violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a Member of Parliament, alleged that he was expelled from his political party without being afforded a fair hearing and without compliance with the party constitution. He contended that the expulsion was mala fide, politically motivated, and intended to suppress dissenting views expressed by him. As the expulsion resulted in the automatic loss of his parliamentary seat under Article 99(13)(a), he claimed that his fundamental rights to equality and freedom of expression were violated.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the expulsion was carried out in accordance with the party constitution and that internal party disciplinary matters are not ordinarily justiciable. They argued that the petitioner had voluntarily subjected himself to party discipline and that the decision to expel him was taken by the competent authority within the party. They denied any violation of fundamental rights.
interpretation_summary:
The Court held that while political parties are voluntary associations, their decisions—when they have serious public consequences such as the loss of a parliamentary seat—are subject to constitutional scrutiny. Where expulsion from a party results in the deprivation of a constitutional office, the process must comply with principles of natural justice and fairness.

The Court found that the petitioner had not been afforded a fair opportunity to be heard and that the disciplinary process did not strictly comply with the party constitution. The Court emphasised that Article 99(13)(a) gives legal effect to party expulsion, thereby transforming what might otherwise be a private decision into one with constitutional consequences.

The Court further held that expulsion used as a means to punish or silence political expression within a party undermines democratic values and may violate Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a). The burden lay on the respondents to justify the fairness and legality of the expulsion, which they failed to do.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the expulsion of the petitioner from the political party was invalid and that the consequent loss of his parliamentary seat was unlawful. The Court granted relief to the petitioner, declaring that his fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) had been violated.
principles_established: Decisions of political parties are subject to judicial review when they have constitutional consequences.
Expulsion of a Member of Parliament must comply with principles of natural justice.
Article 99(13)(a) gives constitutional effect to party expulsion, attracting constitutional scrutiny.
Political parties cannot use disciplinary powers to suppress internal dissent or freedom of expression.
Unfair or mala fide party expulsions may violate Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a).

Karunatilleke v. Dayananda Dissanayake [1999] 1 Sri L.R. 157

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.

legal_issue: Whether the arbitrary refusal by State authorities to permit the petitioner to carry on a lawful activity, without rational justification and in a discriminatory manner, violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that State authorities had arbitrarily refused permission for him to engage in a lawful activity, despite his compliance with all relevant legal requirements. He contended that similarly situated persons were granted such permission and that the refusal was motivated by extraneous considerations, amounting to discrimination and a violation of his freedom of expression and equal protection of the law.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the decision complained of was taken in the exercise of administrative discretion and in the public interest. They denied arbitrariness or discrimination and argued that the petitioner had no absolute right to the permission sought.

The Court reaffirmed that while administrative authorities possess discretion, such discretion must be exercised reasonably, fairly, and without discrimination. Where a petitioner establishes prima facie arbitrariness, the burden lies on the State to justify its decision.

The Court found that the respondents failed to provide any rational or objective basis for treating the petitioner differently from others in similar circumstances. The absence of clear reasons and the unequal application of standards rendered the impugned decision arbitrary.

The Court further held that arbitrary administrative action has a chilling effect on freedom of expression protected by Article 14(1)(a), and that denial of equal treatment in the exercise of discretionary power violates Article 12(1).

legal_issue: Whether the disciplinary and administrative action taken against the petitioner by the respondent authority was arbitrary, unreasonable, and discriminatory, amounting to a violation of the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, a public officer, alleged that adverse administrative and disciplinary action was taken against him without a proper inquiry, without affording him a fair opportunity to be heard, and without objective justification. He contended that similarly situated officers were treated more favourably and that the impugned action was motivated by extraneous considerations, thereby violating Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondent maintained that the action complained of was taken within the scope of lawful administrative discretion and in accordance with applicable regulations. interpretation_summary:

Where executive or administrative power is exercised capriciously, without rational basis, or inconsistently in comparable situations, it violates the guarantee of equal protection of the law.

The Court examined the manner in which the disciplinary process was conducted and found that the respondents failed to demonstrate any objective or rational basis for the differential treatment of the petitioner. The absence of clear reasons, coupled with procedural unfairness, rendered the decision arbitrary.

The Court emphasised that even in matters of discipline and internal administration, public authorities are bound by constitutional standards of fairness, reasonableness, and equality.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(1) of the Constitution was violated. The Court granted relief to the petitioner and awarded compensation. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary exercise of administrative and disciplinary power.
Public authorities must act on rational and objective grounds when disciplining public officers.
Differential treatment of similarly situated persons without justification violates equal protection of the law.
Procedural unfairness may itself be evidence of arbitrariness under Article 12(1).
Administrative discretion is subject to constitutional review under Article 126.

legal_issue: Whether the detention of a minor girl by police officers without lawful basis, without production before a Magistrate, and under coercive circumstances amounted to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and illegal detention in violation of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an Attorney-at-Law acting on behalf of a minor girl, alleged that the child was taken into police custody without lawful arrest, detained for prolonged periods, and subjected to intimidation and coercive questioning. interpretation_summary:
The Court held that the Constitution affords heightened protection to children and that any deprivation of liberty of a minor must strictly comply with constitutional and statutory safeguards. The Court found that the minor was in fact detained under police control and that the explanations offered by the respondents were unconvincing.

The Court emphasised that detention without lawful arrest and without production before a Magistrate violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2). It further held that subjecting a child to prolonged police custody, intimidation, and psychological pressure amounts to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment under Article 11.

The Court reaffirmed that acts of police officers constitute executive action under Article 126, attracting State liability, and that vulnerability of the victim is a critical factor in assessing the severity of the violation.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the minor’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution were violated. No order was made as to costs.
