precedents_cited: Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
Abasin Banda v. S. I. Gunaratne and Others [1995] 1 Sri L.R.
Rifaideen v. Sub-Inspector of Police, Jayalath, Wellawatte Police Station [1998] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Priyankara v. P.C. Sisira Kumara, Police Station, Puttalam and Others [1998] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 683 of 1995

case_title: Dissanayake, Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of K. M. Lal) v. Sujeewa, Sub-Inspector of Police and Others

clauses.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the detention of a minor by police officers without lawful arrest, without production before a Magistrate, and under coercive conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and illegal detention in violation of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner, an Attorney-at-Law acting on behalf of a minor boy, alleged that the child was taken into police custody without lawful arrest and detained for prolonged periods for purposes of interrogation. It was contended that the child was intimidated and subjected to psychological pressure, was not produced before a Magistrate, and that the conduct of the police amounted to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, especially considering the age and vulnerability of the child.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the minor was not formally arrested and was kept at the police station only for purposes of inquiry. They denied any ill-treatment and argued that the actions taken were bona fide and in the interests of investigation.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that children are entitled to heightened constitutional protection and that any form of detention of a minor must strictly comply with constitutional safeguards. The Court found that the minor was in fact detained under police control and that the explanations offered by the respondents were unconvincing.

The Court held that detention without lawful arrest and without production before a Magistrate violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2). It further held that subjecting a child to prolonged police custody and psychological pressure amounts to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment under Article 11.

The Court emphasised that acts of police officers constitute executive action under Article 126 and that the vulnerability of the victim is a crucial factor in assessing the gravity of a fundamental rights violation.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the minor’s fundamental rights under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution were violated. The State was ordered to pay compensation in a sum of Rs. 40,000. The Inspector-General of Police was directed to take appropriate disciplinary action against the officers responsible. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Children are entitled to heightened constitutional protection against abuse of State power.
Detention of a minor without lawful arrest and without production before a Magistrate violates Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
Psychological coercion and intimidation of a child may amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 11.
Police conduct affecting personal liberty constitutes executive action under Article 126.
The vulnerability of the victim is a critical factor in assessing custodial violations.
precedents_cited: Nalika Kumudini, Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of Malsha Kumari) v. Nihal Mahindasena and Others [1997] 3 Sri L.R.
Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Amal Sudath Silva v. Kodituwakku, Inspector of Police and Others [1987] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Dissanayake, Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of K. M. Lal) v. Sujeewa, Sub-Inspector of Police and Others [1998] 2 Sri L.R., S.C. Application No. 721 of 1995

case_title: Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the executive or administrative action complained of was arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory so as to constitute a violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether such action was amenable to review under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the respondents, acting in their official capacities, exercised executive or administrative power in an arbitrary and unreasonable manner, resulting in unequal treatment and a denial of equal protection of the law. The petitioner contended that the impugned decision lacked a rational basis and was therefore unconstitutional.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the action complained of was taken lawfully within the scope of executive discretion. They argued that Article 12(1) does not prohibit all differentiation and that the petitioner had failed to establish discrimination or arbitrariness sufficient to attract constitutional liability.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the scope of Article 12(1) under the newly enacted 1978 Constitution and held that the guarantee of equality before the law includes protection against arbitrary executive or administrative action. While reasonable classification and discretion are permissible, such power must be exercised on rational and objective grounds.

The Court emphasised that Article 126 confers a special and exclusive jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to review executive or administrative action alleged to infringe fundamental rights. Where an action is shown to be arbitrary or lacking a reasonable basis, it may amount to a denial of equal protection of the law.

The Court clarified that not every error or adverse decision gives rise to a fundamental rights violation; the petitioner must establish arbitrariness, mala fides, or discrimination.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner had failed to establish that the impugned executive action was arbitrary or discriminatory so as to violate Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
principles_established: Article 12(1) protects against arbitrary and unreasonable executive or administrative action.
Reasonable classification and discretion are permissible, but must be based on rational and objective grounds.
Not every adverse or incorrect administrative decision amounts to a fundamental rights violation.
Article 126 confers exclusive jurisdiction on the Supreme Court to determine alleged infringements of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.
The burden lies on the petitioner to establish arbitrariness or discrimination.
source: Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Perera v. Premadasa

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the executive action complained of, taken by the Prime Minister in the exercise of political and administrative discretion, was arbitrary or discriminatory so as to amount to a violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether such action was justiciable under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the respondent, acting in an executive capacity, exercised power in an arbitrary and discriminatory manner, thereby denying the petitioner equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1). It was contended that the decision lacked fairness and was motivated by improper considerations.
respondent_argument: The respondent contended that the action complained of fell within the sphere of legitimate executive and political discretion. It was argued that Article 12(1) does not prohibit all differentiation and that the petitioner had failed to establish arbitrariness, mala fides, or unequal treatment amounting to a constitutional violation.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the scope of Article 12(1) in relation to executive and political decision-making under the 1978 Constitution. It held that while Article 12(1) protects individuals against arbitrary executive action, it does not convert every political or administrative decision into a justiciable fundamental rights issue.

The Court emphasised that a clear distinction must be maintained between unlawful discrimination and permissible executive discretion exercised for policy or political reasons. Judicial intervention is warranted only where arbitrariness, mala fides, or unequal treatment is clearly established.

On the facts, the Court found that the petitioner had failed to demonstrate that the impugned action was arbitrary or discriminatory in the constitutional sense.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established and that the executive action complained of did not warrant interference under Article 126.
principles_established: Article 12(1) protects against arbitrary executive action but does not make all political decisions justiciable.
Executive and political discretion is permissible provided it is exercised on rational grounds.
Judicial review under Article 126 is limited to clear cases of arbitrariness, discrimination, or mala fides.
The burden lies on the petitioner to establish unequal treatment in the constitutional sense.
Courts must maintain a distinction between policy decisions and unconstitutional discrimination.
source: Perera v. Premadasa [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Rienzie Perera and Another v. University Grants Commission and Another

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the criteria and methodology adopted by the University Grants Commission for university admissions amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory treatment in violation of Articles 12(1) and 12(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, who were eligible candidates for university admission, alleged that the admissions scheme implemented by the University Grants Commission was arbitrary and discriminatory. They contended that the selection criteria resulted in unequal treatment of similarly situated candidates and denied them equal protection of the law guaranteed under Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the admissions scheme was based on reasonable classification and objective criteria designed to achieve educational equity. They argued that the University Grants Commission acted within its statutory mandate and that the policy was neither arbitrary nor discriminatory in the constitutional sense.
interpretation_summary:
The Court undertook a detailed examination of the scope of the equality guarantee under Articles 12(1) and 12(2). It held that equality does not mean identical treatment in all circumstances and that reasonable classification is permissible if it is founded on an intelligible differentia and bears a rational nexus to a legitimate objective.

In the context of university admissions, the Court recognised that the State is entitled to adopt policies aimed at correcting social and educational imbalances, provided such policies are based on objective criteria and are not arbitrary. The Court found that the admissions scheme challenged by the petitioners was supported by rational considerations and did not amount to invidious discrimination.

The Court emphasised that judicial review under Article 126 is concerned with constitutionality, not with the wisdom or desirability of policy choices.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the applications, holding that the university admissions scheme did not violate Articles 12(1) or 12(2) of the Constitution and that no fundamental rights infringement had been established.
principles_established: Equality under Article 12 does not require identical treatment in all cases.
Reasonable classification is permissible if based on intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to a legitimate objective.
University admissions policies may validly incorporate equity-based considerations.
Courts will not interfere with policy decisions unless they are shown to be arbitrary or discriminatory.
Article 126 jurisdiction is limited to constitutional review, not policy evaluation.
source: Rienzie Perera and Another v. University Grants Commission and Another [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Seneviratne and Another v. University Grants Commission and Another

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any such grounds.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the university admissions criteria and standardisation policy adopted by the University Grants Commission amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory treatment in violation of Articles 12(1) and 12(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, who were students eligible for university admission, alleged that the admissions scheme implemented by the University Grants Commission resulted in unequal and discriminatory treatment. They contended that the standardisation process unfairly disadvantaged certain candidates and violated their right to equal protection of the law under Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the admissions policy was based on reasonable classification and objective criteria intended to address disparities in educational opportunity. They maintained that the policy was formulated in the public interest, fell within the statutory mandate of the University Grants Commission, and did not constitute unconstitutional discrimination.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed the principles laid down in *Rienzie Perera v. University Grants Commission*. It held that equality under Article 12 does not require identical treatment in all circumstances and that reasonable classification is constitutionally permissible if founded on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to a legitimate objective.

In the sphere of university admissions, the Court recognised that the State may adopt policies aimed at promoting educational equity and correcting structural imbalances. Judicial review under Article 126 is confined to examining whether such policies are arbitrary or discriminatory, not whether they are desirable or optimal.

On the facts, the Court found that the admissions scheme was supported by rational considerations and did not amount to invidious discrimination prohibited by Articles 12(1) or 12(2).
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the applications, holding that the university admissions policy did not violate Articles 12(1) or 12(2) of the Constitution and that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established.
principles_established: Equality under Article 12 permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia.
University admissions policies may validly incorporate equity-based considerations.
Courts will not interfere with education policy unless it is shown to be arbitrary or discriminatory.
Judicial review under Article 126 is limited to constitutional scrutiny, not policy evaluation.
Standardisation in admissions is not per se unconstitutional.
precedents_cited: Rienzie Perera and Another v. University Grants Commission and Another [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Seneviratne and Another v. University Grants Commission and Another [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Samarasinghe v. The Bank of Ceylon Ltd.

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the actions of the Bank of Ceylon, a State-owned commercial bank, amounted to executive or administrative action amenable to fundamental rights review under Article 126, and whether the petitioner’s right to equal protection under Article 12(1) was violated.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the Bank of Ceylon, acting through its officers, treated him arbitrarily and unfairly in the discharge of its functions. He contended that the Bank, being wholly owned and controlled by the State, was an instrumentality of the State and that its actions infringed his fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondent Bank contended that it was acting in its capacity as a commercial banking institution and not in the exercise of executive or administrative power. It was argued that purely commercial or contractual activities of a State-owned bank do not constitute executive or administrative action within the meaning of Article 126.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the nature of the Bank of Ceylon and the character of the impugned acts. It held that not every act of a State-owned corporation amounts to executive or administrative action. Where such an entity acts purely in the sphere of commerce or contract, its actions may fall outside the scope of Article 126.

The Court emphasised that the fundamental rights jurisdiction is confined to executive or administrative action and does not extend to ordinary private law disputes merely because one party is a State-owned body. The decisive factor is the nature of the power exercised, not the ownership of the institution.

On the facts, the Court found that the petitioner had failed to establish that the Bank was exercising executive or administrative authority as opposed to commercial discretion.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner had failed to establish that the impugned actions of the Bank of Ceylon constituted executive or administrative action or that there was a violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
principles_established: Article 126 applies only to executive or administrative action.
Not every act of a State-owned corporation is subject to fundamental rights review.
Commercial or contractual decisions of State entities may fall outside Article 126.
The nature of the power exercised, not State ownership alone, determines justiciability.
Fundamental rights jurisdiction cannot be used to convert private law disputes into constitutional claims.
source: Samarasinghe v. The Bank of Ceylon Ltd. [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Gnanatilleke v. Attorney-General and Another; Sirimane v. Attorney-General

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the executive or administrative action challenged by the petitioners amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory treatment in violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether such action was subject to review under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that the respondents, acting in their official capacities, exercised executive power in a manner that resulted in unequal and unfair treatment. They contended that similarly situated persons were treated differently without reasonable justification, thereby violating their right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the actions complained of were taken in accordance with law and within the scope of executive discretion. They argued that any differentiation was based on reasonable considerations and did not amount to unconstitutional discrimination.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the scope of the equality guarantee under Article 12(1) and reaffirmed that equality before the law does not require identical treatment in all circumstances. The Constitution permits reasonable classification, provided it is founded on intelligible differentia and bears a rational nexus to a legitimate objective.

The Court emphasised that judicial review under Article 126 is concerned with constitutional violations, not with correcting every perceived error or unfairness in executive decision-making. Only actions that are arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory in the constitutional sense attract liability.

On the facts of both applications, the Court found that the petitioners failed to establish that the impugned actions were arbitrary or discriminatory.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed both applications, holding that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established.
principles_established: Article 12(1) guarantees protection against arbitrary and discriminatory executive action.
Reasonable classification is constitutionally permissible if based on intelligible differentia.
Not every instance of unequal treatment amounts to a fundamental rights violation.
Judicial review under Article 126 is limited to constitutional scrutiny.
The burden of proving arbitrariness or discrimination lies on the petitioner.
source: Gnanatilleke v. Attorney-General and Another; Sirimane v. Attorney-General [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Palihawadana v. Attorney-General and Two Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the executive or administrative action complained of was arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory so as to violate the petitioner’s right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether such action was justiciable under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the respondents, acting in their official capacities, exercised executive power in an arbitrary and unreasonable manner resulting in unequal treatment. It was contended that the impugned action lacked a rational basis and therefore infringed the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the action complained of was taken lawfully within the scope of executive or administrative discretion. They argued that Article 12(1) does not prohibit all differentiation and that the petitioner had failed to establish arbitrariness or discrimination of a constitutional nature.
interpretation_summary:
The Court examined the scope of Article 12(1) under the 1978 Constitution and reaffirmed that equality before the law protects individuals against arbitrary and irrational executive action. However, the Court emphasised that not every adverse or unfair decision amounts to a fundamental rights violation.

The Court held that judicial review under Article 126 is limited to cases where arbitrariness, mala fides, or discriminatory treatment is clearly established. Where executive discretion is exercised on rational grounds, courts will not substitute their judgment for that of the decision-maker.

On the facts, the Court found that the petitioner had failed to establish that the impugned action was arbitrary or discriminatory in the constitutional sense.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established and that the executive action complained of did not warrant interference under Article 126.
principles_established: Article 12(1) protects against arbitrary and unreasonable executive action.
Not every instance of unequal or adverse treatment constitutes a fundamental rights violation.
Executive discretion is permissible if exercised on rational and objective grounds.
Judicial review under Article 126 is confined to clear cases of arbitrariness or discrimination.
Courts will not interfere with executive decisions merely because they appear unfair or incorrect.
source: Palihawadana v. Attorney-General and Two Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Janatha Finance and Investments Ltd. v. Liyanage and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether actions arising out of a commercial and contractual dispute between a private finance company and other parties could be characterised as executive or administrative action so as to attract the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 126, and whether Article 12(1) was violated.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner company alleged that it was subjected to unfair and unequal treatment in connection with actions taken by the respondents, resulting in a denial of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). It was contended that the conduct complained of justified constitutional intervention by the Supreme Court.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the dispute was purely commercial and contractual in nature and did not involve any exercise of executive or administrative power. They argued that Article 126 jurisdiction cannot be invoked to resolve private law disputes merely by framing them as fundamental rights violations.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that the fundamental rights jurisdiction under Article 126 is confined to infringements arising from executive or administrative action. It emphasised that not every unfairness, illegality, or contractual dispute can be converted into a constitutional claim.

The Court examined the nature of the acts complained of and held that they arose from private commercial dealings and contractual obligations. Such matters fall within the realm of ordinary civil law and are to be resolved through appropriate civil proceedings, not through fundamental rights applications.

The Court further held that Article 12(1) is not intended to constitutionalise private disputes in which no executive or administrative power is exercised.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the dispute was not amenable to fundamental rights review under Article 126 and that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established.
principles_established: Article 126 jurisdiction is limited to executive or administrative action.
Private commercial or contractual disputes cannot be converted into fundamental rights applications.
Article 12(1) does not apply to purely private law disputes.
The nature of the power exercised, not the allegation of unfairness, determines justiciability.
Fundamental rights jurisdiction cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary civil remedies.
precedents_cited: Samarasinghe v. The Bank of Ceylon Ltd. [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Janatha Finance and Investments Ltd. v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arbitrary and unreasonable exercise of executive or administrative power by public authorities, even in the absence of hostile discrimination between classes, constitutes a violation of the right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that the respondents, acting in the exercise of executive and administrative authority, treated them in an arbitrary, unreasonable, and unfair manner. They contended that such arbitrary action, lacking objective justification and procedural fairness, violated their fundamental right to equal protection of the law guaranteed by Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that Article 12(1) is concerned primarily with discrimination between persons or classes and that, in the absence of proof of unequal treatment vis-à-vis others, no violation of Article 12(1) could be established. They argued that mere unfairness or error in decision-making does not amount to a constitutional infringement.
interpretation_summary:
The Court delivered a seminal interpretation of Article 12(1), holding that the guarantee of equal protection of the law is not confined to cases of class-based discrimination. The Court held that arbitrariness is antithetical to equality, and that an arbitrary or capricious exercise of executive or administrative power, even if applied uniformly, violates Article 12(1).

The Court emphasised that equality before the law requires public authorities to act fairly, reasonably, and on the basis of relevant considerations. Decisions taken without rational basis, or in disregard of procedural fairness, are constitutionally infirm.

This judgment marked a significant expansion of Sri Lankan equality jurisprudence by constitutionalising the concept of non-arbitrariness and embedding substantive fairness within Article 12(1).
outcome: The Supreme Court upheld the petitioners’ claims and granted relief, holding that the arbitrary and unreasonable actions of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
principles_established: Arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality under Article 12(1).
Article 12(1) is not confined to class-based or comparative discrimination.
Arbitrary, capricious, or unreasonable executive action violates equal protection of the law.
Equality before the law includes a guarantee of fairness and rationality in public decision-making.
Article 126 empowers the Supreme Court to review executive action for arbitrariness.
precedents_cited: Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
Palihawadana v. Attorney-General and Two Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Wijeratne and Another v. The People’s Bank and Another

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the actions of the People’s Bank, a State-owned banking institution, in relation to its dealings with the petitioners constituted executive or administrative action subject to review under Article 126, and whether such actions violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that the People’s Bank acted arbitrarily and unfairly in its dealings with them, resulting in unequal treatment and a denial of equal protection of the law. They contended that the Bank, being wholly State-owned and controlled, was an instrumentality of the State and that its actions infringed their fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the actions complained of arose from ordinary commercial and contractual dealings of the Bank. They argued that such acts did not amount to executive or administrative action and therefore did not fall within the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 126.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed the principle that Article 126 applies only to infringements arising from executive or administrative action. It held that the mere fact that an institution is State-owned does not automatically render all its actions subject to fundamental rights review.

The decisive factor is the nature of the power exercised. Where a State-owned bank acts purely in a commercial or contractual capacity, its actions fall within the realm of private law and are not amenable to constitutional review. The Court found that the petitioners’ grievances arose out of contractual banking transactions and not the exercise of executive or administrative authority.

Accordingly, the Court held that Article 12(1) was not attracted and that the application was misconceived.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the actions of the People’s Bank complained of did not constitute executive or administrative action and that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established.
principles_established: Article 126 applies only to executive or administrative action.
Not all actions of State-owned corporations are subject to fundamental rights review.
Commercial and contractual acts of State banks fall outside Article 126.
State ownership alone does not determine constitutional justiciability.
Fundamental rights jurisdiction cannot be used to resolve private banking disputes.
precedents_cited: Samarasinghe v. The Bank of Ceylon Ltd. [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
Janatha Finance and Investments Ltd. v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Wijeratne and Another v. The People’s Bank and Another [1984] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Edirisuriya v. Navaratnam and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the impugned administrative actions taken by the respondents were arbitrary, unreasonable, and procedurally unfair, thereby violating the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the respondents, acting in the exercise of statutory and administrative powers, treated him unfairly and without due process. It was contended that the decisions complained of were taken without affording him a fair opportunity to be heard, were based on irrelevant considerations, and amounted to arbitrary executive action violating Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the actions complained of were taken lawfully within the scope of their statutory authority. They argued that the decisions were made in good faith, on relevant considerations, and did not amount to discrimination or arbitrariness of a constitutional nature.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 12(1) is violated not only by overt discrimination but also by arbitrary and unreasonable exercise of executive or administrative power. Where statutory discretion is exercised without adherence to basic principles of fairness and rationality, such action is constitutionally infirm.

The Court emphasised that procedural fairness is an integral aspect of equality before the law. Decisions affecting rights or legitimate expectations must be taken after affording the affected party a reasonable opportunity to be heard and must be supported by relevant and rational considerations.

On the facts, the Court found that the respondents failed to act fairly and reasonably, and that the impugned decisions were tainted by arbitrariness.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been violated. Appropriate relief was granted to the petitioner. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary and unreasonable administrative action.
Procedural fairness is an essential component of equal protection of the law.
Statutory discretion must be exercised on relevant and rational grounds.
Failure to afford a fair hearing may render administrative action unconstitutional.
Article 126 empowers the Supreme Court to review misuse of administrative power.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Edirisuriya v. Navaratnam and Others [1985] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Elmore Perera v. Major Montague Jayawickrama, Minister of Public and Plantation Industries and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the exercise of ministerial and administrative power by the respondents was arbitrary, unreasonable, and influenced by extraneous considerations, thereby violating the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the Minister and other respondents exercised statutory and administrative powers in an arbitrary and unfair manner, disregarding relevant considerations and procedural fairness. It was contended that the impugned decisions were motivated by improper considerations and resulted in unequal treatment, amounting to a violation of Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the decisions complained of were taken lawfully within the scope of ministerial discretion and in the public interest. They argued that the petitioner had no vested right to insist on a particular administrative outcome and that no constitutional violation had been established.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 12(1) is violated not only by discriminatory classification but also by arbitrary or capricious exercise of executive or administrative power. Ministerial discretion, though wide, is not unfettered and must be exercised on rational grounds and for proper purposes.

The Court emphasised that where decisions are influenced by extraneous considerations, political pressure, or personal bias, such action is constitutionally infirm. Equality before the law requires fairness, objectivity, and reasonableness in the exercise of public power.

On the facts, the Court found that the respondents failed to justify the impugned actions on rational and objective grounds, and that the petitioner had been subjected to unequal and unfair treatment.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been violated. The Court granted appropriate relief to the petitioner. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary and capricious exercise of ministerial power.
Ministerial and administrative discretion must be exercised for proper purposes and on rational grounds.
Equality before the law includes protection against decisions influenced by extraneous considerations.
Political or personal considerations cannot justify unequal administrative treatment.
Article 126 empowers the Supreme Court to review misuse of executive and ministerial power.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Edirisuriya v. Navaratnam and Others [1985] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Elmore Perera v. Major Montague Jayawickrama, Minister of Public and Plantation Industries and Others [1985] 1 Sri L.R. 285, Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Mallikarachchi v. Shiva Pasupathi, Attorney-General

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the exercise of prosecutorial discretion by the Attorney-General in instituting or continuing criminal proceedings was arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory so as to violate the petitioner’s fundamental right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the Attorney-General acted arbitrarily and unfairly in the exercise of prosecutorial discretion, subjecting the petitioner to unequal treatment when compared with others similarly situated. It was contended that the decision to prosecute was influenced by extraneous considerations and lacked a rational basis, thereby violating Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondent contended that the institution and conduct of criminal proceedings fall within the lawful discretion of the Attorney-General. It was argued that prosecutorial discretion is exercised on the basis of available evidence and public interest considerations, and that the petitioner had failed to establish arbitrariness or discrimination of a constitutional nature.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that the exercise of prosecutorial discretion by the Attorney-General constitutes executive action and is therefore subject to constitutional scrutiny under Article 126. While recognising that the Attorney-General enjoys a wide discretion in deciding whether to institute or continue prosecutions, the Court emphasised that such discretion is not unfettered.

The Court held that prosecutorial decisions must be based on rational and objective considerations and must not be influenced by mala fides, extraneous considerations, or unequal treatment. Arbitrary or discriminatory exercise of prosecutorial power offends the guarantee of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).

On the facts, however, the Court found that the petitioner had failed to establish that the Attorney-General acted arbitrarily or discriminatorily in the constitutional sense.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established and that the exercise of prosecutorial discretion in the circumstances did not warrant constitutional interference.
principles_established: Prosecutorial discretion constitutes executive action subject to review under Article 126.
The Attorney-General’s discretion in instituting prosecutions is wide but not unfettered.
Arbitrary or discriminatory exercise of prosecutorial power violates Article 12(1).
Courts will not interfere with prosecutorial decisions unless mala fides, arbitrariness, or unequal treatment is clearly established.
Equality before the law applies to the exercise of prosecutorial as well as administrative power.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Mallikarachchi v. Shiva Pasupathi, Attorney-General [1985] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Kularatne v. Chandrananda de Silva and Another

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the petitioner by police officers, without lawful basis and without adherence to due process, amounted to arbitrary and discriminatory executive action violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was arrested and detained by the respondents without being informed of the reasons for arrest and without any lawful justification. He contended that the police acted arbitrarily and abused their powers, thereby violating his right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) and his right against unlawful arrest under Article 13(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the arrest was lawful and carried out in connection with a police investigation. They argued that the actions taken were within the scope of their statutory powers and did not amount to arbitrariness or discrimination in the constitutional sense.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that police powers of arrest constitute executive action subject to constitutional scrutiny under Article 126. It emphasised that equality before the law requires that coercive powers be exercised strictly in accordance with law and on rational grounds.

The Court held that an arrest made without lawful basis or without informing the arrested person of the reasons for arrest is inherently arbitrary. Such arbitrariness offends both Article 13(1), which safeguards personal liberty, and Article 12(1), which prohibits unequal and unreasonable exercise of State power.

On the facts, the Court found that the respondents failed to establish a lawful basis for the petitioner’s arrest and that the detention was tainted by arbitrariness.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution had been violated. The Court granted appropriate relief and awarded compensation to the petitioner. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Police powers of arrest constitute executive action subject to review under Article 126.
Arbitrary arrest violates both Article 13(1) and the guarantee of equality under Article 12(1).
Failure to inform an arrested person of the reasons for arrest renders the arrest unconstitutional.
Equality before the law requires that coercive State powers be exercised strictly according to law.
Abuse of police discretion amounts to unconstitutional executive action.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Wijesinghe v. Attorney-General and Others [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Kularatne v. Chandrananda de Silva and Another [1985] 2 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Abeywickrema v. Pathirana and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of speech and expression including publication.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the impugned executive action taken against the petitioner, purportedly under emergency or security-related powers, was arbitrary, discriminatory, and motivated by political considerations, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the respondents, acting in the exercise of executive authority, subjected him to adverse action because of his political views and activities. He contended that the measures taken against him were not supported by objective or lawful justification, were politically motivated, and amounted to unequal treatment and an unjustified restriction on his freedom of expression.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the actions complained of were taken lawfully in the interests of public order and security. They argued that the petitioner had no fundamental right to insist on immunity from such action and that the measures taken were within the scope of executive discretion.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 12(1) prohibits not only overt discrimination but also arbitrary and unreasonable executive action. Where State power is exercised on political grounds or without objective justification, such action is constitutionally infirm.

The Court further held that restrictions on freedom of expression under Article 14(1)(a) must have a clear legal basis and must be proportionate to a legitimate objective. Executive action taken under the guise of public order, but in reality motivated by political considerations, cannot be sustained.

On the facts, the Court found that the respondents failed to establish a rational and lawful basis for the impugned action and that the petitioner had been subjected to unequal and unfair treatment.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution had been violated. The Court granted appropriate relief to the petitioner. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Article 12(1) prohibits arbitrary and politically motivated executive action.
Equality before the law includes protection against selective or punitive use of State power.
Restrictions on freedom of expression must be supported by lawful and proportionate justification.
Executive discretion exercised for improper or extraneous purposes violates fundamental rights.
Article 126 empowers the Supreme Court to scrutinise misuse of emergency or security powers.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Elmore Perera v. Major Montague Jayawickrama and Others [1985] 1 Sri L.R.
Mallikarachchi v. Shiva Pasupathi, Attorney-General [1985] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Abeywickrema v. Pathirana and Others [1986] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: C. W. Mackie & Co. Ltd. v. Hugh Molagoda, Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the assessment and collection of income tax by the Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue, alleged to be erroneous or unfair, amounted to arbitrary or discriminatory administrative action violating Article 12(1) of the Constitution and was amenable to review under Article 126.
petitioner_claim: The petitioner company alleged that the Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue acted arbitrarily and unfairly in making tax assessments and in refusing relief sought by the company. It was contended that similarly situated taxpayers were treated more favourably and that the impugned actions violated the petitioner’s right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondent contended that the assessment and collection of tax were carried out in accordance with the Inland Revenue Act and within the statutory discretion vested in the Commissioner-General. It was argued that alleged errors in tax assessment are matters for appeal under the tax statutes and do not give rise to fundamental rights violations.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that Article 12(1) does not constitutionalise every alleged illegality or error committed by administrative authorities. In the sphere of taxation, Parliament has provided detailed statutory procedures, including rights of appeal, to challenge assessments and administrative decisions.

The Court held that mere illegality, mistake, or perceived unfairness in tax administration does not, by itself, amount to a violation of Article 12(1). To attract constitutional liability, the petitioner must establish arbitrariness, mala fides, or discriminatory treatment of a constitutional character.

The Court emphasised judicial restraint in fiscal matters and held that Article 126 cannot be used to bypass statutory appeal mechanisms provided by tax legislation.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner had failed to establish a violation of Article 12(1) and that the matters complained of were not amenable to fundamental rights review under Article 126.
principles_established: Article 12(1) does not convert every administrative error into a constitutional violation.
Tax assessments and fiscal administration are primarily governed by statutory procedures and appeal mechanisms.
Judicial restraint is required in matters of taxation and revenue collection.
Arbitrariness or discrimination of a constitutional nature must be clearly established to invoke Article 126.
Fundamental rights jurisdiction cannot be used to bypass statutory remedies.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Samarasinghe v. The Bank of Ceylon Ltd. [1978–79–80] 1 Sri L.R.
Janatha Finance and Investments Ltd. v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
source: C. W. Mackie & Co. Ltd. v. Hugh Molagoda, Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue [1986] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Siriwardena and Others v. Brigadier J. Rodrigo and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Every person held in custody shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the petitioners by military personnel under emergency regulations, without lawful authority and without production before a Magistrate, amounted to arbitrary executive action violating Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that they were arrested and detained by Army personnel acting under the command of the respondents. They contended that the arrests were effected without lawful authority, without informing them of the reasons for arrest, and that they were detained for prolonged periods without being produced before a Magistrate. It was further alleged that the involvement of the military in civilian arrests was arbitrary and unconstitutional.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the arrests and detentions were carried out under emergency regulations in force at the relevant time and were necessary in the interests of national security and public order. They argued that the actions taken were lawful and within the scope of powers conferred on the armed forces.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that even during periods of emergency, executive action is subject to constitutional limits. The involvement of military personnel in the arrest and detention of civilians must strictly comply with the law and with constitutional safeguards relating to personal liberty.

The Court held that emergency powers cannot be exercised arbitrarily and that failure to inform arrested persons of the reasons for arrest and failure to produce them before a Magistrate violate Articles 13(1) and 13(2). Such arbitrary deprivation of liberty also offends the guarantee of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).

The Court emphasised that military officers exercising coercive powers over civilians are performing executive action and are fully accountable under Article 126.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution had been violated. The Court granted relief to the petitioners and awarded compensation. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Emergency powers do not place executive action beyond constitutional scrutiny.
Military involvement in civilian arrests must strictly comply with constitutional safeguards.
Arbitrary arrest and detention violate Articles 13(1) and 13(2).
Arbitrary deprivation of liberty also violates the guarantee of equality under Article 12(1).
Members of the armed forces exercising coercive powers are accountable under Article 126.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Abeywickrema v. Pathirana and Others [1986] 1 Sri L.R.
Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Siriwardena and Others v. Brigadier J. Rodrigo and Others [1986] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Roberts and Another v. Ratnayake and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law and shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the arrest and detention of the petitioners by police officers, without lawful basis and without compliance with statutory safeguards, amounted to arbitrary executive action violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners alleged that they were arrested and detained by the respondents without being informed of the reasons for arrest and without lawful justification. They contended that the police action was arbitrary, unreasonable, and discriminatory, thereby violating their fundamental rights to equality before the law and personal liberty.
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the arrests were carried out in the course of a lawful police investigation and within the powers conferred by law. They argued that the actions taken were necessary for maintaining public order and did not amount to arbitrariness or constitutional infringement.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reiterated that police powers of arrest constitute executive action subject to constitutional scrutiny under Article 126. Equality before the law requires that such powers be exercised strictly in accordance with law and on reasonable grounds.

The Court held that an arrest effected without lawful basis or without informing the arrested person of the reasons for arrest is inherently arbitrary. Such arbitrariness violates Article 13(1) and also offends the guarantee of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).

On the evidence before it, the Court found that the respondents failed to establish that the arrests were justified by law or necessity, and that the petitioners’ detention was unconstitutional.
outcome: The Supreme Court held that the petitioners’ fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution had been violated. The Court granted relief and awarded compensation to the petitioners. No order was made as to costs.
principles_established: Police powers of arrest constitute executive action reviewable under Article 126.
Arbitrary or unlawful arrest violates Article 13(1).
Arbitrary exercise of police power also violates Article 12(1).
Failure to inform an arrested person of the reasons for arrest renders the arrest unconstitutional.
Equality before the law requires strict compliance with legal safeguards in the exercise of coercive State power.
precedents_cited: Velmurugu v. Attorney-General and Another [1981] 1 Sri L.R.
Kularatne v. Chandrananda de Silva and Another [1985] 2 Sri L.R.
Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
source: Roberts and Another v. Ratnayake and Others [1986] 2 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka

case_title: Laxamana and Others v. G. P. S. Weerassoriya, General Manager of Railways and Others

clauses.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.
Provides jurisdiction and procedure for the Supreme Court to hear applications relating to the infringement of fundamental rights by executive or administrative action.

legal_issue: Whether the administrative actions taken by the General Manager of Railways and other respondents in relation to the petitioners’ employment were arbitrary, unreasonable, or discriminatory, thereby violating the petitioners’ right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
petitioner_claim: The petitioners, who were employees of the Railway Department, alleged that the respondents exercised administrative and managerial powers in an arbitrary and unfair manner affecting their service conditions. They contended that they were treated unequally when compared with similarly situated employees and that such treatment violated Article 12(1).
respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the actions complained of were taken within the scope of lawful administrative discretion vested in the Railway Department. They argued that service-related decisions are managerial in nature and that the petitioners had failed to establish arbitrariness or discrimination of a constitutional character.
interpretation_summary:
The Court reaffirmed that administrative decisions affecting public servants are subject to constitutional scrutiny under Article 126 where arbitrariness or unequal treatment is alleged. While recognising that public authorities enjoy a degree of discretion in managing service matters, the Court emphasised that such discretion must be exercised fairly, reasonably, and on relevant considerations.

The Court held that equality before the law requires consistency and objectivity in administrative decision-making, particularly where similarly situated employees are concerned. However, the Court also stressed that not every service grievance amounts to a fundamental rights violation.

On the facts, the Court found that the petitioners had failed to establish that the respondents’ actions were arbitrary or discriminatory in the constitutional sense.
outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that no violation of Article 12(1) of the Constitution had been established and that the matters complained of did not warrant interference under Article 126.
principles_established: Administrative discretion in public service matters must be exercised fairly and reasonably.
Article 12(1) protects against arbitrary or unequal treatment in public employment.
Not every service-related grievance constitutes a fundamental rights violation.
Judicial review under Article 126 is limited to clear cases of arbitrariness or discrimination.
Consistency and objectivity are essential components of equality before the law in administrative action.
precedents_cited: Visuvalingam and Others v. Liyanage and Others [1983] 2 Sri L.R.
Edirisuriya v. Navaratnam and Others [1985] 1 Sri L.R.
C. W. Mackie & Co. Ltd. v. Hugh Molagoda, Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue [1986] 1 Sri L.R.
source: Laxamana and Others v. G. P. S. Weerassoriya, General Manager of Railways and Others [1987] 1 Sri L.R., Supreme Court of Sri Lanka
